note: Both make a sleep that is not sleep the state of yoga: Pattiragiriyar asks when he will sleep without sleeping (தூங்காமல் தூங்கி) and gain bliss; Tirumular says those who slept saw Siva's world, yoga and enjoyment within themselves (தூங்கிக் கண்டார்). 3 names the same state சிவயோக நித்திரை.

The Kural asks why one who knows what hurts his own life (தன்னுயிர்க்கு) does hurtful things to other lives (மன்னுயிர்க்கு); Pattiragiriyar uses the same two words and asks when he will stop killing and eating மன்னுயிர் and think of them தன்னுயிர்போல். The Kural's rule of compassion becomes a condition of finishing tapas.

Tirumular's first mark of one who stands in yama is கொல்லான், he does not kill, before truth, restraint and freedom from drink and lust; Pattiragiriyar makes not killing and eating lives the condition of completing tapas. In both the yogic path begins in the ethics of harm.

Sivavakkiyar lists brick, black stone, the red jati lingam, copper and brass as the things people say Siva dwells in, and asks whether the dance in the hall can be found there; Pattiragiriyar asks when chiselled stone, shaped red paste and tamarind-scoured copper will become the Real. The materials of the image are the same and the answer in both is never.

The Kural's tortoise draws in its five in one birth and is protected for seven; Pattiragiriyar's tortoise draws in its five on seeing a man come (ஆள்கண்டு), and he asks when he will do likewise and subside as a mute. Pattiragiriyar adds the approaching danger and takes the withdrawal into silence rather than into future births.

Tirumular says the five draw in like a tortoise's limbs when the silent letter meets the spoken, and the result is beyond names; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will draw in like the tortoise and take the shape of a mute (ஊமை உரு). Both carry the Kural's image past restraint into silence.

Pattiragiriyar asks to search out and see the Father's dwelling-place (அத்தன் இருப்பிடம்) and then go through the world as a corpse; Tirumular says he is not in the mansion, hall, temple or holy garb but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing. 2614 gives the answer 22 goes looking for, and both put it inside rather than in any building or dress.

In both Death is the one who puts a person into the womb: Tirumular's harsh Kalan sets the base in the womb-pit (கருக்குழி) and they fall in again; Pattiragiriyar's Yama takes him by the hand and makes him an embryo (கருப்படுத்தி). Pattiragiriyar adds the rival act, the Lord shaping him (உருப்படுத்தி), before that happens.

Tirumular: before Death comes in force, which does not ask who you are, do good tapas; Pattiragiriyar: before Yama takes his hand and sends him to a womb, consent to be ruled. Both make the time before Death's arrival the only time there is, and both ask for an act of the will now.

Both make death a lamp put out: Tirumular's flame is taken while the bowl remains and the fools cry over the bowl; Pattiragiriyar's lit lamp goes out and darkness closes in at once, and he asks to learn the way he died and came back. Tirumular's lamp ends in the mourners' ignorance, Pattiragiriyar's in a question about return.

The Kural says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking after it; Pattiragiriyar asks to know the way (வகை) by which he died and came back alive, as darkness follows a lamp going out. Both treat death and the next birth as one continuous passage, and Pattiragiriyar wants the passage itself understood.

Arunagiri is caught in the sorrowful household like a fish in a net (சமுசார வலை மீன்); Pattiragiriyar's mind whirls like a fish in a creel (தூரியினில் மீன்). The trapped fish is the self in the world in both, and in both the way out is the feet, the guru's in Pattiragiriyar and Murugan's in Arunagiri.

Tirumular: those who wear the holy ash without letting it fade will find deeds gone, the Siva state come and the holy feet reached; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will shine wearing the white ash so as to gain the release not had in eight hundred yugas. Both give the ash itself a place on the way to release.
audit_text_issue: 1666 has 'பூசுng', a typing corruption of பூசும்.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks those born and dead in every birth what this ash is that they smear on, and says clarity comes only if they cut off impurity and desire along with the water; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will shine wearing the white ash so as to gain the release missed in eight hundred yugas. The conflict holds if 28 credits the ash with the release; if the ash is only the Saiva's mark worn on the way, as 29's சிவவேடம் suggests, Sivavakkiyar's question still stands but is not denied.

Tirumular's chapter on false guise (அவவேடம்) says fools who put on guises to frighten people into feeding them will not see Siva's feet however they dance and weep; Pattiragiriyar uses the chapter's word, அவவேடம், for the guise he wants to stop wandering in. Both treat the garb worn for a living as the opposite of the Saiva's dress.

Tirumular says the pure Saivas are those who go beyond garb (வேடம் கடந்து) and reach Siva without show; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will excel wearing Siva's garb (சிவவேடம் பூண்டு). The conflict holds if சிவவேடம் is the outward Saiva emblems, which 1438 sets aside; if it means taking on Siva's own form within, the two say the same thing in different words.

Both name Siva by the poison drunk so that others could have nectar: Tirumular's exalted one who drank the poison so the great might drink nectar, Pattiragiriyar's Siva who drank poison for the gods and dances in the hall. Tirumular makes him the giver of knowledge by the path of tapas; Pattiragiriyar asks only to serve his servants.

Tirumular tells the story straight: Brahma and Vishnu sought foot and crown and did not see his form, and Brahma lied. Pattiragiriyar keeps Vishnu's boar digging the earth and not seeing (மால்காணா), sets the light on the hill, and asks when he will be the one to tell of it. Both make the gods' failure the measure of the light.

Tirumular says Vedanta is where craving ends, and those who have truly heard it have let craving go; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will leave behind all of Vedanta and the Veda (வேதாந்தவேதம் எல்லாம் விட்டொழிந்தே) and stay alone in absorption. The conflict holds if 33 discards Vedanta as a teaching; if it means leaving the texts once their hearing has done its work, the two agree, and 229's 'hearing that leaves craving' is exactly what 33 leaves.

Sivavakkiyar calls those who say 'far, far' lazy and those who run through town, country and forest searching mutes, since the Supreme is spread everywhere; Pattiragiriyar asks not to spend his days seeking some other place (மற்றிடம்) but to seek the place already reached (உற்றிடம்) and sleep there. Both put the search close rather than far, and Pattiragiriyar adds that the finding is a sleep.

Sivavakkiyar's frauds, who pose as eaters of kaya-kalpa, smoke ganja at set hours and eat opium and roam the land like dogs; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will stop drinking ganja, opium and toddy and drink the five-fold nectar instead. The same three drugs are the yogi's false intoxication in both, and Pattiragiriyar sets the true drink against them.

Sivavakkiyar's oxen in ochre and matted hair leave their wives to drift, roam every land and beg for crumbs at every house; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will stop fretting from place to place after whoever will give food for the belly. Both see the renouncer's begging round as a wandering for the stomach, not for the Lord.

Tirumular's Lord set the body with nine gates as sluices (மடைவைத்த ஒன்பது வாய்தல்) and the fire in the lotus of the head, and the poet joins hands with him for it; Pattiragiriyar's nine-threaded house (நவசூத்திர வீடு) is the thing he must stop calling 'I' in order to know Siva's thread. The nine-fold body is the maker's work in one and the ego's error in the other.

The Naladiyar's body is a pot seeping filth from nine openings, which the fool addresses in the words of love poetry; Pattiragiriyar's is a worm-nest from which excrement and urine flow and spread. The Naladiyar uses the image against desire for another's body, Pattiragiriyar against attachment to his own, and sets the feet against it.

Tirumular's Lord makes the elements dance like the deed that makes a false puppet dance (பொய்க்கரி யாட்டும் வினை), and that is grace; Pattiragiriyar's body is a puppet (பொம்மை) taken up as the exact match of the two karmas, to be thrown down before praise. The puppet moved by deed is a figure of grace in Tirumular and of bondage in Pattiragiriyar.

Sivavakkiyar tells his mind that the body is a spring of filth that rots if the salt is removed (உப்பை நீக்கில்), and asks how it can desire it; Pattiragiriyar's body is a salted pot (உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம்) that will break and take a womb again. Both make salt what keeps the body, and both set Siva's feet or rule against it.

Arunagiri's great maya is to take as 'I' a leather bag (தோற்பை) of the five elements oozing the mire of desire; Pattiragiriyar's body is a leather bag of rice (சோற்றுத் துருத்தி) carried about till he withers. Both make the body a skin bag with its contents named, and both ask to be rid of it at the Lord's feet.

Tirumular: when the breath rises the dark-smeared temple of the body becomes a gem lamp (மணிவிளக்கு); Pattiragiriyar asks to stand joined in the lamp of the sounding bell (ஓசைமணித் தீபம்), free of desire's net. The lamp lit inside the body is the goal in both; Pattiragiriyar adds sound to Tirumular's light.

Sivavakkiyar: you recite the four Vedas and do not know the foot of knowledge, like ghee hidden in milk; Pattiragiriyar asks to see the great secret the four Vedas called out for and did not see. Both leave the Vedas short of the thing itself, and neither says the Vedas are false, only that they stand outside it calling.

The first stanza of the work asks to burn off (சுட்டறுத்து) the five senses in which the ego hides and to sleep without sleeping; the last of this run asks to burn off (சுட்டறுத்து) all the instruments and faculties and sleep in absorption (நிட்டையிலே தூங்குவது). The same verb and the same sleep frame the seventy-five stanzas, with the senses widened to the whole set of tattvas.

Tirumular: eyes on the nose, breath held within, for those who can sleep (தூங்க வல்லார்க்கு) in absorption seeking the end of sorrow, the body is without fear; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will sleep in absorption (நிட்டையிலே தூங்குவது) with the instruments burned away. Both use the word for sleep for the yogic state, and Tirumular gives the posture and breath that Pattiragiriyar leaves out.

Sivavakkiyar's lotus leaf stands joined with the water and yet is without water, as the Supreme stands in the world and apart from it; Pattiragiriyar's lotus leaf spreads on the water without attachment, as his mind should stand far from kin. The same leaf is the Lord's way of being in the world for Sivavakkiyar and the devotee's for Pattiragiriyar.

The Naladiyar says the scheming of women whose minds are with another man is plainly known and fools still do not grasp it; Pattiragiriyar takes a woman whose mind is elsewhere even in her husband's pleasure as the model for keeping the Lord's feet in his thought. The straying wife is the ethical poem's warning and the Siddhar's figure for devotion; the moral domain and the devotional one use her oppositely.

Tirumular says that even one who makes his bones firewood and fries his flesh cannot reach the gem unless he melts with love (அன்போடு உருகி) and softens within; Pattiragiriyar asks when his body, love and bones will melt (ஆகம் உருக அன்பு உருக என்பு உருக) and the experience of enjoyment join him. Both set melting against burning as the way to the Lord, and Pattiragiriyar's bones melt where Tirumular's are burned to no purpose.

Tirumular: for all who see the holy dance, tears of grace drip, the heart melts and the nectar of bliss wells up in the light within; Pattiragiriyar asks for body, love and bone to melt and the experience of enjoyment to come, with tears like pearls in 61 and the honey of Siva-bliss in 66. The sequence melting, tears, nectar is the same in both.

The Naladiyar's body is a bubble in pelting rain, forming and bursting again and again, and those who see it so resolve to end their wandering; Pattiragiriyar's life is a bubble on water (நீரில் குமிழி) to be left so that the flood of grace may rise. The bubble leads to a resolve in the Naladiyar and to a request for grace in Pattiragiriyar.

Sivavakkiyar mocks those who beat the drum through the town that the body is as unstable as a bubble on water (நீரினில் குமிழி ஒத்த நிலையிலாத காயம்), promise jnana-siddhi and seize others' goods; Pattiragiriyar says the same words of his own life (நிலையற்ற வாழ்வை) and asks to leave it. Sivavakkiyar does not deny the bubble; he denies the preachers, and Pattiragiriyar's saying it to himself is what the preachers do not do.

Tirumular's Shakti moves in the square, rests in the hexagon (அறுகோணம்) and moves in the circle, and Sadasiva is her form; Pattiragiriyar's Mahesvara lives in the hexagon of air and his Sadasiva in the circular path (72). The same shapes house the gods in both, with the square, hexagon and circle in the same order; which centre each shape marks is not fixed in either.

Tirumular lists Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Mahesvara and the five-faced one above them, with bindu, nada and Shakti, and makes Sadasiva common to all; Pattiragiriyar's 68 to 72 climb the same five gods in the same order, each in a shape in the body, ending at Sadasiva in the circle. Tirumular gives the order as cosmology, Pattiragiriyar as a ladder of centres to be seen within.

Tirumular: taking up ida and pingala and twisting at the root in the triangle (முக்கோணிலும்), one may see the feet of the Lord who holds time; Pattiragiriyar asks to worship Rudra who appears in the triangle with its three rings. The triangle is a centre in the body in both, at the root in Tirumular and, by the order of the gods, higher in Pattiragiriyar.

The Kural says the field of the five senses must be crushed and all that was wanted let go at once; Pattirakiriyar watches the mind that roams by the five senses' paths fall burnt. Both make the senses' mind the thing to be killed, not trained.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods; here the 'I' (நான்) dies in the chain that ends in the state of release. Both place the death of the self before the gain.

Kudhambai asks what use hand-cymbals are to the true knower who wanders like the dead; Pattirakiriyar asks when he will have died before the soul leaves the cage. The same figure of the living dead, as a question in one and a state in the other.
audit_text_issue: 1598 is unmarked in the corpus.

note: Tirumular's inner fire, for those who reach the young crescent, becomes a thread-ladder (நூலேணி) for the ready mind; Pattirakiriyar wants to climb the நூல் ஏணி instead of the ladder of skin. If நூல் is thread in both, the image is the same inner ascent; if the pulambal means books, it is a different ladder.

Tirumular says riding the horse swifter than a bird gives joy without toddy and drives off sloth; Pattirakiriyar wants to ride the vaasi instead of wearing out his feet on the earth. Both make the breath a mount, and both set it against a slower bodily motion.

Tirumular has the kalas run through ida, pingala and the unnamed middle channel, and the good rouse the base and join it to the head; Pattirakiriyar rouses the kundalini by awareness and opens the sushumna's latch. The same operation, with the pulambal adding that the opening is a shut door.

Tirumular says moon and sun rise and fall through ida and pingala and life wells up in the middle between them; Pattirakiriyar asks to stand unobstructed in the sushumna that moves between the two. Both locate the gain in the middle, not in either side channel.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 96 சலித்தருப்பது is corrupt or unusual; Tm 793 உயிருக்கு இரந்து is unclear. The channel names are clear in both.

note: Tirumular says that when the fire at the root of the central channel drives the sun and lets the moon drink, the higher siddhis come; Pattirakiriyar leaves the root fire, kindles it in the moon-hall and drinks the milk. The same cipher of fire, moon and drink, with the pulambal's gain being the end of hunger rather than powers.

Tirumular says that for those who set Nandi in love by knowledge there is no impurity, no stain, no pride, no clan, no qualities and no good to seek; Pattirakiriyar asks when he will be without impurity, maya, honour, good and clan. Nearly the same list, as a description in one and a longing in the other.

Sivavakkiyar's crores ran and ran, sought and sought the light mingled within, withered and died; Pattirakiriyar asks to run without running and see without seeking, in himself. The same diagnosis, the light was inside, as a count of the dead in one and a request in the other.

Pattirakiriyar asks to seek and gain the fourth state; Tirumular says one who sees himself sees turiya, but if the turiya he contemplates is not made one with the Lord he is born again. If நாலாம் பதம் is turiya, the Tirumanthiram adds the condition the pulambal does not state.

Tirumular's unripe ones have a magic mirror risen in the mind yet never look at its reflection and go off desiring what is outside; Pattirakiriyar asks to see as light in a mirror instead of surveying the uncounted distances. Both set the mirror within against the search outside.

Tirumular praises the splendour that rises above the six-and-six supports; Pattirakiriyar asks to see the great light of bliss beyond the six adharas as his own gain. Both put the light above the centres rather than in the highest of them.

Tirumular says that for the knower the body itself becomes Siva and for the silent sage it is release; Pattirakiriyar asks to see the body grown from the three malas as stainless. The same body is re-seen, not replaced, in both.

82 asks the Tirodhayi, the concealing power, to show the way to grace; 112 describes the concealing in act, the Lord showing as in a dream and hiding again, and answers it not with a plea but with the resolve to hold the mind in the supreme space.

Tirumular names the three voids, of maya, of space and of the soul pervaded in Siva-Shakti, and ends speech in the pure form beyond them; Pattirakiriyar takes the three voids as given, voids them, voids the first into emptiness and voids that too, and ends in love. The pulambal pushes the Tirumanthiram's series one step further and names a different end.

Tirumular says the great saying 'you are that' ripens into 'I have become that' by Nandi's grace; Pattirakiriyar asks to see the clear sky-reality as 'you' and gain a standing. The pulambal stops at the first stage, seeing as 'you', which 120 then turns toward 'self'.
audit_text_issue: 116 சீ யென்று எழுந்து is uncertain.

note: At 84 the five letters together are the sword that cuts the forest of the mind; at 117 two of the letters, va and ma, are the sword and the rest are contained in the letter a. The weapon is the same, and the second verse takes it apart letter by letter.
audit_text_issue: 117 is flagged uncertain; the sword line is clear.

note: Tirumular says that when the two deeds balance, the sweet grace-power comes as the guru and removes qualities until one becomes Siva; Pattirakiriyar asks the Lord who is beginning and end to take form as grace, come as the guru and take him over. Both make the guru grace itself arriving in a form.

Tirumular says that once the flower called 'self' is laid at His feet, saying 'I' and 'He' is no longer right; Pattirakiriyar asks to know that the one he never knew as 'I' was all along 'you' standing as 'self'. Both dissolve the first person into the Lord, by offering in one and by recognition in the other.
audit_text_issue: tirumanthiram:1607 last line admits two readings, as the marker notes.

note: The Kural cuts off the pride that says 'I' and 'mine'; Pattirakiriyar, after thinking over everything he saw as his own, rests in what he takes as His. The Kural removes the claim, the pulambal transfers it.

Pambatti tells the snake to join the mind to the visible Real as a magnet draws iron, and stay unshaken like a bucket and its rope; Pattirakiriyar asks the Lord to draw him to his feet as a magnet draws iron into its hand. The same pull, with the mind doing the joining in one and the Lord doing it in the other.

Arunagirinathar was drawn to women's breasts as a needle to a magnet and asks for the day grace fills him; Pattirakiriyar asks to be drawn like iron to a magnet to the Lord's feet. One magnet pulls down, the other up, and both poets ask for the same release from the pull.

The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes only from the work they do; Pattirakiriyar asks to go about with no division of caste, as Kapila's agama says. Both deny caste by birth; the Kural keeps a distinction by deeds that the pulambal does not mention.

Sivavakkiyar asks the Siddhars what mind, soul, Shakti, Siva, caste-difference, release and root mantras are, in the seedless seed; Pattirakiriyar wants to live without caste-division on a text's authority. Both refuse caste, Sivavakkiyar by dissolving it with everything else and Pattirakiriyar by citing Kapila.

Earlier in the work the body is a rice-bellows carried about until one withers, to be thrown off to reach the Lord; here it is the bellows the wind blows, thrown off with gambling, theft and karma. The same bellows, filled with food in one and with breath in the other.

Pambatti's body is a torn bellows with nine gates into which the great wind entered, which is how speech arose, food for the burning ground for those who do not know the Lord; Pattirakiriyar's is the bellows the wind blows, to be cast off. Both make the breath in the body a wind in a leather bag.

Tirumular hears the ringing bell as the lamp of the inner breath, the body dazes, and he sees the hall; Pattirakiriyar asks to stand united in the lamp of the sounding bell. Both fuse the heard bell and the seen lamp into one inner object.
audit_text_issue: tirumanthiram:2521 அற்றலும் is obscure; the bell-lamp line is clear.

note: The Arutpulambal asks the Lord of Kannivanam whether the days spent as grass and shrub, as stone and tree, are not enough; Pattirakiriyar asks when he will say 'enough' to births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass. The same list and the same word, போதும், as a reproach to the Lord in one and a hope for oneself in the other.

Arunagirinathar asks not to wander born as sparrow, kite, jackal, beast, worm, fish, elephant and tree; Pattirakiriyar wants to be done with births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass. Both run through the kinds of life as a weariness, and the pulambal adds the inert stone.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging, in order to let clinging go; Pattirakiriyar rests on no object and keeps only the watch for grace. Both leave a single hold when every other is dropped.

99 asks to live in the reality the chattering arts cannot reach; 136 adds the step of examining all the arts to the end first, and names what is seen after them, the truth with no 'you' in it. The arts are not skipped but exhausted.

The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births and the rest cannot; Pattirakiriyar asks to join the Lord without parting and so cut off birth. Both make attachment to the Lord the one means of ending rebirth.

Tirumular's Siva-gnanis wander as the dead while senses and body remain intact, unlike the purifiers and the monkey-glad knowers; Pattirakiriyar asks to be dead without dying under the true guru's feet. The same living death, as a class description in one and a petition in the other.

Kudhambai asks what the darkness of desire is to those who have been cooked without being cooked and seen the open space; Pattirakiriyar asks to be cooked without being cooked beneath the guru's feet. The formula வேகாமல் வெந்து is shared, a finished state in one and a hope in the other.

Tirumular says the Lord makes the elements dance as a deed makes a false puppet dance, and so brings the soul to awareness; Pattirakiriyar calls the Lord the string that makes him dance while he does not know himself. Both put the Lord behind the puppet, and both make knowing the hand the way out.
audit_text_issue: 2344 பொய்க்கரி and பூவியல் கூட்டம் are uncertain

note: Sivavakkiyar asks the sastra-reciter whether the Veda will help when the death-sweat comes, and sets a moment's inner knowing against the whole bag of scripture; Pattirakiriyar names the reality that reading, speaking and worship do not show. Both deny that recitation reaches it.

Arunagirinathar's reality cannot be spoken by debaters, reached by the path of books or by imagined meditation; Pattirakiriyar's is not seen by reading, spoken by the mouth or shown by worship. The same three denials, with worship added by the pulambal.

Tirumular says that if you can tie the horse that rose with twelve legs so that it does not escape, and drink deeply, the body will not leave for thousands of years; Pattirakiriyar asks to bind the leaping twelve-legged horse in the two chains. The same ciphered horse; the Tirumanthiram names the gain (the body kept) that the pulambal leaves unsaid.

Sivavakkiyar says that if one stands the twelve legs still and reaches the five colours, the soul stays within the space and works in the head, and the inquirer becomes Brahman; Pattirakiriyar asks to bind the twelve-legged horse. Two Siddhars with the same count of legs for the breath, and the same stilling.

96 names the three channels plainly, the sushumna moving between ida and pingala, and asks to stand there unobstructed; 144 says the same thing in cipher, leaving the two outer legs and going by the middle one. Set side by side, the plain verse is the key to the coded one.
audit_text_issue: 96 சலித்தருப்பது is corrupt or unusual, as the marker says

note: The Kural's woman says the sea of love certainly exists and the raft to cross it certainly does not; Pattirakiriyar means to cross the sea of desire and climb the shore by kindling the inner homa fire. The same காமக் கடல், the lover's with no way across, the ascetic's crossed by fire.

Tirumular says that when bindu and nada join and meet the moon, nectar wells up and the mantra rising there becomes the oblation; Pattirakiriyar kindles the homa fire within. Both move the sacrifice inside the body, the pulambal keeping the fire and the Tirumanthiram keeping the offering.

Tirumular's dancer has space for his body, the eight directions for hands and the three lights for his three eyes, and dances in the hall of the great body; Pattirakiriyar lights the three lights in the inner house and sees the dance in the heart. Both relocate the dance of the hall into a body lit by sun, moon and fire.

Nondi Siddhar beholds the master's holy dance in the light-space between the eyes, in the middle of the nose-tip, and gains the state of silence; Pattirakiriyar asks to see the holy dance in the heart with the three lights lit within. The dance is inward in both, placed at the brow by one and in the heart by the other.

Tirumular puts the good lady, good yoga, the aim and the Lord himself at the end of nada; Pattirakiriyar asks to be at the central root of nada's end, past all Vedanta and Veda. Both make the end of sound the yogi's station, and the pulambal adds that the texts are what is passed to reach it.

Kanjamalai Siddhar tells the mind that runs about to be caught and corrected and set within the open space of nada's end; Pattirakiriyar asks to stand at the root-centre of nada's end. The same place named in the same term, with the mind's capture as the means in one and the passing of scripture in the other.

At 140 the சூத்திரம் is the string by which the Lord makes the unknowing poet dance; at 150 it is the kite-string that flies and dances on its own once the kite and its loop are gone. The same word for the thread, bound to a hand in one and loose in the open sky in the other.
audit_text_issue: 150 line 1 (பட்டம் அற்றுக் காதற்றில் பறந்தாடும் சூத்திரம்) is obscure; the string-flies-alone reading is doubtful.

note: Both place the goal past eightfold yoga: Tirumular says understanding of every kind lies beyond the eight siddhis that the yoga gives, and Pattiragiriyar asks for the thing beyond what is beyond the yoga. Neither rejects the practice; both refuse to stop at it.

A ladder to release in both: Tirumular's rungs are the thirty-six tattvas climbed upward; Pattiragiriyar's ladder is to be set here, once body and life have parted, to the ancient city that cannot be reached. The image is shared, the rungs are named only in Tirumular.

The first letter as the First Being: the Kural has the world begin from the Primal Lord as letters begin from அ; Pattiragiriyar wants to know within himself the letter that stood as the first beginning. The link holds on the reading of அரி as that primal letter, which is one of two.

Both end the library: Sivavakkiyar says the images, sastras, homa pit, four Vedas and bundled books all came to nothing once he knew the Lord; Pattiragiriyar asks when he will burn the sastras, make the Vedas false and see the one formula that cuts off sorrow.

163 makes the poet the archer, mind as bow and awareness as arrow; 164 turns the figure round, so that it is the Lord who shot the poet dead and wiped out his disgrace. The shooting the poet asked to do is done to him.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 164 is compressed; the line division of வெளியில் வைத்தே ஒளித்து is unsure.

note: The body moved from outside, twice: a ferry driven by poles and a puppet turned by the wind. In 165 the poet wants to know the mover; in 213 he wants to see the body itself as the puppet it is.

The wasp's nest in both: Sivavakkiyar's worm in the fresh-clay cell becomes what it thinks of daily and flies; Pattiragiriyar asks to be shut in the same way and to beg for grace. Sivavakkiyar makes it a lesson in thinking, Pattiragiriyar a figure for confinement and asking.

Fire from bamboo: in Tirumular it is Nandi hidden in the body-temple who rises and removes the malas; in Pattiragiriyar it is the poet himself who hopes to shine out of a birth lower than a dog's. The latent fire is the Lord in one and the soul in the other.

The same image with the same point: the sunstone burns the cotton round it only in the sun's presence. Tirumular says the malas end when the sun appears; Pattiragiriyar asks for grace at the appearing (தோற்றம்) of the noble one. In both the burning waits on the presence, not on the stone.

The sea turtle whose eggs on shore take form while it roams the sea, in both. Sivavakkiyar draws the lesson that thinking of the light within the body is the truth; Pattiragiriyar asks to be reached, or formed, in the same way.

Both use விழுங்கி, swallowing, for what the impurity does to the divine: the darkness swallows grace in 179, the three malas swallow Siva in 183. Together they give the lament's picture of the mala as an eater that must be cut away.

Pattiragiriyar's couplet is Sivavakkiyar's lightning verse in brief: lightning rises and subsides in the sky, and the Lord within subsides within. The source notes the parallel. Sivavakkiyar adds the eye that cannot see itself, which Pattiragiriyar omits.

Verdigris in both: Tirumular's Nandi cuts it away and opens the eye of grace; Pattiragiriyar names it as the three malas that have swallowed Siva and asks when he will separate them. In Tirumular the cutting is done by the guru, in Pattiragiriyar it is still asked for.

151 asks for what lies beyond eightfold yoga; 187 names the step, leaving fixed meditation (நிட்டை) and letting thought and knowing slip, to stand in the open space. The practice is left from inside it.

190 wants the pleasure found with women seen as the Lord; 211 wants the dream of desire for women removed. The conflict holds if 190 is read as a licence for present pleasure; if its past tenses mean pleasures already had and now to be understood, the two agree.

153 keeps the Siddhanta three apart, removing the bond and releasing the soul into the Lord; 194 resolves 'I', 'you' and the other into the one 'you'. They clash on the reading of 194 as an identity claim; if 194 only says the three are all his, 153's distinctions survive.

Both open with knowing awareness by awareness; 158 goes on to forgetting speech and sleeping, 195 to the condition that awareness not stand parted from awareness. The second states what the first's sleep contains.

Tirumular, having known himself, knew nothing else and was questioned through himself; Pattiragiriyar asks for awareness known by awareness with no parting within it. Both describe a knowing with no second thing in it.

Agasthiyar places the hum of Om at the centre of the brows and the fullness called Aum at the suzhumunai; Pattiragiriyar asks to know the hum he heard, what stood within and the Om he uttered as one. Both make the heard sound and the syllable the same thing in the body.

The swan that parts milk from water in both. In Tirumular the parter is the Lord or guru, who turns the soul's deeds into roasted seeds; in Pattiragiriyar it is the seeker, who must part himself from himself to see the Lord.
audit_text_issue: Tm 120 ஆமேவு is obscure; the swan simile itself is clear.

note: Both make being dead while alive the mark of the knower: Tirumular's Siva-gnanis go about dead with senses and body intact; Pattiragiriyar asks to be dead without birth, death, speech, breath, memory or forgetting. Pattiragiriyar adds the stopped breath, which makes his state yogic as well as moral.
166 asks that nothing attach in thought; 210 asks to raise one thought within, awareness itself, with the supreme space shut in the mind. The one thought is the exception to the emptiness of 166.
Two ways of saying that the self must not run on its own: 212 exchanges one's own life for the Lord's, 214 loses my will, the world's hold and self-command and rests on grace.

The puppet moved from outside in both: Tirumular's deed makes a false puppet dance as the Lord makes the elements dance; Pattiragiriyar's body is a puppet whirled by the wind. Tirumular names the mover (deed, then grace); Pattiragiriyar asks only to see the body as puppet.

Both shut a door and turn in: Tirumular locks the breath as with a bolt and turns the gaze back to rest within the eye; Pattiragiriyar bars the head-door and sleeps within thinking of the Lord. The link depends on reading தலைவாசல் as a door in the body, which is one of two readings.

The anril that never parts from its mate is the figure of fidelity in both: in the Naladiyar it is the courtesan's broken promise never to part; in Pattiragiriyar it is the soul that should cling to grace when its companion is parted. The bird is the same, the bond is a lover's in one and the Lord's in the other.
audit_text_issue: 218 line 1 இணை பிரிந்தபோதல் இன்பமுறும் is likely faulty (the anril should have joy only when not parted).

note: Both set bliss beside toddy: Tirumular contrasts the yogi's nectar of knowledge-bliss with the fool's liquor, Pattiragiriyar uses the drunkard's staggering as the picture of bliss itself. The image is shared, with opposite valuation of the drunk.

Both pass the thirty-six tattvas on the way to the goal: Tirumular's devotees go beyond the six sixes and shatter maya by grace; Pattiragiriyar leaves the five sixes and the six for the bare space where the dark mind dies. Each counts the tattvas with a multiplication, and in both the step beyond them is the last.

194 resolves 'I', 'you' and the other into the one 'you'; 229 asks the three as open questions, who am I, who are you, who is the Supreme, and makes their answer the end of tapas. The question and its answer stand in the same work.

Tirumular's Lord is perceived to the measure that one contemplates him; Pattiragiriyar's Lord stood for each in the very way each saw and thought of him. Both make the form of the Lord depend on the conceiver without making the Lord many.

Agasthiyar sets the hum of Om at the centre of the brows and tells the disciple to see the fullness there; Pattiragiriyar asks to see the light-giving bliss straight at the forehead and be fixed. The link holds on the coded reading of நெற்றிக்கு நேர் as the brow centre.
audit_text_issue: Both verses flagged uncertain by the marker.

note: Both begin from not knowing oneself: Tirumular did not know himself, the knower, until Nandi said 'you are the one who knows'; Pattiragiriyar, having asked for knowledge through the whole lament, confesses he does not know even himself and bows to those who went before. Tirumular's verse ends in the gift, Pattiragiriyar's in the asking.

Two poets' apologies to the learned: Sivavakkiyar opens by asking all who have learned to forgive the errors of one who recites like a madman; Pattiragiriyar closes by laying all he has said before the ancients and asking when they will accept it.

The elephant-faced god frames both works: Sivavakkiyar begins with worship of the black-faced wish-tree so that arts and knowledge rise in thought; Pattiragiriyar ends by praising the five-handed one's feet and setting them in his heart for firmness. In both the Siddhar's plainest devotion goes to Ganesha.

Both measure the kin's love by where they stop: Tirumular's wailing wives and children turn back at the edge of the town while others strip and burn him; Pattinathar's embracing wife and children wail but will not take one step past the edge of the cremation ground.
Sivavakkiyar asks whether children, wives and kin, all maya, can come along when Death calls; Pattinathar answers with the scene: they reach the cremation ground and go no further.

Both use the puppet made to dance: Tirumular says Hara's grace makes the spread elements dance like a false puppet and thereby settles the soul; Pattinathar says he is the string puppet and can do nothing if the cord that is the Lord fails. Tirumular describes the five acts, Pattinathar pleads not to be parted.

The Naladiyar says nothing goes with a person but their deeds, not even the body they adorned; Pattinathar says nothing was brought at birth and nothing is taken at death, and draws from it that the wealth held in between is Siva's and is to be given.

On the allegorical reading both share, mother as grace or Shakti and father as Siva, they part on the end: Tirumular says that once the conceit of 'my mother, my father' is gone, the Lord joined with her stands as the mother after, so the Mother remains; Pattinathar's nishtai goes with the mother to the father and then forgets the mother. The conflict depends on taking Pattinathar's தாயை மறந்து as a final state and not a stage.
audit_text_issue: 1129 line 3 is printed with a stray Latin Y (உரைசெய்Yயும்).

note: Both leave the cherished body to scavengers: Arunagirinathar tends a body that ghosts, vultures, jackals and crows will tear and drag; Pattinathar asks whether his is prey for the fox, the vulture and kite, the dog or the fire. In both the body was cherished through lust.
audit_text_issue: 1250 has gaps and corrupt syllables (சேறு஡று, 'வேய்த்த ....... ; ளையோனே')

note: Tirumular says kin is one and God is one, and there is no refuge outside one's own mind; Pattinathar denies permanence to town, kin, name, women, children, glory, wealth and everyone in the country and gives it to the Lord's feet alone. Both reduce the whole circle of belonging to one holding.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which part is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar says karma itself took the form of a woman, became the breasts and flesh men speak of, and threw him into the pit of filth and blood. Both dissolve the woman into her body; Pattinathar adds that he fell in.

The Kural says the greatness of those whose word is full is shown by their hidden words (மறைமொழி); Pattinathar says the graced may be known by their austerity, nature, grace and love and even by their obscure words (இருளுறு சொல்). Both make the dark saying a sign of the great rather than a defect.

Arunagirinathar's miser sends the poor ascetic who asks for food from the upper house to the lower and leaps at him like a dog; Pattinathar's householders stuff their own bellies with the six tastes and will not trouble to feed the renounced. Both are written from the side of the mendicant.

Both say water takes the nature of the ground it lies in; the Kural applies it to understanding, which takes the nature of one's company, and Pattinathar to the Lord or the soul, which stands in each soul according to its ripeness. The image is the same, the domain different.

The Kural says the wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a beautiful woman growing old alone; Pattinathar likens the ungiving man to a fruitless tree, a dried tank and a cow without milk and asks why he was created. Both judge a life by what it yields to others.
audit_text_issue: 257 line 2 கம்பன்னராய்க் obscure.

note: Tirumular says even those who have grasped the meaning and hold the flash of light are infatuated with women who bewilder, and a mind once bewildered cannot be changed; Pattinathar says the demon in woman's form bewildered him with her breasts and stole the substance of his understanding, so that he forgot the Lord.

Sivavakkiyar says people have lost themselves in the bewilderment cast by women with collyrium-dark eyes and can be saved only by a mind that has known truth; Pattinathar says the woman's eyes frightened and her breasts bewildered him and robbed him of awareness. Both name the eyes and the loss of knowing.

The same sequence in both: Arunagirinathar's courtesans melt a man while his wealth lasts and, when it ends, beat him and drive him out; Pattinathar's women swear they would die if parted and, when his hand runs dry, say 'go and come' and strike the back of his head.

Both heap names of containers on the body: Arunagirinathar's bag fed by the two deeds, pot where stench pools and hut the life moves out of; Pattinathar's shed, torn bellows, leather bag fed with rice and pot of wind. Both confess to having loved it; Arunagirinathar asks to give up the delusion that it will not perish.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 263 'பீற்றற் து ருத்தியை' has a stray space (பீற்றல் துருத்தியை).

note: The same closing line, எல்லாப் பிழையும் பொறுத்தருள்வாய்: 245 lists what the poet did not do (learn, melt, meditate, say the five letters, praise, worship), 264 what he did by speech, thought, deed, glance and hearing. Together they make a full confession of omission and commission.

Both watch women at their toilet, turmeric, dots, earrings and the rest, and name the finished beauty as what undoes men; Arunagirinathar asks for the feet to end his desire, Pattinathar asks that his liking (இட்டம்) for them be removed.

Tirumular says to set the five states in nada and the rest, put the corpse-like mala behind and seek the king beyond mind and speech; Pattinathar describes a vision of bliss without elements, senses, objects, qualities, time or the inner instruments. Both reach the end by subtraction of the tattvas.
audit_text_issue: 2575 பினமா மலம் for பிணமா; சத்தாதி சாந்தி uncertain.

note: The Naladiyar says the bellies of the senseless are burning grounds for the beasts and birds they eat; Pattinathar's flesh-eaters feed the inert pot of the body with killed lives and are themselves bitten by Death. Both make the eater's body a place of the dead.

note: Sivavakkiyar says that even if you kill one creature with another and make it your food, and lie and steal in the market, lovingly joining the Lord brings the gods within you that day; Pattinathar says those who kill and eat will have no answer when Death seizes them. The conflict holds on the plain reading of 1239, where joining the Lord overrides the deed; on its softer reading, that sinners are not shut out, Pattinathar's own 276 agrees with it.

note: 250 said the poet had been thrown into the pit from which filth and blood pour and could not see the bank to climb out; 270 names the same pit and asks the Lord for the climbing. The complaint becomes a petition.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Pattinathar calls his own body a pot of rice and curry and the woman's body a pit of filth and blood. Both strip the body to a vessel of waste; the Naladiyar aims it at the lover's eye, Pattinathar at both bodies at once.

The Kural says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods anxiously and then say they have no support; Pattinathar asks what being on earth is worth for those who will not feed the guests who come yet live in prosperity. Both treat hospitality as the test of a household.

257 asked why the Lord created men who give nothing, like fruitless trees and dry tanks; 275 asks why he made the harsh, the lustful and the cruel, who grow like tall palmyras without knowing the good. The same question widens from the ungiving to the wicked.
audit_text_issue: 257 line 2 கம்பன்னராய்க் obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: The same catalogue, town, kin, name, women, children, glory, wealth; 249 says none of it lasts and only the feet do, 277 asks what use any of it is even while it lasts. The second stanza drops the affirmation and keeps the question.

Tirumular says the kin who cling and follow are worse than one's deeds and that the road of rebirth can be closed by lighting awareness while in the body; Pattinathar counts the mothers, fathers, wives and children of uncounted births and asks how many more. Both treat kin as the recurring content of birth rather than its consolation.

The Naladiyar ends its funeral-drum stanza with சாவார் சாப்பிணம் சுமப்பார், the dying carry the dead; Pattinathar's mourners are சாம்பிணம், corpses that will die, rolling and crying round the corpse that has gone. Both make the funeral a procession of corpses; Pattinathar adds that the dead man at least left his desires.

Tirumular says the quality that comes to those who have seen the holy dance in the hall comes to those who hear of it too, and compares it to drink; Pattinathar says that whenever he sees the dance of the Lord of the little hall his eyes well and his heart and inner self melt. Both describe the dance as an intoxication of the seer.
audit_text_issue: Tm 2779 line 2 is obscure (உண்டார்க்கு உணவுண்டால்).

note: The Kural defines virtue as what proceeds without envy, craving, anger and harsh speech; Pattinathar's 'wealth' is a life without partiality, hot anger, slipping from good or daily seeking. Both define the good by what it abstains from, and both place anger in the heart (நெஞ்சில் / உள்ளத்து) rather than in act.

The Kural asks where the life of the one who conceals hides when the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal; Pattinathar asks for a wealth that never says 'there is nothing' to askers without even looking at them. Both treat refusal of the asker as a kind of killing.

The Kural says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh and that hell does not open its mouth for the eater; Pattinathar heads his conditions for wealth with not killing and not eating what was killed. Both put killing and eating together and before the other faults.

The Naladiyar says even kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left; Pattinathar says crowned kings and all the rest burn to a fistful of ash, and that even seeing it people cling to life. The Naladiyar's lesson is impermanence; Pattinathar's is that seeing it does not teach.

Sivavakkiyar says people have seen the body lying there and the life slipped out, and still do not take it in; Pattinathar says people have seen kings burnt to ash and still think only of this grasping life. Both separate seeing death (காண்) from realising it.

Both name the same three bodily needs, food, sleep and pleasure: Sivavakkiyar uses them to level caste (they are alike for you and me), Pattinathar names them as the day's three conditions (உபாதி) and asks the Lord to remove them. The same facts serve an argument about birth in one and about release in the other.
audit_text_issue: 287 சஞ்சிதமாம் sits oddly in the list; ஆலமுகந்தருள் is read as ஆலம் உகந்து.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks what the life of Namban is, dancing surrounded by dogs in the loveless forest where ghouls eat corpses; Pattinathar tells his mind that near the Lord the bull charges, the serpent bites and ghosts and bhutas follow, and that its only destination is where the dwellers of the corpse-forest go. Both approach the Lord through the cremation ground and its company.
audit_text_issue: 1461 is flagged uncertain; how its two halves join is unclear

note: In 240 the poet is a string puppet who cannot move if the cord that is the Lord fails; in 290 the Lord is named as the one who makes all beings eat, sleep, embrace and dance on the rope of the two deeds. The personal confession becomes a doctrine of a single mover working through karma.

The Kural says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like that crowd breaking up; Pattinathar asks where the kings' wealth and their hand-built theatre halls (நாடகசாலை) are once the Lord's mind turns. Both use the theatre for the vanishing of wealth; Pattinathar makes the Lord the one who empties it.

On the reading of 273 in which 'all is Siva's doing' is the poet's own conclusion, 294 states it outright: apart from the Maker's word there are no deeds, and grand talk, stilts and dancing achieve nothing. On the other reading of 273, where the line is the learned men's excuse, 294 supplies the doctrine they misuse.
audit_text_issue: 294 தம்முன் தம்பி அத்தாசை is obscure.

note: Arunagirinathar calls Thiruttani the physician of the disease of birth and asks to cut birth's root; Pattinathar says there is a medicine against dying for one already born, and that it is remembering the Lord's feet. Both borrow the Siddhars' medical language for devotion rather than for herbs or breath.

Tirumular says that when the inner maya and the three impurities go and one chants சிவாய, those letters end karma that is hard to remove; Pattinathar says chanting the Lord by the five letters without flagging brings the release that is not being born again. Both make the five letters the means and the end of birth the result.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 296 'செவியாமல் நீ£செபித்தாற்' has a stray £ and செவியாமல் is probably சலியாமல்; Tirumanthiram 2714 'தீர்fப்பதும்' has a stray f.

note: The Naladiyar's body is a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, called 'broad-shouldered one' by the fool; Pattinathar counts the openings one by one, rheum, wax, mucus, spit, wind and urine, and says the mind took this grass hut for firmer than stone. Both reduce the body to its leaks; the Naladiyar aims at the lover, Pattinathar at the mind's own trust in its body.

Tirumular says the mind made firm as stone stands before Siva while the body is brief as lightning; Pattinathar reproaches the mind for taking the body for firmer than stone (கல்லினும் வலிதாக் கருதினை). The same stone is misplaced in one and rightly placed in the other: the firmness belongs to the mind turned to Siva, not to the body.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 2141 last line is obscure (சிலை stone or bow; சிவமுன் இடைக்கே unclear).

note: The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; Pattinathar names the Siva-bliss as what stands free of 'I' and 'mine' (எனதற நினைவற) along with the two deeds and the malas. Both make the end of the two possessives the threshold; the Kural's reward is a higher world, Pattinathar's is the Lord himself.

The Naladiyar's firm-minded see the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts; Pattinathar's catalogue includes the bubble on water (நீரிற் குமிழி) and then says the body is worse, a stain of maya. The Naladiyar makes the image the mark of understanding; Pattinathar treats it as too kind.

Tirumular says the wealth that seemed lasting is like writing on water and tells one to conquer the senses; Pattinathar applies நீர்மேல் எழுத்து to the body itself, among the frost, the rainbow and the dream. The same image moves from possessions to the possessor.

Arunagirinathar names his body as a string of bags, of deceit, of flesh, of anger's toddy, of wind, of rubbish, of pus, and a carcass for dogs; Pattinathar's string runs through chest, casket, hamlet, pot, top, ship, cage, bellows, log, shirt and corpse. Both are catalogues of the body in short phrases ending in a plea; Pattinathar's adds the brief things and the maya stain.
audit_text_issue: 534's praise half is partly obscure (வெள்ளுத்தி மால், சிள்ளிட்ட காட்டில்), as the marker notes; the catalogue half is clear enough for the link.

note: The Kural says the friendship of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its nest (குடம்பை) behind; Pattinathar names the body a hut (குரம்பை) from which the bird that is life flies off, in the middle of his catalogue. Both use the one bird and the left nest; Pattinathar makes it one name among forty for what he is laying down.

Tirumular says to take refuge in the shade of the Pure One's holy feet and the leaping sea of deeds will not reach you; Pattinathar asks refuge at the lotus of the feet when he lays down the body that sailed the sea of birth with a cargo of sin. Both place the refuge at the feet and both set it against a sea of karma.

The second and third agavals share the top spinning on the rope of desire (ஆசைக் கயிற்றிலாடும் பம்பரம்), the bellows for rice, the casket or shackle of the two deeds and the ship of disease or of birth; the second ends 'enough, enough' and asks to be ruled, the third adds the roll of the mind's faults and ends in refuge. The second describes the body, the third hands it over.

The Naladiyar lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which of them is the garlanded woman; Pattinathar goes limb by limb and sets bone, sweat, mucus and wax against the flower and fruit each is called. Both dissolve the praised woman into her matter; Pattinathar does it against the poets' conventions by name.

Arunagirinathar repeats the questions men ask, whether the eyes are vel or carp, the hair cloud or forest, the breasts Meru or tusks, and asks not to drown in such women's eyes; Pattinathar repeats the same conventions (cloud for hair, lily for eyes, lotus bud for breasts) and answers each with the body's matter. Both quote courtly praise in order to refuse it.

On the reading in which Sivavakkiyar rebukes those who count the breast that grew and rose as maya and tells them instead to examine the body of the jiva that holds grace, Pattinathar is the man rebuked: he strips the breast and every limb down to bone and pus and the womb's impurity. The conflict depends on that reading of 1372's first line; if its கொங்கை is a figure for pride, the two do not meet.

Both close on the same surrender: 304 ends 'I know nothing, whatever is, is your doing' (ஏதுமொன்றறியேன் யாது நின் செயலே), and 350 opens 'nothing at all is my doing; all is yours'. 304 asks for union beyond the tattvas; 350 turns the same formula to the problem of why evil has come to one who did no evil in this body.

Both ask for the state in which 'you and I' are one: Pattinathar asks for a day when நீயும் நானுமாய் stand in the space beyond nada, Arunagirinathar for the bliss in which 'you and I' become one enjoyment after deeds, malas, death and birth end. Both set this union beyond the body and its tattvas.

The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives before any other plan. Pattinathar says rolling so that the devotees' feet touch one's head tears the leaf of fate. On the Kural's plain reading fate is unbeatable; on Pattinathar's, devotion beats it. The conflict depends on taking கிழிப்பது as cancelling fate rather than only ending its grip on the mind.

Both claim that devotion breaks the writing on the head: Tirumular says that when his heart joined the Lord's feet the Lord broke up his தலைவிதி, and Pattinathar says the devotees' feet on his head tear the விதி ஏடு. Tirumular has the Lord do it; Pattinathar gives the act to the Lord's servants.

309 asks that at death someone teach him the five letters, since he will no longer be able to recite them himself; 346 lists the five letters recited within (உள்ளே எழுத்தைந்தும் ஓதவுண்டு) among the ascetic's possessions. The deathbed request shows what the possession is for.

Both deny that the outward signs of the ascetic matter: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one quits what the world condemns, and Pattinathar says forest, air, rags and bowl are nothing without inner love. The Kural's test is conduct, Pattinathar's is love, but both move the mark inward.

note: 311 says the true lovers reach release even living in the house with women; 347 describes those free of attachment from the outside: they bathe when they sweat, eat when hungry, sleep, and look like worldly people. Together they say that the renouncer and the householder cannot be told apart by what they do.

note: Both make standing among people a function of money: the Naladiyar says a man with a few coins gains rank whatever he wears, while one with nothing is lower than a corpse though well born; Pattinathar says mother, wife, child and kin all become enemies once wealth is gone. The Naladiyar counsels on wealth, Pattinathar draws the conclusion that only the Lord's feet are free of the dependence.

Both make the fate of the body after the life leaves a matter of indifference: the Naladiyar asks what it matters whether the corpse is dragged with a rope, buried with care or thrown anywhere; Pattinathar lists forest, shore, city, house and porch as the places where the body may fall and gives the life a companion that does not depend on which.

Both watch the mourners rather than the dead: Tirumular's town wails, burns the body, bathes and stops thinking of him; Pattinathar's mourners are themselves corpses-to-be (சாம்பிணங்கள்) wailing beside a corpse. Tirumular shows that grief ends; Pattinathar that the grievers end.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:314 பத்தும் புகுந்து is open to several readings.

note: 316 confesses that the poet cannot do what Siruthondar, Thiruneelakanda and Kannappar did and asks how else to become a servant. Tirumular's verse answers the question: even making one's bones firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach the gem; only those who melt with love do. Pattinathar's own answer comes at 324, in melting and tears.

Both describe the desired body as a vessel of filth: the Naladiyar's pot that seeps from nine openings and churns with slime, dazzling the fool with its dark skin; Pattinathar's pus-hole, pit of filth and hidden wound. The Naladiyar blames the fool's eye; Pattinathar asks for the state that leaves the pleasure behind.

Tirumular reproaches the dull who call the body filth (மலம் என்று உடம்பை மதியாத) and hold some other place sacred, since the whole cosmos is grasped in the strong body. Pattinathar calls the body a filth-pit and a hidden wound and asks to rise out of it. On the reading that Tirumular means the human body as such, and not only the yogi's, the two value the body oppositely; Pattinathar's verse is about the woman's body as an object of lust, which narrows but does not remove the conflict.

Both poets describe themselves as foragers: Pattinathar wanders night and day for prey (இரைக்கே) round the pit at women's waists; Arunagirinathar carries a body that stinks like a corpse from house to house, speaking sweetly for whatever feast comes. Each asks the Lord to end the circuit, Pattinathar by being taken and ruled, Arunagirinathar by bowing at the feet.

Both describe the state in which the mind has ceased as a drink or a sleep of bliss that does not lift: Tirumular's drinkers of the nectar of Siva's bliss in the samadhi where the mind melts do not leave it standing, sitting or lying; Pattinathar asks to stay in the drowse of the sleep of bliss, free of thought and of its absence. Tirumular names it samadhi; Pattinathar keeps the word for sleep.

Both make melting the heart of worship: Tirumular commands 'melt your love and praise the Lord' and says Nandi answered when he melted; Pattinathar asks for the heart that breaks and softens into mud, melting and melting, with tears running down the chest. Tirumular reports that it worked; Pattinathar still asks when it will come.

Both refuse to court the rich for a living: Tirumular says do not wither praising petty-minded men for their wealth in hope of sustenance, but praise the Lord with one's true home in mind; Pattinathar refuses to follow the rich, speak of his troubles and show his teeth, and asks instead for solitude at the bound of supreme bliss.

Both make the company of the Lord's people the ground of release: Tirumular says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva if one has kinship with those whose minds have joined Siva's bliss; Pattinathar says he has stayed where those who praise the Lord are, will not leave the company of the good, and so will not be born again.

311 says forest, air, rags and the begging bowl are nothing without inner love and that true lovers reach release at home. 321 asks for exactly that outward life, house left, begging, toothless, attached to nothing. The two stand together only if 321's begging is the form love takes for this poet, not its substitute; 311 sets the condition under which 321's wish is worth having.

The Kural curses the creator if even begging is needed to live: let the one who made the world wander and perish. Pattinathar lists loincloth, porch, leaves, water and the Lord's name as enough, and 345 adds that when hunger comes Siva gives. On the Kural's plain reading a life sustained by begging is an indictment of the world's order; on Pattinathar's, it is the life in which nothing is lacking. The conflict holds if both speak of the same begging; the Kural's chapter is about want forced on a man, Pattinathar's about want chosen.

Tirumular lists curd, ghee, copper, mercury, brick, bilva and gold as materials any one of which can be the Sivalinga; Pattinathar asks whether the brow-eyed one will dwell in stone and copper and expects the answer no. On the reading that Pattinathar denies the Lord's presence in the material image, the two conflict directly; the conflict softens only if his line means that the Lord is not confined to stone, which the preceding list of the Lord's dwellings does not say.

note: Sivavakkiyar names brick, black stone, the red lingam, copper and brass as the things people say Siva dwells in and sends them to know themselves instead; Pattinathar asks whether the Lord will dwell in stone and copper and places him in the word, the sky, the jnani's house and the devotees. Both make the same denial; Pattinathar supplies the positive list that Sivavakkiyar's verse leaves to the dance in the hall.

note: Both set kin below deeds: Tirumular says the kin who cling and follow are worse than one's karma and tells one to light the lamp of awareness before the life leaves; Pattinathar says kin go only as far as the cremation ground and that only tapas done before goes further. Each names what one should secure while alive, awareness or austerity.

The Kural says to do virtue without delay, since at death it is the companion that does not perish; Pattinathar measures property to the house, wives to the street and children to the burning ground, and says what follows is the pair of deeds, merit and sin. The Kural names only the good companion; Pattinathar adds that sin follows just as faithfully.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether goats, lands, elephants, armies or a crore of horses will come and stand beside you, and answers that only the alms thrown and the dharma done gladly do; Pattinathar's wealth, wives and children stop at the house, street and burning ground, and only merit and sin follow. Both use the image of what accompanies one, and both make deeds the only companion.

Tirumular's drinkers of Siva's bliss keep it standing, sitting and lying down; Pattinathar's detached ones bathe, eat and sleep like everyone else and have no fixed observance. Both place the attained state inside ordinary postures and acts rather than in a visible discipline.

note: The Kural says that removing the ruinous hunger of the destitute is where wealth should be stored; Pattinathar's teaching to his heart is to hold wealth as nothing and look at the face of the hungry (பசித்தோர் முகம் பார்). The Kural keeps wealth and redirects it; Pattinathar has already dismissed it and keeps only the looking.

Both have Siva as the beggar: Tirumular's righteous one, with no one of his own, dwells in the burning ground, eats alms and is the model renouncer; Pattinathar's Siva takes a holy guise, walks the street and asks him for alms, and that asking is the poet's initiation. In Tirumular the Lord's begging is an example; in Pattinathar it is the means by which he takes a disciple.

Both describe release as leaving the yogic and psychological apparatus behind: Tirumular puts away the five states and the false thirty-six tattvas and stands as one; Pattinathar climbs past the eight-limbed yoga, the six supports and the five states into the open space. Tirumular ends in standing as one, Pattinathar in being swallowed by bliss.

Both have the nectar that wells for the one who has gone within: Tirumular's seeker goes within the bright flame in the full lotus and the nectar flows; Pattinathar drinks the milk that wells from the red moon in the open space beyond the six supports. Both place the drink above the centres, and both make it the mark of arrival rather than a stage.

Both make the body food for the scavengers before it is dead: Arunagirinathar's mass of filth and worms is food for jackals, vultures and crows and stinks the moment life leaves; Pattinathar's fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog each already call it theirs. Both end on the folly of having cherished it.

The same roll of claimants on the body: here fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog say 'mine'; at 428 dogs, jackals, ghosts and vultures hold the fat belly to be theirs while 'we' call it ours. 428 turns the image into a reason not to harm anyone.

Both follow the loving ones to the moment they leave: Tirumular's storehouse loses its fastenings, the nine gates shut and the loving ones wept and went; Pattinathar's mother calls him a corpse, the wives say 'go' and the sons break the pot. Pattinathar adds the conclusion, that the only attachment left is to the Lord.

Pattinathar calls the begging bowl, the loincloth and the verandah wealth without lack, proclaimed by the Veda; the Kural says that if one must live by begging, let the world's maker wander and perish. On the Kural's plain reading begging is the worst of lives; for Pattinathar it is the chosen one. The conflict holds unless the Kural is read as about the poor who beg from need rather than the renunciant.

Tirumular allows that the true garb receives alms but adds that a garb saves only those who have understood; Pattinathar's list of the beggar's goods makes no such condition. 363 supplies it from the poet's side, the beggar's way being that of those clear in true knowledge.

Both set the bundled book against the Lord: Sivavakkiyar's shastras recited and books tied in bundles ended as nothing once he knew the Lord; Pattinathar's fools roll up the all-pervading light and carry it under the arm instead of keeping it in thought.

Both poets use deliberately foul anatomy of the woman's body to break desire: Arunagirinathar's well, channel of old stains and rotting hole; Pattinathar's seven stenches ending at the yoni and the mud of the senses. Both close by turning on the poet's own mind that clung.

note: Sivavakkiyar argues that caste has no substance, since all bodies are the same five elements through the same gate; Pattinathar does not argue but acts, resolving to beg from any caste as part of lacking nothing. The doctrine of one becomes the practice of the other.

Tirumular's Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while their senses and body remain intact; Pattinathar's knowers of true jnana wander like ghosts and lie like corpses. Both describe the jnani by his resemblance to the dead and set him against other kinds of ascetic or ritualist.

Pattinathar tells the heart that good and evil come only as Brahma wrote, so that even worship changes nothing and the right stance is not to waver; the Kural says those who toil without flagging will see fate's back. On Pattinathar's plain reading, no effort alters the outcome; the Kural claims effort can. The tension softens only if 365 is read as counsel for the mind's peace rather than a claim about causation.

Tirumular lists what becomes needless once the Life of life is within (recitation, desire, dying, going about); Pattinathar lists the vows, Vedas, Agamas, fire rites, japa and pujas and calls them pretence. Tirumular's list is of things outgrown, Pattinathar's of things false, but both set the whole ritual apparatus aside.

note: Tirumular makes the heart the temple, the body the shrine, the soul the lingam and the senses the lamps, so that worship is translated into the body; Pattinathar goes further and names each outer item by its absence, a chakra not drawn, a lingam not built, a heart that does not think. Tirumular's inner temple is still furnished; Pattinathar's inner puja has nothing in it.

Sivavakkiyar asks what mantra it is to circle a planted stone and mutter while the Lord is within; Pattinathar answers with the worship the guru taught, which has no planted lingam and no spoken mantra. Both rest on the Lord being within the worshipper.

note: Both set the household against its end: the Naladiyar's man sees the corpse carried and the kin wailing yet marries and believes there is joy here, and the funeral drum answers him; Pattinathar's wife, sons and house, real day by day, went away as a lie, an old tale and a dream. The Naladiyar's warning is before the fact, Pattinathar's report is after.

The pot that breaks: Tirumular's potter shapes pots from the tank's clay and people keep the shards of a broken pot but not a broken body; Pattinathar's kin, wife and livelihood are clay pots struck with a stick. In Tirumular the pot is the body, in Pattinathar the household, but both make the potter Brahma's making the reason it breaks.

Pattinathar says the body is fit for nothing but to be fuel for fire; Tirumular says that if a jnani's body is burned the whole land burns with fever, and it should not be given to dogs and jackals. On Tirumular's reading the jnani's body is a thing of power to be entombed, not burned; on Pattinathar's it has no use at all. The conflict holds for the jnani's body, since Pattinathar makes no exception for it.

The Kural says the false embrace of women of wealth is like embracing a stranger's corpse in a dark room; Pattinathar lists going to the harlots as the one act of a heart that refused self-knowledge and the guru. Both place the courtesan at the far end from knowing what is real.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether a planted stone will speak while the Lord is within and makes the pot and ladle the whole argument; Pattinathar says only that he will not praise stone, plaster and copper as gold, and keeps the Lord's feet within. Pattinathar's refusal is personal and does not deny that others may worship the image; Sivavakkiyar's is a verdict on the image.

Tirumular once held the body a thing of shame and cherishes it now that the Highest has made it his temple; Pattinathar holds the stone, plaster and copper images apart and keeps the feet inside the body instead. Both move worship inward, but for Tirumular the body itself becomes the shrine, while for Pattinathar (387) it stays a disgust even as it holds the feet.

Arunagirinathar tells his own life from the embryo in his mother's body, born with desire and raised with love, to ask for love for the feet; Pattinathar tells his mother's ten months and her breast to ask in what birth he will see her. The same beginning is told from the child's side in one and from the mother's debt in the other.

The life as a bird: the Kural says body and life are friends only as a bird that flies off leaving its shell or nest; Pattinathar's mother dandled him so that the sky-bird would not fly away, that is, kept the life in the infant body. Pattinathar uses the Kural's figure for what the mother held back for a time.

The Kural says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today; Pattinathar says the same of his mother, enthroned, then in the street, then ash, and adds what the Kural does not, that the whole of it is Siva. The Kural's observation becomes a Saiva conclusion.

Tirumular's town wails, burns the man, bathes and stops thinking of him, which is the verse's reproach to the world; Pattinathar is the one who will not come to sprinkle the milk and does not grieve, and gives as his reason that all is Siva. The same refusal to mourn is folly in Tirumular's townsfolk and knowledge in Pattinathar.

430 asks what a mother who bathed, kept vigil, conceived, bore, raised and named a son can do if the son turns mad for God; 396 is that son at her pyre, counting the fire she set in his belly among the fires of the gods. The later verse states the mother's loss in general; this one lives it.

The body as a vessel with nine openings that seep filth: the Naladiyar's fool praises the pot that leaks from nine holes because its dark skin dazzles him; Pattinathar calls it a nine-mouthed wound and names the cure. The Naladiyar's image serves to shame desire, Pattinathar's to ask for medicine.

note: Both set the hut or wound of nine gates against medicine: Arunagirinathar kept trying worthless medicines and yogas for his ashen body until his mind cried enough and turned to the feet; Pattinathar says the one medicine for the stinking nine-mouthed wound is the dust of the devotees' feet. Both move the cure from the body to the feet.

note: Tirumular's people wander searching everywhere in the land for Nandi who is fragrant within the body and do not know the meaning that stands within it; Pattinathar's pilgrims run from festival to festival while the Lord of Arur is here and never seek the inner sign. Pattinathar adds the figure of seeking fire while the lamp burns.

The same method of breaking lust by naming the body's openings: 359 runs through the stinking mouth, eyes, body and yoni and asks how the mind clung; 405 fixes the womb-mouth two fingers above the dung-mouth and says the lover in the chariot street is already dead.

The Kural defines virtue as what proceeds without envy, craving, anger and harsh speech; Pattinathar's list of what the mind will not give up has lying, flesh and anger beside not thinking of the Lord and not reciting the five letters. The Kural's ethical list is kept and the Saiva items added to it as the same kind of thing.

Both ask for the end of rebirth after following the body to the fire: Arunagirinathar's townsfolk burn it to ash and he asks for grace not to seek this birth again; Pattinathar counts his mother, Brahma's hand and his own feet as worn out and asks not to enter another womb.

The Kural says do virtue without saying 'later', since at death it is the companion that does not perish; Pattinathar says speak the Lord's name before Death, the dimming eye, the mourners and the pyre. Both make the time before death the only time, and differ in what is to be done in it, virtue in the Kural and the name in Pattinathar.

The Naladiyar says the body lasts like water on a grass tip, so do good right now, for people will say 'he stood, he sat, he lay down, and with his kin wailing he was gone'; Pattinathar's five 'befores' end at the same wailing kin and the pyre. Both reason from the suddenness of the end to an act now.

Tirumular makes Siva himself the renouncer who dwells in the burning ground and eats alms; Pattinathar's happiness is to worship the serpent-wearer, take alms and eat, and sleep at the temple gate. The beggar's life is the Lord's own in one and the devotee's in the other, and both call it the renouncer's.

Pattinathar names taking alms and eating them among the four things that alone are happiness; the Kural says that if one must live by begging, let the world's maker wander and perish. On the Kural's plain reading begging is a life not worth the world's making; for Pattinathar it is the whole of the good life. As at 357, the conflict holds unless the Kural is confined to the needy.

The Kural says not asking, even from those who give gladly, is worth ten million times more; Pattinathar goes beyond not asking: he will not go even when called with insistence, and eats only what is brought to where he sits, though the body waste. The Kural's restraint on asking becomes a refusal of the giver's house.

The Naladiyar's worthy man goes before no one except those who embrace him and say 'come in, eat'; Pattinathar will not go even to those, and accepts food only if it is carried to him with eagerness. The Naladiyar allows the welcoming host as the one exception; Pattinathar removes it.

Tirumular's Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while their senses and body remain intact, set against ritual purifiers and chattering knowers; Pattinathar tells his heart to want no display or garland and to go about like the dead. The same formula for the jnani's outer life, in Tirumular as description and in Pattinathar as instruction to himself.

note: The vultures at the stinking body: the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures crowd in and tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; Pattinathar's heart is asked whether it has not seen the vultures hop, strip the skin and eat. Both end the body's story at the birds and use the sight as the argument against loving it.

Sivavakkiyar turns the rule of leavings on the one who keeps it, since the hand and the water are already touched by mouths; Pattinathar goes a step further and makes the saliva itself the object of inquiry, so that examining it reveals oneness and heals the mind. Sivavakkiyar refutes the rule, Pattinathar makes its object a means.
