note: Tirumular says there is no need of purification for one who stands free of pollution; Pattinathar says one who examines the pollution itself and stays with it comes to oneness and a mind without disease. In both the purity rite is superseded by a state, though Tirumular's state is being clean of pollution and Pattinathar's is seeing through it.

The Kural asks why one who knows what is hurtful to his own life does hurtful things to other beings; Pattinathar tells the heart not to intend harm to anyone, since the body one would protect by harming belongs already to the dogs and vultures. Both ground harmlessness in the self, the Kural in the self's own knowledge of hurt, Pattinathar in the self's having no body to defend.

Tirumular says silence is when speech and mind are both still, and one whose speech alone is silent is merely mute; Pattinathar's freed ones keep the mind in silence while the body works, suffers or plays like the water carrier swinging her arms. Both place silence in the mind and not in the mouth or the limbs; Pattinathar adds that the limbs may do anything.

357 makes the renunciant's marks (loincloth, bowl, verandah, poor food) the wealth without lack, and 360 and 363 repeat the inventory; 429 says the freed mind stays in silence whatever the work or austerity, so that no outward form is the mark. The later verse does not cancel the beggar's way but denies that it is required.

Sivavakkiyar says children, wives and kin are maya and none of them can come along when Yama calls; Pattinathar has the desire for children and kin itself refuse to forget him. Both treat the bond of kin as the thing that does not leave.

Pattinathar's five senses say they will not subside and he turns to the Lord; Tirumular says the senses come under control of themselves once one meets the Lord alone. Both place the subduing of the senses with the Lord rather than with effort.

Kakapusundar's dance comes when one is without desire and anger and has forgotten mother and kin; Pattinathar's lust and anger refuse to pass and his kin-desire refuses to forget. The same two items block the same goal from opposite sides.
The body as a bubble on water: the Naladiyar praises those firm enough to see it so and end their wandering; Pattinathar confesses that his thought takes the bubble for permanent.
Tirumular's streaming body goes like a bubble on flowing water into the Supreme; Pattinathar's water-bubble body is what desire wrongly holds as lasting. One image, used for merging and for delusion.

Tirumular's body-tenders end mounted on a pyre of rough logs; Pattinathar sees bodies burn on the log before his eyes and still thinks he will stay. Both make the cremation log the refutation of the body's care.
The Kural calls taking what does not last for lasting the lowest understanding; Pattinathar confesses that very thought in himself, and adds that it is held fondly (ஆதரவாய்).
Tirumular addresses those who feel the unstaying state as lasting and the perishing hut as permanent; Pattinathar is such a one speaking of himself.

Tirumular prescribes thinking of women as Death come to kill so that desire falls away; Pattinathar states it as his experience, Death taking a woman's form to deceive him, while his desire has not fallen away.

Sivavakkiyar: gathered from atoms through every kind of womb you were born human and now lose yourselves in books; Pattinathar counts the same passage through the orders of birth and asks whether it is not yet enough.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:455 கிடமாய் uncertain.

note: Arunagirinathar asks how many bodies, countless as sand, he has filled, in the sea, on hills and in springs; Pattinathar's litany of births as elements, gods and demons is the same count put to the Lord as a plea that it suffice.

Arunagirinathar blames deeds that the flower-born Brahma ordained for his failure to wear ash and say 'Hara Hara'; Pattinathar counts being cut up by Brahma's written leaf among what he has suffered, and three verses later complains that the Lord never gave him the ash.
audit_text_issue: 838's opening lines on the women and the young man are of uncertain construction, as the marker flags.

note: Tirumular's Siva is the mad one who cuts off the births of those who renounce; Pattinathar's whole complaint assumes the same, that ending birth and death is the Lord's act to do, and charges him with not having done it.

Tirumular lists holy ash first among the emblems, then earrings and the rudraksha string, as the marks of the Siva-yogi; Pattinathar asks the Lord for exactly these, the ash in 467 and the rudraksha and garb in 468, as things to be given rather than put on.

Sivavakkiyar asks those who smear burnt ash and take up the garb in which of their mantras the Lord actually stirs, so the dress is an empty sign; Pattinathar begs the Lord to give him that very garb, as the means of seeing the world as a thing to leave. On the reading that Sivavakkiyar rejects the garb as such, and not only the garb without inner practice, the two cannot both hold.

Tirumular's flawless light took over his debts, made him stainless and gave his feet; Pattinathar asks for the same sequence in the imperative, the ruining impurity crushed and the Lord's look bringing him near.
The tiger skin, with the crescent and the ash, is what Tirumular's great love lies entwined with; Pattinathar's longing fastens on the same skin at the waist and asks whether he will not see it.

Tirumular has Muyalakan lying under the dancer whose body is space and whose hands are the eight directions; Pattinathar asks to see the dance on the struck-down Muyalagan with the lifted foot and slim waist. The cosmic and the iconic Nataraja, one dwarf under each.

The gods delighting in the konrai-haired one who shares half his body with the bright-browed lady, in Tirumular's invocation; Pattinathar's gods cry victory as the beauty grows in the great Mother's half, after the konrai in 490.
audit_text_issue: 16 கோது குலாவிய (lines 1 and 4) is obscure

note: Tirumular: when the truth beyond speech is attained the five hard to curb subside and knowledge shines; Pattinathar asks for the silence beyond speech and the self-purity beyond assault as the states that would end the senses' refusal of 444.
audit_text_issue: 498 prints 'வாக்கிற்து' for வாக்கிறந்து.

note: Tirumular's Lord gave the open space of grace in great bliss, last in a list of gifts; Pattinathar's வெட்டவெளி that ends burning sorrow is the same expanse, asked for rather than received.

Tirumular asks the Lord to stand where he can be seen, since who else is kin to his servant; Pattinathar, after asking to see the form, says he has nothing but the Lord. The same claim of sole refuge, in both cases attached to seeing.

Tirumular's Lord ended word and feeling and set him in the form beyond, so that 'we passed beyond words'; Pattinathar's guru of grace strikes him into the state beyond word and mind. Both make the passage past language the Lord's act.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 505 வசோகசத்தில் looks corrupt (perhaps அசோக சத்து).

note: Tirumular's Supreme told him the one thing beyond telling and entered him; Pattinathar's Lord is named guru in the act of striking him into what is beyond word and mind. In both the guru gives what cannot be said.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 505 வசோகசத்திற் is likely corrupt (read அசோக சத்து); the first phrase is clear.

note: The same verse as Azhuganni 33 with the ஆத்தாடி refrain: the bow to Ganesa and the one who came and showed his form. The Azhuganni reads தற்சொரூபம், the self's form, where this reads தன்சொரூபம், his own.

Both say the grace that frees comes in the guru's form: Tirumular's grace-power comes as the guru when the two deeds balance; Pattinathar's Lord took the guru's shape to cut birth and the senses, and 527 has him destroying the two deeds.
The body as a fort: the Meynjanap-pulambal asks when it will seize the fort of the body-city; here the fort of deceit, with its six centres and fifty-one letters, is burned down.
Azhuganni 35 is the same couplet with the refrain; both burn the six supports and the fifty-one letters as a deceitful fort.
Azhuganni 36 combines this line on the tattvas losing their heads with the line on the five beginning with speech that appears here at 513.

Both have the guru take the disciple past the thirty-six: Nandi makes their nature known and then stands beyond them; Pattinathar's guru burns them and cuts the root of birth. Tirumular keeps the tattvas as something learned; Pattinathar only destroys them.

Tirumular's ninety-six (thirty, thirty and thirty-six) live in a walled temple and run off when it falls; Pattinathar's sixty die inside the fort when it burns. In Tirumular the constituents outlive the body; here they are killed with it.
The Kural says cutting off the pride that says 'I' and 'mine' enters the highest world; Pattinathar's guru cuts the ego (ஆங்காரம்) at the root. Pattinathar adds that Om itself goes with it.

Tirumular faults those in whom the light of Om rises but who never gain the ego-free experience; Pattinathar goes a step further and has Om and ego ruined together, so that even the pranava is not kept.
In the first part of the lament (முதல்வன் முறையீடு) the poet asks whether the open space that ends burning sorrow will not come to him; here, in the woman's voice, he says he has become it.
Bhadragiriyar asks when he will see clearly the bare void grown in the open space; Pattinathar's speaker has become the open space and sees everything else as a dream.

In the Kural the town, not knowing the woman's worth, makes the lover a present of gossip; Pattinathar's speaker, whose state is now visible, expects to be the country's song and the lookers' talk. The lover's gossip becomes the jnani's.

Tirumular says those who have set Nandi in love by knowledge have no caste, no stain and no qualities to take on; Pattinathar's speaker, having realised, asks whether caste or the sastras will have her, and the answer the Tirumanthiram gives is that the question no longer applies.
Pambatti says those who have seen never tell and those who tell have never seen; Pattinathar asks the same as a double question, have the tellers seen, have the seers told.

The Agappei tells the inner demon to just stay still and says it has told the formula (சூத்திரம்); Pattinathar's speaker was made to stay still and says she does not know the formula. Both make சும்மா இருத்தல் the teaching, and differ on whether its rule can be stated.
Azhuganni 37 is the same couplet with its ஆத்தாடி refrain: no bathing, no flowers, the heart a bare void.

Tirumular says that those who recite, worship and gather flowers without love have minds like a stone in a mossy pond; Pattinathar's speaker drops the flowers and bathing altogether and finds her heart an empty void, which she cannot yet read as gain or loss.

Tirumular's Being stays mingled within like light in a gem and is farther than far if put into words; Pattinathar's Lord stays mingled like the light within a ruby and is the greatness his devotees do not speak of. Same image, same conclusion about speech.

Both warn that a void can be mistaken for the goal: Tirumular says the foolish call the wordless void in which turiya subsides the Supreme; Pattinathar confesses she fell into the void without devotion and took it for a fitting sleep.
audit_text_issue: 553's second line is grammatically awkward.

note: The Kural says those who have learned here and seen the true thing reach the path of not returning, so that learning is the way to the real; Pattinathar says the cause is not learning and not hearing but what is shown by a hand. The conflict holds on the reading of கற்று as learning the true texts, which is how Parimelazhagar takes it; if the Kural means only 'having learned to see', the two agree.

Both use the same Sanskrit term: Tirumular's Nandi is வாசாமகோசரம், beyond speech and mind, where conduct, love and the Veda end; Pattinathar's Lord took his seat in வாசாமகோசரம் and is the knowledge of knowledge.

Tirumular says there is one God in all ten directions and no direction where he is not; Pattinathar says his state is not contained by the ten directions and he is one body unbroken in every direction. Pattinathar's verse has no refuge or deeds, only the pervasion.

Both deny that pervasion lessens him: Tirumular's Lord, being everywhere as all that moves and does not, stands without lessening; Pattinathar's is not lessened by an atom though every being in every world exists.
audit_text_issue: உண்டாலும் is glossed as 'exist'; 'eat' is likelier.

note: The light within the ruby twice in the same lament: at 550 he stays mingled in the speaker like that light, and at 563 he is that light for those who set a noble mind on him. The first is indwelling, the second the condition of seeing it.

At 547 the speaker's strung doctrine collapsed when she saw all as the Supreme; 568 adds that for those who string a frame he takes the strung state, so the collapse is hers and not a fault in those who hold a doctrine.

The Kural says to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging, in order to let clinging go; Pattinathar says he held her as the hold of those who hold to nothing. The Kural commands the soul to hold; Pattinathar has the Lord do the holding.
Pattinathar tells his heart elsewhere that to stay in the open space without liking or disliking is joy; here, in the woman's voice, he dwelt in her in that open space.

Tirumular takes the void as his way and rests in the void that has dropped even that imagining; Pattinathar says the true life became bare void for her. Both make the void the end and not a loss, though Pattinathar leaves the tone open.
518 asks whether he came as a form or to destroy form; 576 answers with what she saw, the one who cast the spell losing his own form.
audit_text_issue: 576 புண்மாயமிட்டவனை is obscure, likely a corruption (புன்மாயம்?); the second line's sense is not fixed.

note: Tirumular's virgin, and virgin undone, bore the five gods; Pattinathar's virgin palm bore fruit. In Tirumular the paradox belongs to Shakti as mother; in Pattinathar to the soul taken by the Lord, whose maidenhood was destroyed at 531 and who is a maiden again at 528.
audit_text_issue: tirumanthiram:1118 line 2 (துன்னியங fகைவரைப்) is corrupt.

note: In the Thiruppugazh civet is the scent of women who seek money with deceitful hearts; in Pattinathar every place reached smells of civet, and 579 calls it the natural scent of grace. The same perfume is applied in one and innate in the other.

The same image in the same words: Tirumular's Nandi drew him in as hot iron draws in water (இரும்பிடை நீர்); Pattinathar's Lord swallowed her like water taken up by iron (இரும்பு நிறை நீர்). Both are of absorption with nothing left over.

Tirumular's streaming body goes into the Supreme like camphor in a rising flame; Pattinathar's Lord swallows her like fire eating camphor without remainder. In Tirumular the image is of the body's ending, in Pattinathar of the union itself.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:581 line 2 மக்கினம்பட்டு is obscure; the camphor line is clear.

note: Azhuganni's stanza has the same two formulas, the guru's form taken to cut off birth and the cause come to cut the thieving senses, with the refrain ஆத்தாடி; the line is shared property of the pulambal tradition, not one poet's.
audit_text_issue: Azhuganni கள்களப் for கள்ளப்; the verse is unmarked.

note: Both make the lowest understanding a mistake of perception: the Kural's paltry mind takes what does not last for what lasts; Pattinathar's shell-for-silver people cannot reach the Lord. The Kural's object is impermanence, Pattinathar's the Supreme.

Tirumular ends speech in the pure form beyond the three voids; Pattinathar's Lord is the Brahman that does not speak and the great light past speech. In both the end of words belongs to the Supreme itself.

Tirumular's disciples become the reality mixed in the shoreless light as ghee mixes in pure milk; Pattinathar's Fullness is spread through all as sugar in milk. Same vessel, but Tirumular's image is of the soul merging and Pattinathar's of the Lord pervading.

The Kural makes the Primal Lord first of the world as the letter A is first of letters; Pattinathar says he is not born of letters and not held in a book. Not a conflict, since the Kural's letter is a simile, but Pattinathar refuses the medium the Kural uses.
audit_text_issue: 595 line 2 நாட்டினரிகள் likely a misprint for நாட்டின் நரிகள் (jackals).

note: Sivavakkiyar's Lord enters his heart and makes it his temple, as the water is held in the coconut; Pattinathar's sets his feet in a heart of stone as a lily blooms in it. Both make the heart the shrine, and in both it is the Lord who enters, not the devotee who builds.

Sivavakkiyar: recite the Sama and the four Vedas and you still do not know Siva; Pattinathar: ride the Veda-horse at a gallop and you do not know him. Both place knowing after reciting and locate it within intent, not text.
Both end speech at the Supreme: Tirumular's pure form beyond the three voids is where words come to their end, Pattinathar's silent Brahman is the light at the place where sound subsides within Om.

Sivavakkiyar asks what he can say of what has no grammar, there being nothing within him but the Lord and I; Pattinathar, looked at by the Lord, finds nothing but him and no place to speak from. Both make the end of the self the end of saying.

The Kural says cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging, so as to let clinging go; Pattinathar names the same thing பற்றற்ற பற்று and adds that the Lord came to earth to show it. The Kural's paradox is made a person.

Tirumular names the three voids, of maya, of space and of the soul pervaded in Siva-Shakti; Pattinathar takes the scheme as known and places the Lord beyond it as a first void and whole First that comes and swallows the soul.

Sivavakkiyar's sinners do not know the Lord who is in them like ghee hidden in milk; Pattinathar's supreme light holds and swallows him as milk holds ghee. One uses the image for the unseen presence, the other for accomplished union.

Tirumular says that beyond the light in the void there is nothing here to compare it with; Pattinathar's guru is the substance without equal or simile. Both put the Supreme past comparison, and Pattinathar then apologises (622) for having compared.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 2462 தொற்பதம் is probably a misprint for தொம்பதம் or தொல்பதம்.

note: Tirumular's experience is in the three voids where words cease; Pattinathar names those who have learned and realised the three voids as the judges of his failed words. The three voids are the point where both poets expect speech to break down.

The Naladiyar's petty-minded say 'we are rich' and never think where they must go, and their wealth vanishes like lightning; Pattinathar's boast 'all this earth is our holding' is the same speech, confessed in the first person after the vanishing.

Sivavakkiyar calls children, wives and kin maya and asks whether they can come along when Death calls; Pattinathar says he took children and wives for real and lost the Lord. Both make the error one of taking them as true rather than of having them.
Sivavakkiyar's fine body stinks when the Arbiter calls and is carried only as far as the cremation keeper; Pattinathar's body already has the corpse-smell while he chases money for it.

Sivavakkiyar asks how many flowers he threw, mantras he recited and temples he circled in vain; Pattinathar says he performed Siva's worship through countless births and lost the Lord. Both renounce the ritual path from inside it, having done it.

Tirumular says release comes with joy to worshippers who offer food, lamps and incense and think on him in love; Pattinathar says Siva-worship through countless births did not free him. The conflict holds if Pattinathar's பூசை is the same offering-worship Tirumular commends; it dissolves if Tirumular's condition, love and thought, is what Pattinathar lacked.

The Naladiyar asks what it matters whether the body is dragged with a rope or buried once the dancer has left it; Pattinathar's man who could not bear an ant on his body consents at death to its binding and burning. The body that was everything becomes a thing one lets others dispose of.

The Kural says that for those bent on ending births even the body is excess; Pattinathar says the body is one's own enemy and he died not knowing it. The Kural states the ascetic's view, Pattinathar the cost of not holding it.

Both stanzas place the Lord beyond the three voids as முதற்பாழ், the first void: in the Arutpulambal he comes and swallows the soul, in the plaint he dances there unpraised while the heart trusts a life that is itself a void.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 639 துப்பாழாய் is obscure and may be corrupt.

note: The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; Pattinathar's heart, given a birth in which to share rice, thought gold, house and women permanent instead. Both make giving the lasting use of a passing thing.

The Naladiyar says share the food of blameless wealth from the day it comes, because it turns like a cart wheel; Pattinathar adds that it came by earlier deeds and was not got today, and that the destitute and the learned were owed a share.

Tirumular's dying man leaves while the kohl-eyed wife and the wealth stay behind; Pattinathar's jewelled lord on a golden throne does not see the gold come along when Yama takes his hand. Same scene from the same side.

The Naladiyar says those who live on earlier austerity and do none now will stand outside the house grieving; Pattinathar says gold and women come only from austerity done before, and the heart that does not hold to the guru now is blind. Both treat present fortune as spent merit.

Arunagirinathar asks to join the devotees before his body falls into Death's tongue like a frog into a snake's mouth; Pattinathar says he has already become the frog in the serpent's mouth, trusting gold. One prays before the image, the other confesses from inside it.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether children, wives and kin can come along when Death calls; Pattinathar asks who among kin, parents, brothers and children will help when one dies. The same rhetorical question put to the heart.

The Kural pictures the body and life parting as a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; Pattinathar ends his list of everything that stays with கூடு, the cage or nest, left while 'you' went. The nest is the body in both.

Arunagirinathar names the body a leaking bag of wind among his string of bags; Pattinathar calls it the wind-bellows and the oozing corpse. Arunagirinathar asks to be rid of it, Pattinathar faults the heart for feeding it instead of the hungry.

The Naladiyar says give at once what comes to hand, for those who gave first escape the waste land through which Death drags his captives; Pattinathar's heart gave not a nut's worth of rice and did not ask who would stand by it when Yama's messenger drags it. Giving is the only provision for that journey in both.
The Naladiyar's firm see the body as a bubble in pelting rain; Pattinathar's heart trusted the water-bubble life as certain. Same image, opposite minds.

Tirumular says that if one door is closed inside the bag, light shines in the body and the black-daubed temple is lit with a gem lamp; Pattinathar's Siva-siddha shows how to open the house and summon the open space by light in the holed bag. Both make the body a bag with a door and light the thing to be found in it, though one closes the door and the other opens it.
audit_text_issue: Both verses' senses are flagged uncertain; 655's third line is cipher.

note: Tirumular makes the Lord's feet the eight letters and his anklets twice five and fifty-one; Pattinathar's Lord stands as five letters, eight letters and fifty-one. The same letter-counts name the same Lord, and in both the counting ends in a single subtle thing (the tender letter, the feet).

Sivavakkiyar demands the straight truth of the unripe letter (பிஞ்செழுத்து) that stands first among the five; Pattinathar's Lord stands as the tender letter behind the five, eight and fifty-one. The same cipher-word for the one letter behind the counted ones.

Sivavakkiyar's householder rejoices beside his mansions with cattle, wealth, wife and children when Death's messengers strike all at once; Pattinathar's heart trusted children, wives and kin and thought it would last for all time.

The Kural says the gambler's winnings are like the hook swallowed by a fish; Pattinathar is the kendai fish writhing on the hook of women's maya. The same hook, baited with winnings in one and with women in the other.

664 names the Lord who ate the hunter's leavings as the one the heart failed to reach; 673 adds his sale to a bard and names the heart's fault as ஆணவம், so the two stories of the Lord's stooping frame the heart's pride.
The plaint opens with the heart as a dog wandering the market and here has it as a dog poking its head under every eave; the first is lust, the second homelessness without Sivaloka.

Arunagirinathar wastes away like a frog that has eaten poison, playing with women who strip his wealth; Pattinathar wanders like a fish that has eaten poison, having missed the light. Both are creatures that swallowed their own death and go on moving.
audit_text_issue: 668 lines 1-2 (ஐமூன்றும் எட்டும் ஒன்றாய்) are cipher; the fish line is clear.

note: 661 is the kendai fish writhing on the hook of women's maya; 668 is the fish that has eaten poison and wanders. The same fish, caught in the first and dying in the second.
audit_text_issue: 668 line 1 (அஞ்சுமுருவாகியைமூன்றுமெட்டுமொன்றாய்) is unkeyed cipher and may be corrupt.

note: The Kural says that for those bent on ending births even the body is excess; Pattinathar says the escape he failed to make was to leave the country the five ruled, the body, as the Pandavas left their kingdom. Both make leaving the body itself the renunciation that counts.

Sivavakkiyar asks what use a hundred crore Agamas and mantras recited for a hundred crore days are beside the one letter in the heart; Pattinathar says thinking on tantra and mantra left him confused because he did not see the light above bindu and nada. Both put the practice below what it points at.

Tirumular sets bindu and nada above the letters and says the three impurities leave when one stands fierce with SIVAYANAMA; Pattinathar used mantra and tantra and stumbled, because he did not see the light where bindu melts into nada. He does not deny the mantra's power but makes the sight of the light its condition.
audit_text_issue: Tm 930's letter-count (ஆறெட்டு, ஆறும் பதினாலும்) is unexplained; the bindu-nada and mantra lines are clear.

note: The Naladiyar asks whether spices, flowers and finery can remove the body's foulness, which eating strengthens; Pattinathar's body stinks however it tries not to, a salt-pot leaking its ooze. Both say the stink is the body's nature, not a lapse.
audit_text_issue: 670 ஆறாத நாடு is obscure

note: Tirumular says that taking up ida and pingala and twisting at the root in the triangle (மூலத்து முக்கோணத்துள்) one may see the Lord's feet; Pattinathar names the three-cornered chakra risen at the root as the place where the Maiden was not praised. The same triangle at the root is the practice's starting point in both; Tirumular gives the method, Pattinathar the omission.
audit_text_issue: 2173 ஏலங்கொண்டு is obscure; 674's வாலை is not fixed by the Tamil.

note: Tirumular puts the supreme Shakti and the truth above the adharas, beyond the sixteen; Pattinathar's climb ends past the six centres and nada-bindu at the crown-space (உச்சி வெளி). Both place the goal above the named centres rather than in any of them.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1705 line 3 (போதா லயத்துஅ விகாரந்தனிற்போத) is unclear and possibly corrupt.

note: Kakapusundar says that those who stare at the nose-tip calling it the sushumna wander in vain like madmen and perish, and moves the seat to the uvula; Pattinathar counts not keeping his eyes open on the nose-tip among the failures that spoiled his body. On the reading that 682 recommends the nose-tip gaze as a practice, the two disagree about whether it is the way or a false way.

Tirumular says that with both gazes set at the middle of the nose there is no withering, no ruin for the house and no self, and we become Siva; Pattinathar says that for not watching the nose-tip his body was spoiled and his understanding lost. The gain in the one is the loss in the other, the same practice seen from its two sides.

Tirumular says moon and sun rise and fall through ida and pingala over the two fortnights and life wells up in the middle, and tells the reader to understand and discern it; Pattinathar says that not knowing the nature (இயல்பு) of ida and pingala he hesitated with obstruction. The nature Tirumular teaches is what Pattinathar says he lacked.
audit_text_issue: 793 உயிருக்கு இரந்து is unclear

note: The Kural says the friendship of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell; Pattinathar says he was bound by believing this body and life would be permanent. Both deny the bond between body and life any permanence; the Kural states it as a fact, Pattinathar as the error he lived by.

Tirumular matches the four paths to four kinds of people, devotees in chariyai, servants in kiriyai, yogis and siddhas in jnana; Pattinathar names the same four, chariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana, as what he failed to look to. Both hold the four as the whole of the way; Pattinathar does not rank them, Tirumular does.

Sivavakkiyar calls those who run through town, country and forest searching 'mutes' and tells them to know the Supreme straight within themselves; Pattinathar says he wandered as far as Kasi, legs weary, instead of watching the breath. Both set the search outside against the one within; Pattinathar names the inner thing as the breath (வாசி), Sivavakkiyar as the Supreme spread everywhere.

Pattinathar names the breath (வாசி) as the thing to watch instead of going to Kasi, without saying what it is; Kakapusundar defines it: what comes and goes is the vaasi, and so are the sun and moon in the sky, and the siddha is the one of clear mind. The definition fills in what Pattinathar's rhyme only names.

The two are one poet's two accounts of the same time.

note: 812 ends by asking not to enter the prison of the womb (சிறைக் கருப்பாசயம்) again; 833 describes that prison cell by cell and ends with the same request, this prison escaped, not to enter the prison again.

Tirumular says that in the womb maya joins her brood to the soul, thought arises, karma takes hold and maya's bonds begin; Pattinathar is dragged into the womb by the deeds of bad company and comes out with the five guards set over him and desire's rope tying him to the body in bonds (பாசம்). Both locate the start of bondage in the womb and name the bonds.

Tirumular says the Lord is not in the mansion, hall, courtyard, temple or holy garb but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing; Pattinathar says the gods and Vedas crowd into the shrine of Marudur and do not come out, while the light sprouts inside the one-pointed mind. Both put the finding inside the person, not the building.

Sivavakkiyar says that whoever recites the beginningless mantra of five and three in the heart will see a hundred crore of the five great sins fly like cotton; Pattinathar says one utterance of 'he of Marudur' makes every sin, even the unblamed ones, vanish from where thought can reach. The one text has the mantra and the other the place-name, but the claim that a word undoes deeds is the same.

Tirumular says that standing in the chakra and saying SIVAYANAMA makes the three impurities cry out and leave; Pattinathar says saying the Lord's name once makes all sins hide and vanish. Tirumular removes mala, Pattinathar sin, so what is removed differs; the removing word is the same kind of thing.

Pattinathar uses பூரணன், the Full One, as a name of the Lord beyond the Vedas and the inner faculties; Agasthiyar says that those who call pooranam God must say what pooranam is and defines it as the sixteen kalas guarded in the body. The medical Siddhar turns the devotional epithet into a technical term, so his verse qualifies Pattinathar's usage rather than contradicting it.

Tirumular makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the gate and the senses the lamps; Pattinathar makes the mind a room swept with love and lit with the lamp of grace and the Lord's bedchamber. Both house the Lord in the person, but Tirumular's senses become lamps while Pattinathar's five buffaloes are driven out.

The Marudur agaval farms the heart and this one cleans it, with the same stages: deceit or lust removed first, love laid down, truth as manure or canopy, the five senses as cattle to be fenced out or buffaloes to be driven off, grace as the sprout or the lamp. In 821 the Lord is the fruit that grows; in 845 he is the guest invited in.

At Marudur the poet counts the endless wombs and the threefold pain of birth, bearing and death and asks for the thought to cross; at Kazhumalam he counts what the wombs have made of the world, every being his parent and his child, his eater and his food, and asks the Lord to take one flower and one word as the whole rite. The weariness is the same; the second verse widens the family and lowers the price.

Tirumular says he once held the body to be a thing of shame, then found the true substance within it and now cherishes it as the Highest One's temple; Pattinathar says those who do not know the body as impurity entire are the ones who sink in lust and do not worship. The conflict holds if Pattinathar's முழுமலம் is a doctrine about the body and not only a cure for lust; Tirumular's verse was written against exactly that doctrine.

824 lists what the body is, hair, skin, wound, blood, bone, marrow, slime, worms, excrement, nerves and disease, and finds no self in it; 849 states the conclusion, the body is impurity entire, and makes not seeing this the root of lust. The agaval gives the evidence and the venba the thesis.

Tirumular compares the soul striving by its deeds in its three states to a blind man whose eyes are open, who sees only the step ahead and feels his way with a stick; Pattinathar's unenlightened self is a man who cannot see, for whom the pit becomes the road and the road the pit, stumbling from one to the other. Tirumular's blind man still finds his way; Pattinathar's is only released by the Lord's look.

Tirumular says anyone can give a green leaf to God, grass to a cow, a mouthful to another and a kind word; Pattinathar says if there is no flower the leaf will do, if no leaf then water, and if nothing then the heart. Both make the smallest offering sufficient; Pattinathar goes one step further and makes the heart alone enough.

The Marudur kovai opens by saying the Lord gives release even to devotees who offer a green leaf; the Kazhumalam kovai closes by saying that when even the leaf and water fail, the heart is an equal offering. The two kovais frame one claim, that grace is not priced by the offering.

The Kural condemns those who, unrenounced in heart, live by deceiving as though renounced; Pattinathar confesses to exactly that false outward service and asks whether the Lord will take it anyway. The confession turns the Kural's verdict into a plea, and it leaves the verdict standing.

Both wear feet as an ornament (பூண்): Tirumular's devotees wear the holy feet of the great one and have no deeds left; Pattinathar's clarity is to wear the feet of the Lord's devotees. The ornament is the same, but Pattinathar steps one rank lower, to the servants' feet.

The first sight of the woman in both: the Kural's man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a rare peahen or human; Pattinathar's hero sees the grace of a golden peacock and red-streaked eyes and love is born. Pattinathar states the effect (காதல் விளைத்தன) where the Kural leaves the man reeling.

The millet field as the place of wooing: Arunagirinathar's Murugan speaks his desire to the parrot of the millet field; Pattinathar's youth 'like Murugan' (சேயனையார்) will not leave the field by day. Pattinathar's comparison names the myth the Thiruppugazh tells.

Gossip as a gift to the lovers: the Kural's man says the town made him a present of gossip; Pattinathar's friend tells the hill lord that his partings spread the gossip (அலர) and that the field's vengai now bears his name. In both the rumour is turned toward the match rather than against it.
audit_text_issue: 876 பேசுகயாவரும் / பூசுகையார் / தேசுகையார் / கூசுகையாது is awkwardly printed and the syntax of the first line is not secure.

note: The woman's heart runs ahead of her to the absent man: the Kural's woman's heart climbs as she thinks of his return; Pattinathar's girl says her mind has run here and gone worshipping after the pitiless hill lord. Pattinathar adds the devotional verb தொழுது.

The same figure with the same claim: those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; Pattinathar's Ekambar is the one who makes us cross the sea of birth (பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர்). The Kural names no god; Pattinathar names Ekambar of Kachi.

The Kural's king with all six, army, people, wealth, ministers, allies and fort, stands among kings as the male leads its herd; Pattinathar grants the same horses, elephants, infantry, chariots and parasol and says kingship and drum never shine without Kambar's ash on the brow. One condition is added that the Kural does not have.

Both make the ash the real protection: Tirumular calls it armour (கவசம்) that ends deeds and brings the Siva state; Pattinathar makes it the one thing without which an army and a parasol cannot make a king shine. Tirumular's gain is release, Pattinathar's is the kingdom's lustre.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1666 line 1 has a corrupt 'பூசுng' (Latin letters in the Tamil).

note: Both rank the Brahmin of Veda and the six duties below the devotee: Tirumular says feeding ten million such Brahmins does not equal a handful given to the ash-wearing servant; Pattinathar says the Brahmin who keeps the Veda and the fire but does not worship at Ekambam stands among the hunters.
audit_text_issue: 1861's third line is compressed.

note: Both deny that birth sets rank: the Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from what one does; Pattinathar says one born at the bottom of a killing, flesh-eating clan is best of all if he loves the Lord's anklets. The Kural's measure is work, Pattinathar's is devotion, and both set it against descent.

Both make devotion override every other mark: Tirumular's ash-wearers who cry 'our master' are gods walking on earth; Pattinathar's lowest-born lover of the Lord's anklets is உத்தமர் for all. Pattinathar goes further by naming the clan's killing and shamelessness and still ranking its devotee first.

The same Ravana story in the same two beats: Arunagirinathar's Ravana pulls up Kailasa, has his twenty arms crushed under one toe and is afterwards given a sword by Siva; Pattinathar's demon has ten heads and twenty arms slackened under the toe and, when he sings, receives the good sword.

Both make the dance a destruction: Tirumular's dance in the golden hall is the dissolution of the world; Pattinathar's drum splits the cosmos and his foot crushes the earth. Tirumular adds that the dance is bliss and wonder; Pattinathar that it grants boons.

The three thousand Brahmins of Tillai (Puliyur) appear in both as the Lord's worshippers: Arunagirinathar's three thousand worship daily by sacrifice; Pattinathar's bow together and know nothing but their duty. Pattinathar praises them for love where 884 set Brahmin rite at nothing.
audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 484 'எழில் புநன்மு வாயிர' looks corrupt (probably புலி மூவாயிர, Puliyur's three thousand).

note: The bangles that slip from the wrist announce the man's parting in both: the Kural's woman asks whether her slipping bangles do not already say the lord of the shore has left; Pattinathar's mothers search the street for the white bangles that fell from the girls wasted by the begging Lord.
897 sets the Lord's right foot on the neck of thunder-voiced Death as a mark of his form; 908 tells the story behind it, the Brahmin of Kadavur saved and Death crushed, and names the place.

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and escaped, so give while you can; Pattinathar says the Lord crushed Death so that the Brahmin of Kadavur might live. The conflict holds if the Markandeya story is taken as a claim that one man did escape; if the Naladiyar speaks of ordinary men and the verse of a miracle, they need not clash.

Both say Death can be leapt past: the Kural's one who has the power of austerity can; Pattinathar's Brahmin of Kadavur lived because the Lord crushed Death. The Kural credits tapas, Pattinathar the Lord's act for a devotee.

Tirumular makes the heart the temple and the body the shrine; Pattinathar lists a dozen shrines and then tells those with thinking hearts (நினைவார் தரு நெஞ்சினீர்) to come to Kachi. The thinking heart is the condition in both, but Pattinathar still sends it to a place, which Tirumular's verse makes unnecessary.

Both speak to the heart as a separate party in a parting: the Kural's woman's heart climbs at the thought of the man's return; Pattinathar's mother asks her faltering poor heart where the eloped girl now walks on the stony path. The love is a lover's in one and a mother's in the other.

In both the bangles know before the woman is told: in the Kural they register the lord of the shore's parting before her mind does; here they tighten at the mere news of the chariot, so that the slipping bangle of separation runs in reverse.

Both refuse the deferral of 'today, that day, some day': the Naladiyar puts Death behind the one who asks when, Pattinathar puts the god's leaving behind the one who says 'we will serve tomorrow'. The Naladiyar asks for virtue as far as one can; this verse asks for service without a day's gap.

Two Siddhar prefaces on mad reciting: Sivavakkiyar asks the learned to forgive the errors of one who recites like a madman; Pattinathar says the true servants will take even such babbling as Veda. The apology is the same; Pattinathar supplies the hearers who make the poor words good.

Arunagirinathar confesses he has no great poetry of devotion and that tattvas learned led only to argument; Pattinathar says words that do not shine with wisdom are Veda when they praise Ekambar. Both set the name praised above the poem's learning.

Both dress the cosmos on the god: Tirumular makes the sky the linga, the sea its bathing hall, the stars its garland and the directions Nandi's garment; Pattinathar makes the stars the garland, the sea the garment, the directions the shoulders and the earth the loins. Tirumular pictures a linga in worship; Pattinathar a body with breath, speech and eyes.

Tirumular says the Lord himself stands as the directions, the gods, body, life, tattvas, ocean and mountain; Pattinathar says the same thing member by member and adds, as Tirumular does in his last line, that he is also the one who works it, blinking the eyes that make and destroy.

Both make the sects' quarrel a fault of the sects and not a division in the god: Tirumular's six roads lead to one city and the quarrellers bark at a hill; Pattinathar's quarrellers each see their own colour in a crystal that has none. Neither verse ranks the roads.

The same crystal that takes the colour of what lies against it: in the Kural it is the face showing what is strongest in the heart; in Pattinathar it is the god showing each sect its own belief. The figure explains an appearance by its neighbour in both, but the Kural reads a man and Pattinathar excuses a god.

Tirumular's Lord comes as the many souls and, dwelling with them in form, is one with them and not one; Pattinathar's souls rise in him like waves in the sea, in him and yet apart. Both keep the Siddhanta double statement rather than resolve it.

Tirumular calls those who speak of the unspeakable mutes and says the Lord shows himself to thought grown still as water without waves; Pattinathar's list of self-cancelling predicates ends that only those who shrink their standing in words can know him. Both make the limit of speech the condition of knowing.

Two Siddhar boats: for Sivavakkiyar the body is the boat and the open water the end, so act while it lasts; for Pattinathar the body is the sea itself, with hair for foam and hunger for sharks, and the god's feet are the ship. The same figure carries opposite valuations of the body.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 961 has misprints: ஐவகைனெடுங்காற், உருகிய்வார்வப், தூம்ச்சோதிச்.

note: Tirumular's boat across the sea of deeds is austerity and virtue, made fruitful by the Lord; Pattinathar's ship across the sea of the body is the Lord's feet, with love as sail and restraint as rope. The sea is deeds in one and the body's own humours in the other.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:961 has misprints (உருகிய்வார்வப், தூம்ச்சோதிச்) as the marker notes.

note: Both take the body apart by the physician's categories: Arunagirinathar's bellows of bile bound by the three humours and the senses, Pattinathar's wind and bile joined with the five winds beating. Arunagirinathar asks for the end of such birth; Pattinathar makes the voyage across it the god's own act.

Both confess that their words are too poor for the god and that learning did not help: Arunagirinathar has no great poetry and learned tattvas only to argue; Pattinathar's harsh poor words cannot reach him, so he lays knowledge itself at the feet with everything else.

Tirumular says that to take the poison from the salt sea as nectar is the intent of the shining-throated Isa; Pattinathar hails him as the one who took poison as nectar (நஞ்சினை அமிர்தா நயந்தோய்). Both make the swallowing a disposition, not a rescue.
audit_text_issue: 2688's line 3 can be construed several ways.

note: Both make the five letters the container of the world: Tirumular says by them the Lord made the elements, the wombs of birth and the wide world; Sivavakkiyar says the cosmos and beyond, the three gods and the letters of Om are all held within them.

The same siddhi with the same proof: Tirumular sets the two breaths in the upper palate so that grey hair and wrinkles change and one becomes a child; Sivavakkiyar raises the breath from the channel to the skull so that the old become children and the body reddens. Both seal it with Nandi's or the Mother's authority.
audit_text_issue: Tm 805 line 3 ந்யாலம் is a misprint for ஞாலம்.

note: Both follow the body to the cremation ground and no further: Tirumular's town wails, burns the corpse, bathes and stops thinking of him; Sivavakkiyar's fine body stinks and is handed to the cremation keeper. Sivavakkiyar adds the jealous man ready to kill for a body that ends this way.

Tirumular says that even having recited, people are mutes who know nothing unless they join the beginning and the end; Sivavakkiyar asks the sastra-reciter whether the Veda will help when the death-sweat comes, and sets a moment's inner knowing against the whole scripture-bag.

Ghee within milk is in both the figure for the Lord present but unseen: Tirumular says the Stainless one is there as ghee in milk yet they do not desire that light; Sivavakkiyar says the Veda-reciters do not know the Lord within them as ghee hidden in milk.

Both say recitation of the Lord's letters removes what binds: Tirumular's SIVAYANAMA makes the three impurities cry out and leave; Sivavakkiyar's five-and-three mantra makes a hundred crore of the five great sins fly like cotton. Tirumular speaks of mala, Sivavakkiyar of sins, so the thing removed differs.

The Kural asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Sivavakkiyar says the Sama and four Vedas and all the sastras, recited in safety, leave one not knowing Siva. Both deny learning any worth apart from the Lord, though Sivavakkiyar's route is inward perception, not bowing.

Read as cipher, both describe one practice: Arunagirinathar asks that the breath be run from the root through ida, pingala and the middle way up the pillar; Sivavakkiyar says set aside the two conches and blow the one stream, and union follows. The Thiruppugazh names the channels; Sivavakkiyar codes them.

Both set one letter above the recited Vedas: Tirumular says what is ours lies in one letter of our Lord, and mastering it brings one to the far shore; Sivavakkiyar says that knowing the one letter among the five brings the Dancer's 'fear not'. Neither names the letter.

Tirumular says those who recite the first of the Dancer's letters stand as one in creed with him, and that is the sign for seeing the Dancer; Sivavakkiyar says the one who knows the one letter sees the Lord dance in the hall. Both make a single letter the condition of seeing the dance.

The Naladiyar says no one has leapt clear of Death and tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; Sivavakkiyar asks the builders of long houses with shut doors whether they mean to live, and shows them standing helpless when Death's sound comes. The Naladiyar draws the lesson of giving, Sivavakkiyar of holding to the feet.
audit_text_issue: Naladiyar 6 line 1 பிழைத்தெரிணஇக் is garbled

note: Both say use the body while it lasts: the Naladiyar tells those with a sturdy body to take the fruit it can yield before it departs like mist; Sivavakkiyar says make yourself firm while the boat lasts, for when it breaks there is no one left in the open.

Both price the body at death at nothing: Arunagirinathar's body, after the whole life from womb to pyre, is not worth a handful of ash; Sivavakkiyar's, when Yama's summons comes, will not fetch the price of a potsherd. Sivavakkiyar adds that sacrifice and household are counted among the same possessions.

Tirumular tells the devotee to seek through lands, towns and holy temples, sing 'Siva Peruman' and bow, and the Lord will then take the heart as his temple: outer chariyai leads to the inner one. Sivavakkiyar counts his own flowers, japa, libations and circlings of Siva temples and calls them done into the void (பாழிலே). On the reading that 990 dismisses the rites as waste rather than as a stage he outgrew, the two disagree about whether temple service leads anywhere.

Tirumular says the Lord is not in the mansion, hall, courtyard, temple or holy garb but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing; Sivavakkiyar says the jnanis who have found where the Lord dwells do not raise their hands to the god in a built temple. Both locate him away from the shrine; Tirumular names the condition (longing given up), Sivavakkiyar the result (no hands raised).

967 shows crores running and seeking the light mingled within until they wither and die; 992 names the error, that the lazy call the all-pervading Lord 'far' and run through town, country and forest, and gives the remedy, perceive him straight within and stand.

Both use one gold under many ornaments for the gods: Tirumular says the many gods appear many as ornaments do though they are gold, and makes the Mistress their cause; Sivavakkiyar says Mal and Isa are one gold in differing forms and that sectarian quarrel misses it. The image is the same, the conclusion drawn (Sakti as cause, or sects as error) differs.

Tirumular ranks the ways: those who know only bathing cannot join the Lord, and he is within the minds of those whose knowledge is clear. Sivavakkiyar tells the daily fire-kindlers and bathers that the fire and water are within them and only that knowing joins the light. Both keep the rite's elements and move them inside.

Both turn on the whispered ear-mantra: Tirumular calls the gods who do ear-mantras and lay out the oblation kitchen for their own gain a cruel gathered mantra; Sivavakkiyar calls the mantra muttered with the mouth covered a trappers' purse snapping shut. Tirumular's target is self-interest in the rite, Sivavakkiyar's the secrecy itself.

Both poets report the same event in the first person: Tirumular brought the bright reality in and made his heart its temple on earth, and swears it is truth, not falsehood; Sivavakkiyar says the Lord entered his heart and made it his temple, hidden like water in a coconut. Sivavakkiyar adds the consequence, that he no longer opens his mouth before the world.

Tirumular makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the tower gate and the soul the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar says temple and tanks are in the mind. Tirumular builds the inner temple as a full correspondence to the outer one; Sivavakkiyar asks what the outer one is at all.

Tirumular says that for those clear through and through the soul is the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar denies that Siva dwells in brick, black stone, the red lingam, copper or brass and says that self-knowledge is what makes the Lord's dance appear. Both move the linga from stone to the self.

The two verses share their last line, சுருக்கம் அற்ற சோதியைத் தொடர்ந்து கூடல் ஆகுமோ, and the same shape: an outer practice (fire and bathing in 994, Vedas and ash in 1001) set against an inner act (knowing fire and water within, speaking the truth with a melted heart) that alone reaches the light.

The Kural says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from the work they do; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the Paraiyar woman and the Brahmin woman differ in flesh, skin, bone or pleasure. The Kural still allows distinction by deed; Sivavakkiyar's bodily test allows none.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Sivavakkiyar says there is no mark of caste on flesh, skin or bone. The Naladiyar replaces caste with merit; Sivavakkiyar removes it and puts nothing in its place.

Tirumular says there is no need of purification for one who stands free of pollution (துடக்கு); Sivavakkiyar says Veda, mantra, worlds, seed, moon and light are all spittle, so purity has no ground anywhere. Tirumular sets purity aside for one who has passed beyond it; Sivavakkiyar denies it was ever coherent.

1008 asks what mind, thought, life, Sakti, Sambhu, release, root and root mantras are in the seedless seed; 1009 repeats the list with அற்று after each and names what stands where all of them are absent as Sivayam ripened in the seed. The question is answered by negating every term it asked about.
audit_text_issue: 1009 விலைந்ததே read as விளைந்ததே; 1008 இதினெனதென்று insecure

note: 993 says gold is one and the forms differ, and applies it to Vishnu and Siva; 1010 says ear-ring, bracelet, wire and anklet are one gold, and applies it to castes, with the five elements and the one womb-gate as the shared substance. The same figure does the work against sect and against caste.

Tirumular says that for those who set Nandi firmly in love there is no impurity, no pride, no caste and no qualities to take on; Sivavakkiyar asks what caste is when all bodies are the same water, the same five elements and the same gold. For Tirumular caste falls away at a stage of knowledge; for Sivavakkiyar it never had a nature.

The Kural says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking after sleep, a cycle that resumes; Sivavakkiyar says the dead are not born, as milk does not return to the udder or the fallen fruit to the tree, and denies it four times. On the plain reading of 1011 the two make incompatible claims about what follows death; on tradition's softer reading (not born into this body again) the conflict dissolves.

Tirumular's Siddhanta premise is that the soul is reborn until it rests in the Lord and birth is cut off (பிறப்பறுந்தானே); cutting birth is an attainment. Sivavakkiyar's plain statement that the dead are not born again makes rebirth not a bond to be cut but a thing that does not happen. The tension holds on the plain reading of இறந்தவர் பிறப்பதில்லை.

1013 ends with the impurity rolled into word-gurus (சொற்குருக்கள் ஆனதே) and 1014 opens with the same words, then extends the list: light-bodied gurus, true gurus, sat-gurus, gurus of deeds, puja and sastra are all the same clotted blood. The antadi chain crosses the tool's chapter boundary.

The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Sivavakkiyar says blinking at a rosary and counting places are nothing beside looking at one's own mind. Both set the inner change above the outward mark of the devotee.

Both place the moon on the left and the sun on the right: Tirumular as a breath practice, the sun's breath set on the left and the moon's on the right so the axle-pin holds a thousand years; Sivavakkiyar as the Lord's two eyes in a body mingled with the devotee's. On tradition's reading of 1017 the eyes are the two breaths, and the image is the same practice described as a form.

993 makes Vishnu and Siva one gold under two forms; 1018 makes them salt dissolved in water, one measure with no seam, and adds the penalty for dividing them, a hell entered for nothing. The second figure is the stronger: gold keeps its forms, dissolved salt has none.

Tirumular praises Siva as the One who ends the flawed birth of Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, placing Vishnu among the born below the Lord; Sivavakkiyar says the lord of Tillai and the lord of Arangam are the same he, and curses those who rank one above the other. On the reading that Sivavakkiyar's 'he' is Siva at both shrines, the two verses disagree about Vishnu's standing; if his 'he' is a Supreme beyond both names, Tirumular's hierarchy is not contradicted.

978 says those who recite the four Vedas do not know the foot of knowledge; 1021 tells its hearers to perceive the fitting books within themselves and sing. The attack is on recitation without inward perception, not on books as such, and 1021 states the condition under which they are allowed.
audit_text_issue: 1021 line 3 (செற்றமாவை யுள்ளரைச் செருக்கறுத்து) is hard, but line 1 carries the link.

note: 980 names an unreachable mantra that is five and three and promises that reciting it burns off the five great sins; 1022 repeats the five and three become one letter and names it, ராம. Read with 974, the two verses make the ராம verses part of the mantra argument rather than a Vaishnava intrusion.

Tirumular assigns the letters: A is the soul, U the supreme, MA the impurity, SI is Siva, VA the form, YA the soul; Sivavakkiyar asks whether U arose within A and whether A and U could stand without SI, and tells the yogis to explain. The question presupposes a scheme like Tirumular's and probes how its letters generate one another.
audit_text_issue: 1023 lines 1 and 2 as printed ask the same thing twice (அவ்வு / உவ்வு), likely a copying slip.

note: Both run the நீ catalogue, earth, sky, number and letter in 972, virtue, cosmos, strength, sleep and awareness in 1024, and both end at the feet; 972 asks to reach them, 1024 asks them to stay even when the poet forgets.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart and that those who do not bathe in them wander over hollow and height; Sivavakkiyar asks the seekers of holy waters where the bathing is, answers that it is within, and names the water as the five letters. Sivavakkiyar makes the mantra itself the tirtha; Tirumular leaves the inner waters unnamed.

Both have a door at the palate that opens: Tirumular says if the two breaths are set in the upper palate there is no Death and the door opens; Sivavakkiyar says open the hanging gate and look, and maya leaves and the light appears. Tirumular's result is a renewed body, Sivavakkiyar's the light, but on tradition's reading the gate is the same place.

1031 says that opening the hanging gate makes maya leave and the light appear; 1032 repeats the gate in every line, calls it the whirling gate, and says the one who opens it becomes the truth that was inside. Vision in one verse becomes identity in the next.

The two verses make the same promise under the same oath: 968 raises the breath from the channel to the skull and the old become children; 1033 holds the light risen in the root channel for four nazhigai and one lives as a child and becomes Brahman. Both close on the poison-eater's and the Mother's feet or oath.

Arunagirinathar asks that the breath run from the root up the pillar through the six centres to the Supreme; Sivavakkiyar says the light sprung in the root channel, held within, makes one a child and Brahman. Both start at the root (மூலம்) and rise; the Thiruppugazh ends at the dancing foot, Sivavakkiyar at a renewed body.
audit_text_issue: 188 நாலங்குலம் and the சிகாரம் line are obscure

note: Tirumular says the Lord stands as the food one eats and the medicine, and has become the five letters; Sivavakkiyar tells the hearer to worship the five letters before death and not to lose footing by taking them as medicine. Both put mantra and medicine side by side; whether 1034 affirms or warns against the equation depends on the reading of மருந்தெனப் பதம்கெடீர்.

Tirumular says the fifty letters are all the Vedas and Agamas and that, once known, the fifty become the five letters; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the fifty-one letters are not held in one letter and says the mantra and the four Vedas sprouted from the root five letters. The same reduction, fifty to five to one, in both.

Tirumular says the ground at the root is நமசிவாய and that spoken it becomes வாசி, the yoga of the breath; Sivavakkiyar says the five letters Sivaya are the means that calls back the breath gone out through the doorless gate. Both bind the five letters to the breath, Tirumular by the word வாசி, Sivavakkiyar by the claim.
audit_text_issue: 890 obscure throughout; தராதலம் repeated four times with no fixable sense

note: Both verses define the Lord by denial: 973 not Hari, not Brahma, not great, not small, beyond turiya; 1037 not form, not space, not great, not small, not even speech, and not bound to the gate. 1037 adds the poet's own cipher, the வாசல், to what the Lord is not.

Tirumular states the Siddhanta position that the soul, the Lord and the bond are each beginningless (அனாதி); Sivavakkiyar runs the same word down to the senses, the disputing books and Sadasiva and demands that the yogis say which of them it fits. The question does not deny Tirumular's claim but presses on what the word is doing when it is given to everything.

Both set curd at hand against a fool who goes elsewhere: Tirumular's ritualist eats bitter things while ghee, milk and curd stand by; Sivavakkiyar's reciter leaves the curd in the pot and searches the town for butter. In both the dairy at home is the knowledge already within.

Tirumular's seekers lose it in the sea and look in a pond, not knowing he has entered the body; Sivavakkiyar's reciters look in the town for what is in the hanging pot. Both say the search is misplaced, not that it is too weak.

The potter's pot against the body: Tirumular says people keep a broken pot's shards but not the broken body for a moment; Sivavakkiyar grades the pots, clay restacked, bronze treasured, the body thrown out as stinking.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 158 line 1 (வளத்திடை முற்றத்தோர்) is hard to construe but does not affect the image.

note: Both run wife, kin and gathered wealth into the burning ground: Arunagiri's body falls like a broken pot and is left at the pyre; Sivavakkiyar's wealth is the very firewood that burns it, and the kin cannot follow Death's summons.

The Kural's life flies off like a bird leaving its shell; Sivavakkiyar's life slips out and the body lies there. Both make the parting sudden and the body the thing left behind; Sivavakkiyar adds that people have watched it and learned nothing.

Tirumular's knower has no impurity, no caste and 'no good to seek'; Sivavakkiyar's heart that has reached knowledge has 'nothing good' left in it, like a burnt forest. Both put the knower past the pursuit of good, though Sivavakkiyar's line also admits the darker reading that the fire leaves nothing.

Both make the body the Lord's shrine: Tirumular names heart as temple, flesh as shrine, mouth as tower gate and soul as the linga; Sivavakkiyar makes Tillai's hall the body built of the five, with the nine gates as its doors.
audit_text_issue: 1051 line 3 (கருவிநாதம் உண்டுபோய்க் கழன்றவாசல்) is syntactically loose; the marker flagged the verse.

note: For both the temple within is seen by the breath: Tirumular's breath rising swiftly lights the dark temple like a gem lamp; Sivavakkiyar's breath settled near the heart lets one see the devotees' temple in the eight directions.

Tirumular says people cling to body after body without knowing the bond between body and life; Sivavakkiyar makes that bond a riddle, which took which, and answers that the life does not die with the body.

Both parcel the Lord's work out by letters: Tirumular's one, two and three letters make the world, the pair and the light, and 'the great letter' brings delusion; Sivavakkiyar gives A the worlds, U the form and M the world's delusion. In both a letter is charged with maya.

Both promise escape from death through breath: Tirumular's yogi who holds prana and apana together and stays still has no Yama; Sivavakkiyar's eater of the mantra, which he says is the rising breath, has no death.
audit_text_issue: 1056 line 2 மறத்தில்ஊறல் unclear

note: Tirumular says chant சிவாயநம in the right way and no birth follows; Sivavakkiyar says those who merely 'eat' mantras are deluded, since a mantra is the breath and not the sound. He does not reject the five letters (1045, 1059), so this limits what chanting is, rather than contradicting it.
audit_text_issue: 1056 line 2 மறத்தில் ஊறல் is unclear.

note: Lightning within lightning: in 1057 it shows that the Lord and the self are one flash, so Tamil cannot say it; in 1088 the lightning rises, spreads and subsides to show the Lord in the self subsiding into the self, which the eye cannot see as it cannot see itself.

The banyan and its seed: the Naladiyar's tiny seed grows a vast shade to show that a small virtue in worthy hands spreads wide; Sivavakkiyar's banyan is folded back into its seed to show that the whole is already within the self. The same tree, growing outward in one and inward in the other.

Both map the five letters onto the body. Tirumular puts NA at the feet, MA at the navel, SI and VA at the shoulders and YA as the light above; Sivavakkiyar puts NA at the two legs, MA at the belly, SI at the shoulders, VA at the mouth and YA at the two eyes. The scheme is shared, the placements differ at VA and YA.
audit_text_issue: 941 line 3 சீயுரு தோள்வவ்வாய் is unclear in word division.

note: Both describe the coiled serpent of three turns in the body as the thing to be worked: Tirumular's serpent of three coils with the yantra and the twelve finger-breadths keeps the body from perishing; Sivavakkiyar's sleeper of three rings is roused as sound through the root channel to the crown.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 728 is technical throughout; நான்றவிம் is doubtful.

note: The two verses share the closing cry என்னமாயம் ஈசனே. 1043 asks it of what people do with the fallen body; 1076 of the body's growth from pollen and flower and the fall of the senses. Together they frame birth and death as one maya.

1064 reworks 1063 line by line: the letter in the three mandalas becomes three threes the gods seek, the mantra of mother and father gains the moving nada, and the one letter in which there is nowhere else to speak becomes the mandala in which it appears.

Both end with the Lord coming to speak once the human speaker falls silent or recites the one letter: 1067 contains the five senses in one letter and keeps silent; 1104 dismisses a hundred crore Agamas and recites the single rising letter.
audit_text_issue: 1067 line 2 அலைந்தருள் செய்கிறார் reads oddly; sense of the line insecure

note: Tirumular's five senses draw in like a tortoise when the silent letter meets the spoken one, and reaching Om gain inner light; Sivavakkiyar's five of desire are contained in one letter and silence, and the Lord speaks. In both the gathering of the senses follows the letter rather than effort.
audit_text_issue: 2158 line 1 begins with a stray 'Y' before ஊமை

note: Two creatures that become by thought: the turtle whose eggs hatch on the shore by her brooding from the sea (1062) and the worm in the wasp's clay nest that becomes a wasp by brooding (1070). 1062 applies it to contemplating the light within; 1070 to becoming what one thinks.

Tirumular's two breaths set in the upper palate open the door and end death; Sivavakkiyar's good gate opened and passed leads to the boundary gate and no more birth. Both set the body's upper opening against the nine ordinary ones.
audit_text_issue: 805 line 3 ந்யாலம் is a misprint for ஞாலம்.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from deeds; Sivavakkiyar says the one origin became the differences of caste and every being. Both deny that caste is primordial, the Kural by pointing to work and Sivavakkiyar to the one source.
The two verses share the cry என்னமாயம் ஈசனே: 1043 on the body thrown out at death, 1076 on the body's growth from pollen and the senses' fall. Birth and death are framed as one maya.

1078 asks how one can live with men who do not bow daily to the Lord; 1093 laughs at those who do rites to stone and asks whether gods can be stone. Read together, the daily bowing 1078 demands is to the Lord who stands as guard within (1093), not to the image.

Tirumular's Siddhanta formula is 'neither one nor two nor nothing, yet one'; Sivavakkiyar's answer to the deniers is 'neither not nor a thing, the two joined'. Both refuse the void and refuse plain duality in the same breath.

1054 asks whether body took life or life took body, and answers that the life does not die; 1083 takes the life beyond the body into its dealings with maya, where life and maya kill and eat one another, so that the survival 1054 asserts is not yet release.
The pupil in the eye: in 1042 the gods see by it while claiming 'mine' and 'yours'; in 1085 the Lord stands as the pin in the eye, the truth the gods cannot know, and dwells within once birth is cut.
1074's good gate and gate of knowledge, passed through to the boundary gate, is 1086's upper gate opened to the light beyond the sky. Both end in no more birth or no more maya.

Both promise childhood through breath: Tirumular's yogi with the breaths set in the palate sees grey hair and wrinkles change and becomes a child; Sivavakkiyar's knower of the root breath can stay a child long and become the Supreme.

Pattirakiriyar's pulambal asks when he will know, within himself, the one who stands within him, with lightning that rises and subsides into the sky; Sivavakkiyar states it: the Lord within subsides within and is all he has known. The same couplet, a plea in one and a claim in the other.
1071 has Siva at Kasi teaching the name of Rama; 1095 asks whether there can be two gods, ours and yours. The Rama verses put the second claim into practice.

Tirumular turns the one who blazes at the root opening upward with the breath and burns Death in the yoga of fire; Sivavakkiyar opens the fire-chamber in the pit that takes no embryo and can then stay on earth and push the worlds aside. Both read the fire at the root as the way past death.

Both make the puja inward: Tirumular's heart is the temple, the soul the linga and the senses the lamps; Sivavakkiyar's elements are the Vedas, water the bath and the feet the linga. In both the rite is kept and its objects replaced.

Tirumular says curd, ghee, copper, fire, brick, bilva or gold, any one of them clearly known, can be the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar asks whether gods can be stone and can only laugh. The conflict holds if Tirumular means the material object is to be worshipped as Siva; if தெளிவுறக் கண்டு means that knowing makes any thing the linga, Sivavakkiyar's Lord 'mingled within you' is not far from it.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1720 line 4 (தென்தியங்கு ஒன்றை) is unclear.

note: Tirumular says the Lord is a cow of stone to those who stand apart without knowing him; Sivavakkiyar says stone cannot be god at all and the Lord is the guard within. Tirumular's stone is what the Lord becomes for the unknowing; Sivavakkiyar's is what the knowing should never have mistaken.

Tirumular: those who know only bathing cannot join him, he is within the minds of those whose knowledge is clear. Sivavakkiyar: the frog that lives in the water gains nothing, think of the root with the inner eye. Both set inner thought against the bath and keep the bath's goal.

Tirumular: kin is one and God is one, and there is no refuge outside one's own mind; Sivavakkiyar: there are not two gods, ours and yours, since the first form is one here and there. Both make the oneness of God a reproach to sect.

The Naladiyar says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are only words, and austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Sivavakkiyar asks 'what good castes?' and demands to be told how the Brahmins came to be. Both empty the word; the Naladiyar refills it with conduct, Sivavakkiyar with blood.

Tirumular assigns the linga's material by varna, crystal for Brahmins, gold for kings, komalam for Vaishyas, bana stone for Shudras; Sivavakkiyar says every caste is the same monthly blood grown into a body and asks what good castes there are. The conflict holds if Tirumular's rule treats varna as a real difference in worship; if it only records custom without ranking it, as its own text allows, the two can stand together.

1075 lists caste among the forms the one origin took; 1100 gives the mechanism, the oozing pollution that grows into the good castes, and refuses to let the life be spoken of apart from the blood it settled in.

The Kural says that giving up craving at once yields a nature that does not shift; Sivavakkiyar says that once the wanting is renounced the thing wanted is quickly seen. Both make the gain immediate on the dropping of the want, though the Kural's gain is a state and Sivavakkiyar's is a sight.

Tirumular says recitation is not needed once the Life of life has come within; Sivavakkiyar says Vedas, Agamas and true books ended as dust once he knew the Lord. Both put scripture before knowledge in time and after it in worth.

Tirumular's fifty letters are all the Vedas and Agamas and, once known, become the five; Sivavakkiyar's hundred crore Agamas and mantras are useless beside the one letter within. Both compress scripture into a letter, Tirumular to five and Sivavakkiyar to one.

Tirumular says the twenty thousand eight hundred kinds of karma, mantra and yoga only tire the body and come down to four; Sivavakkiyar says a hundred crore Agamas recited for a hundred crore days are no use beside one letter. The reduction is the same gesture at a different number.

1094 mocks the dawn-and-dusk bathers; 1105 turns their காலைமாலை into காலன், Death that is the alternation of morning and evening, and says settling in thought beyond both ends him. The rite's hours become the thing to escape.

Tirumular's yogi seeks the Lady dancing where there is neither night nor day and becomes a child that age does not touch; Sivavakkiyar's practitioner, free of morning and evening and settled in thought, has no Death. Both place the deathless state outside the alternation of day and night.

1106 gives the counts of mandalas and says the Lord dances in the mandala of the dance; 1107 asks where in the eight he stands and answers with places in the body, the root channel at the legs, the eyes, the closed directions, the upper two.

1103 says scripture ended as dust once the Lord was known; 1110 goes further back and says that at the beginning there were no four Vedas at all, only light and no word. Scripture is late in time as well as spent in use.

Tirumular says none but those who eat having put flesh away can reach the Lord's feet, whatever their offerings; Sivavakkiyar says calling flesh impure is folly since the Lord sprouted in flesh and never stood apart from it. The conflict holds if 1111 defends eating flesh, as 1112's address to Saivas suggests; if it only denies that flesh is apart from God, Tirumular's rule of abstention is untouched.

The Kural says the standing of life lies in not eating flesh, and hell will not release the eater; Sivavakkiyar says the Saiva who rejects flesh grew on milk made of blood and is flesh himself, so the rejection is folly. The conflict holds if 1112 is a defence of eating; the Kural's ground is the killed creature and Sivavakkiyar's is the eater's own body, so each leaves the other's reason unanswered.
audit_text_issue: 1112 line 3 மதிரமாக விட்டதேது is unclear.

note: 1096 turns the rule of pollution on its keepers, who find impurity in seclusion, birth and the bath alike; 1113 turns the rule of leavings on them, since the purifying hand and water are themselves leavings. The same move on two rules.
audit_text_issue: 1113 உண்டகல்லை and 1096 lines 1 and 3 are insecure

note: 1098 asks how the Veda-reciting Brahmins came to be, since every body grew when the monthly blood stopped; 1111 asks how the Lord could stand apart from flesh. One argument, from the body's origin, applied to caste and to the horror of flesh.

1172 repeats 1114 almost word for word, replacing the recited books and learning of line 1 with the cherished mantras and the Agamas (ஆதரித்த மந்திரம் அமைந்த ஆகமங்களும்). Together the two stanzas put secular learning and sacred scripture under the same test: both vanish in sleep.

Both are fables of creatures busy inside an enclosure while death waits: the Naladiyar's turtle plays in the pot with the fire lit beneath, Sivavakkiyar's cocks and chicks quarrel in the guarded coop until the old jackal gets in. The Naladiyar names its moral (Death waits his moment); Sivavakkiyar leaves the coop and jackal unexplained.
audit_text_issue: 1116 கூவமான் obscure, possibly corrupt

note: Both use tarnish on metal for the covering over the self. In 1118 verdigris on copper is burnt off by heating until the light of the hall shows; in 1145 the tarnish is cut from red gold and the god within is known that day. The metal changes from copper to gold, and the means from heating to cutting.
audit_text_issue: 1118 line 2 அம்பினில் எழுதொணாத unclear

note: Kural 269 says leaping past Death becomes possible for those with the power of austerity (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). 1119 says Death who came hunting is bewildered and goes for those who can see within themselves (தேடிவந்த காலனும் திகைத்திருந்து போய்விடும்). Both make a discipline, not a god's favour, the thing that turns Death away; the Kural's is tapas, Sivavakkiyar's inward seeing.

Both make the pair of deeds the knot to be undone before release. Tirumular has the two deeds balance (இருவினை ஒப்பு) so that grace can enter and impurity leave; Sivavakkiyar asks for the knot of the two quarrelling deeds to be cut (இருவினைப் பிணக்கறுக்க) so that the unquarrelling joy can be had. One word is balance, the other cutting, but the end is the same.
audit_text_issue: 2262 line 1 reads இருவிடை; the link relies on emending to இருவினை

note: Tirumular says those without truth, knowledge, restraint and devotion are not Brahmins, whatever they are called. Sivavakkiyar shows the outward rule failing from the other side: the Brahmin who shuns fish bathes in fish-water and wears deer-hide. Both deny that purity of diet and emblem makes the Brahmin; Tirumular supplies the inner standard, Sivavakkiyar only the exposure.
