Kural 259 ranks not killing one creature above pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). 1122 says the sacrifice the Brahmins perform is itself goat-flesh (ஆட்டிறைச்சி அல்லவோ யாகம்). The Kural compares merits and leaves the rite standing; Sivavakkiyar calls the rite killing and the priests' meat-rule a lie.

Tirumular says he once held the body a thing of shame, then saw the true substance within it and now cherishes it as the Highest's temple. Sivavakkiyar says the Lord entered the true inner self as water enters a tender coconut and took the body as his temple (கோயில் கொண்டபின்). Both make the body the temple by the Lord's dwelling; Sivavakkiyar adds silence toward the world as the consequence.

Tirumanthiram 975 assigns the five letters: SI is Siva, VA the form, YA the soul, and MA impurity. 1125 turns the assignment into a path: pass beyond NA and MA, rest on SI, find VA and YA within it as the teaching of wisdom, and the Shakti pierces the crown. What is a table of meanings in Tirumular becomes an order of ascent in Sivavakkiyar.
audit_text_issue: 1125 நாடொணாத சியின்மேல் is awkward; the marker flagged the verse uncertain

note: Tirumanthiram 2236 states as doctrine that the soul is beginningless and bound by five impurities that came without beginning (அனாதியே). 1126 asks the same of letter, soul, elements, books and guru (அனாதியோ?) and gives no answer. Sivavakkiyar turns what Tirumular asserts into open questions, and sets scripture and guru among the things questioned.

Both rank inner lamps. Tirumular's root lamp, seen lamp and higher lamp (மேலை விளக்கு) lead to release; Sivavakkiyar's blue lamp at the brow is held until, above the inner light, a higher light (உள்ஒளிக்கு மேல்ஒளி) is seen. In both the first light seen is not the last.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 1128 has misprints: உற்றிருநது (உற்றிருந்து), அரிந்தவன் (அறிந்தவன்).

note: Tirumanthiram 510 says those who know only bathing cannot join the Lord, who is within the minds of those whose knowledge is clear. 1129 says scooping water and pouring it into water is done in vain, and that thought on the root and seed reaches Siva's state. Both set the water rite below inner knowing; Sivavakkiyar's tone is mockery, Tirumular's a ranking.

1131 asks where body, breath and desire stood before conception, form and grace; 1132 answers, body in fire and desire in wind, with the same refrain that Sivayam cuts the doubt. Read together they show the refrain working as the answer to any question, since 1131 already closes with it before the answer is given.
audit_text_issue: 1132 line 2 repeats காயம் and தேயு from line 1 where 1131 asked about உயிர்ப்பு; probably a copyist's doubling, so the breath's answer is lost.

note: Tirumular says those who did evil to the ascetics who taught the one-syllable mantra will be born as outcaste dogs and outcastes in a hundred forms. Sivavakkiyar says the sectarians who stoned the jnani in the street reaped sin (பாதகங்கள் ஆகவே பலித்ததே). Both make abuse of the knower a sin that returns on the abuser; Tirumular names the return as low birth, which is the very slur Sivavakkiyar's stanza puts in the abusers' mouths.
audit_text_issue: 1133 line 2 (கூதரைப் பறைச்சிமக்கள்) is hard to construe; the stoning and its result are clear.

note: Tirumanthiram 965 says the fifty letters are all the Vedas and Agamas, and once known they go and become the five letters. 1137 says what rose as sheath, pierced the body and was born as the land is the five letters, while the fifty-one letters stand filling the vessel. Both rank the whole alphabet of mantra below the five syllables; Sivavakkiyar counts fifty-one where Tirumular counts fifty.
audit_text_issue: 1137 ஈசனார் அருந்திட and ஆசயம் are doubtful.

note: 1170 repeats 1138 with its middle changed: the ten letters become ajapa's three letters, the swelling lotus becomes conch and discus and all the sky, and the heart of those who join becomes the yogis who took a share and the five supreme gates. The frame (the body-linga's pedestal, the lion-roar, nothing but Sivayam) is the same, so the variable middle shows what the poet counted as interchangeable.

Both count the body's gates in cipher. Tirumanthiram 457 has eight that go out, eighteen that come in and nine gates, with the serpent and four horses; 1142 has five sets of eight gates and shapes that the deluded circle. Neither count is explained in its stanza, and the two do not match, which shows the cipher was not a fixed code even between parent and child text.
audit_text_issue: Both flagged uncertain; 457 recurs as 2926 with a different line.

note: Tirumanthiram 669 says the fire at the root of the central channel drives the sun and lets the moon drink, and the siddhis follow. 1143 has the yogi kindle the root fire (மூல அங்கி) with the breath so that the honey's chamber opens and the moons enter the staff. The same sequence of root fire, breath and nectar is the mark of the good yogi in both; Tirumular ends in powers, Sivavakkiyar in a 'measure taken in the flesh'.

Tirumanthiram 2962 says 'see, there is one God for the world', and tastes the fruit நமசிவாய. 1145 says one and only one, the whole world is one, and ends in the refrain சிவாயம். Both tie the oneness to the five-letter mantra; Sivavakkiyar adds that the one is found by cleaning the self like gold.
audit_text_issue: 1145 line 4 அரிந்ததே is probably a misprint for அறிந்ததே.

note: Tirumanthiram 214 says that when steadfast Brahmins pour the oblation, sky and earth, the quarters, the gods and great wealth all flourish: the homa sustains the world. 1146 says the homa pit (ஓமகுண்டம்), with Vedas, shastras and books, is fierce babble that came to nothing once the Lord was known. The conflict holds on the plain reading of each; it softens only if 1146 means the rite is empty for the knower alone and 214 speaks of the land at large.

Kural 34 says that to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர). 1146 calls installed images, homa, Vedas and bound books fierce babbling (கடும்பிதற்று) that ended as nothing when the Lord was known. Both dismiss outward religion as noise; the Kural's standard is a clean mind, Sivavakkiyar's a knowing of the Lord.

Tirumanthiram 2614 says he is not in the mansion, the hall, the courtyard, the temple or the holy garb, but in the hidden place in the heart of those who have given up longing. 1148 asks what temple or palli is, and says the Lord is seen in the shrine of the body by one who bows in the shrine of wisdom. Both deny the Lord to the building and give him to the inner person; Sivavakkiyar names the mosque or Jain shrine alongside the temple.

1148 says the Lord is seen in the shrine of the body (காயமான பள்ளி) when one bows in the shrine of wisdom. 1163 builds that shrine item by item: mind as flower and water, heart as the temple, breath as the linga, the five senses as incense and lamp, and no fixed hours. The second stanza furnishes what the first only named.

Both turn on ஊத வல்லீரேல், 'if you can blow'. 1149 lists metals by number and promises gold of the eighth touch; 1157 names the bellows, the smith and the golden light and promises a pillar of flame and a dancing light with 'you' left beside it. Read together, the alchemy of 1149 is given its yogic sense in 1157: the blowing is breath, the gold is light.
audit_text_issue: 1149's counts (six, four, three, two, one) are unexplained

note: Tirumanthiram 1611 says that for those to whom silence has come, release comes and the powers stand before them. 1150 says silent-wisdom yogis whose inner dirt is uncut stay dirty even in the forest, and only those who have cut it have cut off birth. Sivavakkiyar grants silence its name but denies that it does anything by itself; the mind's dirt, not the vow, decides.
audit_text_issue: 1150 line 3 மவினஞான is a misprint for மவுனஞான.

note: Tirumanthiram 1437 defines the attainment of Siddhanta as being neither one nor two nor nothing, yet one, and leaving the sects and the formless. 1151 denies form, light, scent, size and even the speaking breath, and asks who can see the rare straightness that stands as one. Both reach the one by denials, and both deny even the categories a devotee would hold on to (form, light).

Kural 1 makes the letter A the first of all letters as the Lord is the first of the world. 1152 begins with the one letter within which the whole world rose (ஓரெழுத்து உலகெலாம் உதித்த அட்சரம்). Both ground the world in a first letter; the Kural uses it as a comparison, Sivavakkiyar as the first rung of a mantra ladder that ends in his own refrain.

Tirumanthiram 966 says that by the five letters the Lord made the five elements, the wombs of birth and the world, and by them stands seated. 1153 says the root bindu and nada became the five elements and the five letters and stood pervading all. Both make the five syllables and the five elements two forms of one making; Sivavakkiyar names bindu and nada as the source where Tirumular names the Lord.

Tirumanthiram 230 asks whether thread and tuft are Brahman, answers that the thread is cotton and the tuft hair, and gives the true thread as Vedanta and the true tuft as knowledge. 1156 asks whether loincloth, thread and tuft were born with the Brahmin, and whether the Vedas rose in his mind at birth. Both strip the emblems of any natural standing; Tirumular keeps them as signs of something inner, Sivavakkiyar offers no replacement.

Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns. 1156 says the loincloth, thread and tuft did not come with birth, so they are not what a Brahmin is. Both deny that outward marks make the religious man; the Kural speaks of the ascetic's hair, Sivavakkiyar of the Brahmin's thread, and the Kural supplies a conduct test where Sivavakkiyar supplies none.

Tirumanthiram 820 says that if the breath rises swiftly inside the body, the temple daubed with black is lit with a gem lamp. 1157 says that if one blows the bellows with a right mind, the great pillar blazes and spreads, and only the dancing light and 'you' remain. In both the rising breath lights the dark body; Tirumular's figure is a lamp in a temple, Sivavakkiyar's a smith's fire.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 820 line 1 (பையினி நுள்ளே படிக்கத வொன்றிடின்) is obscure; the link rests only on lines 3-4.

note: Tirumanthiram 1837 says those who strew great flowers and cry 'our Lord's red feet' never come to know the holy one. 1158 says those who spread out heaps of copper and throw flowers at it, in guise and with incense, are like butchers sharing out a goat, and asks what worship that is. Both deny that flower-puja reaches the Lord; Sivavakkiyar adds the butcher's comparison and the collected copper, making the rite trade as well as show.

Tirumanthiram 1852 says worship offered where moon and sun shine goes to the asuras, and worship where they do not shine is the great worship of Nandi. 1160 says those who melt the line beyond sun and moon into the one letter in the void are not born again. Both place the goal beyond the sun and moon, which yogic tradition takes as the two side channels; Tirumular speaks of worship, Sivavakkiyar of the end of birth.

Tirumanthiram 890 says the ground at the root is the heat and is நமசிவாய, and the yoga of that ground is the breath. 1162 places the uttered mantra in the chamber of the muladhara, at the seat of seed and blood, and says it is truly Sivayam. Both make the lowest centre the place where the five letters sound; Sivavakkiyar names the generative fluids there outright where Tirumular speaks of heat.

Tirumanthiram 1823 makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine, the mouth the tower gate, the soul the linga and the five thieving senses the bright lamps. 1163 makes the mind flower and water, the heart the temple, the breath the linga and the five senses incense and lamp. The match is close enough to be a borrowing; Sivavakkiyar changes the linga from soul to breath and adds that the Dancer keeps no hours.

Tirumanthiram 234 says the land where Brahmins live does not decline and its king prospers because they make the oblation at dusk and dawn (அந்தி சந்தி). 1163 says the dancing Lord has no dusk and dawn (அந்தி சந்தி இல்லையே). The conflict holds if 1163 denies that timed rites have any standing; it dissolves if it means only that the inner worship it describes is continuous, leaving outer rites to others.

Tirumanthiram 979 says SIVAYA joined becomes the soul's enjoyment and knowledge, grace settles in the clarified soul, and becoming that Siva is release. 1165 says that clarified (தெளிந்து) in the five letters Sivayam one may become a god, rule the sky and grasp the truth. Both make clarity in the five letters the way, and both rank the truth or the Siva-state above what else the mantra gives.

Both make the body a clay pot. The Naladiyar's pot seeps filth from nine openings and only a fool calls it a woman; Sivavakkiyar's false pot (பொய்க்குடம்) tosses on the water when it holds only the five, and sits content when it has scooped up Siva. The same vessel is a cause for disgust in one and, filled rightly, a seat of delight in the other.

Tirumanthiram 1531 calls the Lord the thief-chief who enters and leaves the hollow hut of the body (கள்ளத் தலைவன்). 1167 ends by telling the hearer to bind tight the thief who knows the theft (களவறிந்த கள்வன்). If Sivavakkiyar's thief is the Lord, the stanza asks for what Tirumular's laments the lack of: holding the one who comes and goes. If it is the mind, the image is the same and the thief different.

Tirumanthiram 2204 ends its states of deep sleep with turiya as a void beyond words (வாக்கிறந்த பாழ்). 1168 describes the truth of the blissful nature where speech has died and mind has died (சொல்லிறந்த மனமிறந்த). Both place the goal past speech and mind; Sivavakkiyar adds that even the inner Brahman dies there, and that night and day, the states themselves, are gone.
audit_text_issue: 1168 line 4 சொல்லியாற is obscure, perhaps corrupt.

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew, skin and flesh and asks which part is the woman. 1169 lists what ten months of the womb's impurity became, two hands, two feet, two eyes, a body of sound, taste and smell, and says the 'pure' body is that impurity. Both take the body apart to deny it worth; the Naladiyar's aim is desire for a woman, Sivavakkiyar's pride in one's own body and birth.

Tirumanthiram 934 says Nandi is seated by the five letters and within the five letters (அஞ்செழுத்துள்ளே அமர்ந்திருந்தானே), making mantra, diagram and Lord one. 1171 says the thing itself is not the five letters nor the three (அஞ்செழுத்தும் மூன்றெழுத்தும் அல்ல காணும் அப்பொருள்). The conflict holds if 934's 'within' means identity, as its circling of the word suggests; it dissolves if 934 means only that the Lord dwells in the mantra, which 1171 also allows by pressing the five into the heart.

Both stanzas look behind the five letters. 1171 says the thing is not the five nor the three, and that knowing 'that letter' colours the five; 1182 asks what stands as the first of the five, what the heart's letter is, and what the sword of the five letters cuts. One answers with a hidden letter, the other leaves the questions open, but both refuse to let the mantra be the end.

Tirumanthiram 2987 says that reciting the Lord's thousand names holds one within a thousand protections. 1174 says the name Rama in the mouth of the spiteful comes as disease and blockage, and only in the mouth of the loving stays settled. Sivavakkiyar makes the effect of the name depend on the heart that says it; Tirumular's promise has no such condition.
audit_text_issue: 1174 line 3 நோய் அடைப்பதாம் is ambiguous (blocks disease / comes as blockage).

note: Both open with the water rite: 1129 'you scoop water and pour it into water', 1175 'what is the water you scooped and poured?'. 1129 goes on to offer thought on the root and seed as what reaches Siva; 1175 only widens the mockery to the kneaded ball, the muttering, the guise and the shut eyes, and calls the performers gurus. The second stanza is the first without its positive half.

Kural 274 likens the man who hides in austerity and does what is not austerity to a hunter in a bush snaring birds. 1175 asks what the false guise (கள்ள வேடம்) and the shut eyes are for, and calls the mumblers fools and then gurus. Both treat religious show as a hunter's cover; the Kural says what the hunter takes, Sivavakkiyar only exposes the bush.

Thiruppugazh 520 traces the poet's life from a drop like dew in the womb (பனித்துளி), growing to a doll of nine gates. 1176 says the seed set in the mother's womb becomes a drop like dew (பனித்துளி போலாகுமே) and what is born of it is impurity. The same dewdrop opens both accounts of the body; Arunagiri's ends in a plea for the feet, Sivavakkiyar's in a rebuke to the proud.
audit_text_issue: 1176 line 3 (உன்னிதொக் குளழலும்) is garbled; the dewdrop line is clean.

note: Kural 278 says many bathe as though distinguished and go about concealed, with impurity in their minds (மனத்தது மாசாக). 1177 addresses those who bathe daily to remove dirt whose dirt is never removed, and asks where the dirt was. Both say water misses the dirt that matters; the Kural reports it of hypocrites, Sivavakkiyar tells the bathers where to cut.

Kural 298 divides purity: outer purity comes by water, inner purity is seen through truth. 1177 says daily bathing leaves the dirt and asks where the dirt was, so that it can be cut there. Sivavakkiyar's 'where' is the Kural's 'inner'; the Kural grants water its outer purity, Sivavakkiyar grants it nothing.

Kural 357 says that if the mind ponders and knows with certainty what is, one need not think again of birth. 1178 tells those lost in recited books to ask for themselves what birth, death, thought and standing are (நீர் நினைந்து பாருமே). Both put the mind's own inquiry above learning as the way past birth; Sivavakkiyar names the books as the obstacle.

Tirumanthiram 2957 says that for those who set Nandi firmly in love by knowledge there is no impurity, no pride and no caste (குலமில்லை). 1179 says that for the jnanis who have known the Lord within themselves there is not the least thing called caste difference (சாதிபேதம்). Both deny caste for the knower rather than for everyone; Tirumular's knower reaches by love, Sivavakkiyar's untaught (போதியாமல்).

Naladiyar 195 says 'good caste' and 'bad caste' are words with nothing behind them, and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage. 1179 says caste difference does not exist at all for those who have known the Lord within. Both empty the word of substance; the Naladiyar replaces birth with merit, Sivavakkiyar with knowledge, and only Sivavakkiyar says there is nothing there (இல்லையே).

Tirumanthiram 1658 ranks the wearers of the garb by line: men of low birth put it on to rise, men of the right line to become gods, and the outcast ones are to be weeded out. 1179 says there is not the least caste difference for the knower. The conflict holds if 1658's குலம் words mean birth-caste, as its first line (இழிகுலத்தோர்) suggests; if they are words for conduct, as its own marking allows, the two need not clash.
audit_text_issue: 1658 flagged uncertain; the குலம் compounds are unsettled.

note: Tirumanthiram 809 says to raise the tongue by the way of the body's water, drink the honey-water and say Sivaya nama. 1180 says to fold the tongue back toward the nose (நாக்கை மூக்கையுள் மடித்து), go by the channel of sound and hold the pair pressed. Both give the khechari seal, the tongue turned back, as the practice; Tirumular ends in nectar and the mantra, Sivavakkiyar in every direction becoming Brahman.

Tirumanthiram 647 says that in the eighth stage of practice grey hair and wrinkles do not appear. 1180 opens with the claim that in the first cause the body does not age (ஆக்கை மூப்பது இல்லையே), and gives the tongue and channel practice that reaches it. Both make the body's ageing stop as a result of yoga; Sivavakkiyar locates the agelessness in the source rather than in a counted year.

Tirumanthiram 977 says five elephants live in the forest, the five letters are their goad, and for those who hold all five together the First beyond the five can enter within. 1181 counts fives that make trouble and fives that sit within, and says that for those who can sustain the fives, the fives sit settled within as Sivayam. Both make mastery of the fives the condition for the Lord's settling within; Sivavakkiyar multiplies the count to twenty.

Kural 340 asks whether the life that lodges in the body has no home of its own. 1183 asks where life was before it took up the body, what joins life and body, and tells the jnani who took a body to answer. Both treat the body as the soul's lodging and ask after the soul's own place; the Kural's question is about impermanence, Sivavakkiyar's about origin.

Thiruppugazh 1313 traces an ascent from the four-petalled lotus through the centres to bindu, nada and the sound beyond, and asks to be sent out by the root gate into the light. 1184 sets the curling letter at the mouth, raises the pressed letter in the fire, mingles the six lotuses (ஆறு பங்கயம்) and reaches the place beyond. Both are compressed itineraries of the yoga of the centres; Arunagiri's is a plea, Sivavakkiyar's an instruction without its last clause.
audit_text_issue: 1184 is a fragment without a finite verb; 1313's ஆர மூணுபதி / நுறு பத்தினுடன் எட்டு are unresolved.

note: Both answer 1131's questions about what was before form, conception and grace. 1132 says the body was in fire and desire in the wind; 1185 says life entered as sound, the body was blood, and understanding is the root support before grace. The two answer sets do not match, which shows that the refrain, not the physiology, is what the poet holds fixed.
audit_text_issue: 1132 line 2 repeats line 1's காயம் ... தேயுவில் where 1131 asked about உயிர்ப்பு; probably a copyist's doubling.

note: Tirumanthiram 1087 says the many gods appear different as ornaments appear many though they are one gold, and the Mistress is the cause of Siva, Brahma and Vishnu. 1186 says 'our god, your god' are not two, and that the difference is the speakers' own. Both make the plurality of gods a seeming; Tirumular explains it by one material in many forms, Sivavakkiyar by human partition (பங்கு கூறு).

Thiruppugazh 257 asks why the deceitful siddhas and those confused by the six sects consecrate many gods, fix names and set up images, dividing themselves only to be reborn. 1186 says those who parcel the one Lord into 'our god, your god' make a difference that is theirs alone. Both charge the sects with manufacturing plurality; Arunagiri includes the siddhas among the dividers, which is a charge Sivavakkiyar would turn back on the sects.

Tirumanthiram 311 says the able live joined to the one way while others say knowledge is many, and that the unlearned do not know God mingled in all. 1187 says the one that is Hari and Brahma and fills the cosmos is one foot, and that those in guise who say 'it is spread out' and make it many should look with understanding and see it one here and there. Both make plurality the error of the unknowing and pervasion the mark of the one.

Tirumanthiram 1666 says that for those who wear the holy ash gladly and never let it fade, deeds will not stay and the Siva state will come. 1188 addresses those who smear burnt ash and take up the guise and asks in which of their mantras the Lord comes and moves, implying none. The conflict holds if 1188's question is a denial, as the stanza's tone suggests; if it only asks for the right mantra, it leaves the ash untouched.

1174 says the name works in the mouth of the loving and turns to disease in the mouth of the spiteful. 1188 asks in which daily mantra, former or root, the Lord moves. Read together, 1174 supplies the answer 1188 withholds: not in any mantra as such, but in the heart that says it.

Both read the letters of Om as a pair joined by a third. Sivavakkiyar makes A life and U the body, joined by Siva; Tirumular makes A the Lord and U the Lady spread through the world, rising together as sound. The same letters carry two different pairs.

Both say that nothing one owns goes along with one and only the deed does. The Naladiyar says it of all deeds at death; Sivavakkiyar says it of gifts and dharma, which return like a bolted horse while elephants, armies and horses do not.

Both take the gifts customarily made to Brahmins and redirect them: Tirumular to the ash-wearing devotee, worth more than feeding ten million Vedic Brahmins; Sivavakkiyar to 'the Vedic one who dwells within', the Lord in the body.
audit_text_issue: 1861 line 3 syntax compressed

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes only from what one does; Sivavakkiyar mocks renouncers who claim to be Brahman yet keep caste distinctions. Both deny that caste marks anything real.
audit_text_issue: 1210 line 4 திடுக்கமுற்ற may be a corruption of திடமுற்ற.

note: Tirumular says that for those who set Nandi firmly in love there is no caste; Sivavakkiyar says that those who claim to be Brahman cannot also keep caste. Both make caste fall away at the point of realisation, Tirumular by grace and Sivavakkiyar by consistency.

Both separate owning books from understanding them. The Naladiyar distinguishes scholars who keep books from those who understand and teach; Sivavakkiyar calls those who stack books and recite liars, and asks what fixity and knowledge they have.

Tirumular says those who recite many praises and hymns lack understanding and wither within; Sivavakkiyar asks the reciters of sastra what letter they actually abide in. Both set realised knowledge above recitation.

Both trace the body from the white seed through the womb to its form. Tirumular gives the measures (eight finger-breadths in, four out, a body of eight spans); Sivavakkiyar gives the stages (seed, water, form) and asks the knowers to explain them.
audit_text_issue: 464 அக்கரம் எட்டும் obscure

note: Tirumular says siddhi, release and true knowledge cannot be known unless the Lord takes form and gives grace; Sivavakkiyar says he did not know the formless Mother until she came in form, and names the guru as the form that made it clear.

Both set the Lord's real form against the installed image: Tirumular makes earth the pedestal, sky the linga and the sea its bathing hall; Sivavakkiyar calls those who name a made stone the ancient substance poor fools and points to the maker. Tirumular elsewhere defends the temple (516), so the agreement is on where the Lord's form is, not on whether to worship the stone.

Both describe the ascent through the central channel: Tirumular through the sushumna in the narrowed stalk of the eight-petalled flower to the gathered light; Sivavakkiyar through the channel, raising the fire and crossing the six lotuses to the space beyond. The vocabulary differs, the route is the same.

Both put the cutting of birth before the mantra. Tirumular says the five letters show the way of grace to those who have cut the reckoning of the womb's way; Sivavakkiyar says the truth of the five letters can be known only by one who has slain deceitful birth.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether the knowledge of silence can be spoken by the mouth at all; Tirumular distinguishes true silence, in which speech and mind are both still, from mere muteness. Tirumular's distinction qualifies the claim: unsayability is not the point, the stilled mind is.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1896 line 4 அச் சுத்த்ததை is a misprint (சுத்தத்தை).

note: Both place a triangle at the root of the body: Tirumular's twisting in the triangle at the root with the two channels leads to the Lord's feet; Sivavakkiyar's mantra rises in the root centre whose base is the முச்சதுரம், the three-cornered figure.
audit_text_issue: 1217 தீட்டமாய் is unexplained; 2173 ஏலங்கொண்டு is obscure.

note: Tirumular makes the heart the great temple, the body the shrine and the soul the linga; Sivavakkiyar says the one who knows the light in the heart lotus has no need to raise hands to the god in a seen temple. Both locate the temple in the body.

Tirumular lists lamps, flowers, sweeping and bathing the image as the servant's path to the Lord; Sivavakkiyar says the knower does not raise his hands to the god in a seen temple. The conflict holds if 1220 means that temple worship is useless; if it means only that the knower has passed beyond it, Tirumular's path remains for those who have not.
audit_text_issue: 1502 line 1 garbled (தீப miடல்மலர்)

note: Both use the eye that sees everything but cannot see itself. Tirumular uses it for the Lord, who sees all and is not seen; Sivavakkiyar for the self, which cannot be its own object, so that he has not known the one who stands within him.
audit_text_issue: 1226 line 3 கண்ணிறி விலாமையால் looks misprinted (perhaps கண் அறிவு இலாமையால்); the eye-image survives it.

note: Both hear the unceasing sound within and see the hall there: Tirumular's ringing bell is the lamp of the inner breath, and he heard the sound and saw the hall; Sivavakkiyar's conch of nada sounds whether he lies, sits or walks, inside the hall that cannot be contained.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 2521 line 4 அற்றலும் கேட்டது is obscure, possibly for அரற்றலும்.

note: Both say the mantra's letters are not the end. Tirumular: when nama falls away there is no more seeking, and to join the great silence that is Siva is release; Sivavakkiyar: the five letters and the three are not that thing, until 'that letter' is known, when they become it.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1013 line 3 (நமவற ஆதி நாடுவது அன்றாம்) is obscure.

note: 1189 gives each letter of Om and of Sivayam a cosmic function, creation, form, delusion, clarity; 1237 says the three letters and the five are not the thing itself. The second verse keeps the letters from being taken as the goal that the first seems to make them.

Tirumular says to speak the truth as well as one can; Sivavakkiyar says there is no need to speak the truth, because the false enjoy lies and the truthful have no hearers, and confesses that he was afraid to open his mouth. The conflict holds if 1238 is a settled claim; if it is a complaint to the Lord about his own fear, the two need not clash.

The Kural says virtuous action is not killing, and killing brings every other evil deed; Sivavakkiyar says that even one who kills for food, lies and steals may, if he can lovingly join the Lord, know the gods within himself that day. The conflict holds if 1239 makes realisation override the moral law; if it means only that the sinner is not shut out from the Lord, the Kural's ranking of deeds is untouched.

1238 confesses the poet's fear of speaking truth in a world where liars enjoy their lies; 1241 gives the image for it, truth pulled up like a weed among the paddy, and the conclusion that the world of such speakers is hell.
audit_text_issue: 1241 line 3 (விரகிலே முளைத்தெழுந்த மெய்யலாது) is ambiguous; the link does not depend on it.

note: The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar says those who draw pond water without a drop of moisture in the mind achieve nothing, and that cutting the mind's dirt makes the light, you and I one. Both make the inner state the whole of it.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart and those who do not bathe in them wander; Sivavakkiyar asks those who pour away water in rites to think of root and seed instead. Both replace the outer bath with an inner object.

Tirumular lists the bathing of the image among the works of the temple that are the servant's path; Sivavakkiyar says those who daily do worship to copper only bewilder themselves, when holding the light within is release. The conflict holds if 1249 condemns image worship as such; if it condemns only image worship in place of inner knowledge, Tirumular's path for the servant stands.

note: Tirumular says that once the meaning is grasped and samadhi is in hand there is no need of sounded chant or purification; Sivavakkiyar says that holding the measureless light within is release and that muttering and finger-counting are bewilderment. The Kural speaks of those with impurity in their minds who bathe as if distinguished and go about concealed; Sivavakkiyar says those who dip in the tank do not cut the dirt of the mind. Both charge the bather with a dirty mind under clean water.
audit_text_issue: 1252 வண்டுலங்கள் / குண்டலங்கள் are loose rhyme-words of uncertain sense.

note: Tirumular says the hall where the Lord dances is the whole world, his feet and the five letters; Sivavakkiyar addresses the Lord as the five letters dancing in the sky and the consciousness spread out as sparks. Both make the dance, the mantra and the pervading Lord one thing.

1226 says the eye cannot see itself, so the self within cannot be known; 1258 pushes the image further: the unlookable look, when it comes, looks back at the one looking. Not-knowing in the first verse becomes a reversed seeing in the second.

Both say the Lord is mingled everywhere as a hidden essence is in its substance: Tirumular's jaggery in cane, ghee in milk, juice in fruit and fragrance in flower; Sivavakkiyar's oil in sesame, repeated in 1263 for the Lord hidden in every letter.

Tirumular says there is no dharma outside the Veda and the wise gained release by reciting it; Sivavakkiyar says he has seen no Veda, since he has no burning birth to escape. The conflict holds if 1260 rejects the Veda as a way; if it means only that one already free needs no Veda, Tirumular's claim for those still bound is not denied.

Both contract the mantras: Tirumular's fifty letters, which are all the Vedas and Agamas, become the five letters once their order is known; Sivavakkiyar's five crore mantras are held in the five, and the five, four and three become a single letter within oneself.

Tirumular says the gods go about the eight directions saying 'there he stood, there he lay', while he praises the Lord who dwells within his own heart; Sivavakkiyar calls those who seek the dancing Lord here and there sinners and tells them to seek within. Both set searching in places against finding within.

Both measure the breath in finger-breadths (எண்விரல், நால்விரல்) and end in the five letters: Tirumular's breath goes out twelve, eight return and four are lost, and gathered it is the mantra; Sivavakkiyar's mantra rises amid the four gates and eight fingers.
Sivavakkiyar makes the body Shakti and the life in it Siva, so the Lord's form is the living person; Tirumular makes the human body's shape the Sivalinga, Chidambaram and the dance itself.
Lines 2 and 3 of 1269 recur almost unchanged in 1373 (the four Vedas recited, the knowledge, the poison-throated one, Brahma and Vishnu); both resolve the gods and the Vedas into the five letters.
Sivavakkiyar fixes the one god as the dancer of the hall at Thillai, with a threefold 'no'; Tirumular widens the same dance: Chidambaram and the holy dance are everywhere Siva is.

Both count the Lord into the elements: 1231 piles up fives and threes and ones and asks who can see him, 1273 gives the qualities five to one from earth to sky and asks the same question in the same words.
1146 lists the fire pit, the four Vedas and the bound books and says all this ended as nothing when the poet knew the Lord; 1276 asks the priest what each of them is.
The Kural ranks one abstention from killing above a thousand oblation-pourings, leaving the rite its lesser merit; Sivavakkiyar takes the next step and asks what the fire pit is at all.
Tirumular's Siva-gnanis go about as the dead while senses and body remain; Sivavakkiyar's jnanis have nothing to think whether they sleep, wake or let the senses scatter.

Both set a single letter above all recitation: Tirumular says life can be won by one letter uttered without another, Sivavakkiyar that the one letter the reciters recite is one and that nada, the gods and he are one in it.

Tirumular's eight siddhis come when the fire at the root of the central channel drives the sun and lets the moon drink; Sivavakkiyar rouses the root fire with the wind, seals the gates and sends it up the spine through the root nadi.

Tirumular says no one sees the one letter in the sky and the world knows only letters on water; Sivavakkiyar says the Beginning settled in the one letter cannot be seen or known on this earth or in song.

note: Both count the Lord's letters: Tirumular's one letter becomes the world, two join as two, three make the light; Sivavakkiyar's three and two and five make gods and worlds, and the one letter that appears is the end of speech.

Tirumular says the knowing soul, the Lord and the bond are all beginningless; Sivavakkiyar says the soul is not beginningless, only the truth mingled with all things is. Tirumular says the five letters protect the soul when Death lays hand on it; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the mantras one has learned can be recited when one is dead, and locates the real mantra in the mind. He does not deny the five letters, but moves them from learned speech to inner knowing, which limits what the recited formula can do.

Both make the body the temple: Tirumular's heart is the great temple, the flesh the shrine and the soul the linga; Sivavakkiyar says temple, tank, fire, air and Siva are one and those who know this body become the vision itself.
Tirumular says Parashakti stood as his body and life and became his awareness; Sivavakkiyar states the same as doctrine: Shakti is your body, and the jiva within it is Siva.

note: Both count letters without giving the key: Tirumular says by one letter he became all, by two he is two, by three the light springs up; Sivavakkiyar asks whether A holds the rest, arose from itself, or joined with U, and leaves the answer to the jnanis.

Tirumular says the Lord is not in the mansion, hall, temple or ascetic's garb but in the heart of those free of longing; Sivavakkiyar says temples, tanks and gurus known by their badges only confuse, and knowing Hara is like sitting with one's own parents.

Both verses have the Lord as oil in the sesame seed; 1259 adds that he came gently into the poet after true tapas, while 1367 turns the image into a rebuke of fools who swing between outer routes and dares them to straighten the dog's tail.

Tirumular's Lord is ghee in milk, juice in fruit and fragrance in the flower, mingled everywhere; Sivavakkiyar's is oil in the sesame seed. Tirumular leaves the image as praise; Sivavakkiyar uses it to ask why anyone looks elsewhere.
audit_text_issue: Tm 2639 காலினில் ஊரும் is unclear, as the marker notes; it does not affect the link.

note: Tirumular says that wearing the holy ash gladly without fail makes deeds fall away and brings the Siva state; Sivavakkiyar asks what use the ash is to one born and dead in every birth, and makes the cutting of malam and desire the condition of seeing. The conflict holds if 1380 denies that the ash does anything; it eases if the poet only ranks it below inner cleansing.

Both verses set ash-smearing beside Vedic recitation and babbling as things that do not bring the Lord: 1001 says he does not come for them, only for a melted heart that speaks the truth within; 1380 says cut malam and desire instead and see in the sound of nada.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and all else is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar asks what the ash on the body is for and puts the cutting of impurity and desire in its place. Both put inner cleanness over the visible sign.

Tirumular asks what use it is to write the cause beyond all signs on the outside of a palm leaf, without the guru's joining; Sivavakkiyar asks in which letter the Lord sits inside the palm leaf while the crowd recites. Both say the book cannot hold what it names.

Tirumular says that once samadhi is in hand sounded chant, purification and even the mind become needless; Sivavakkiyar says that once the First is seen there is no light, no word and not even the five letters. Both set a stage past the means they otherwise teach.
audit_text_issue: 1383 line 4 அஞ்செழித்தும் is a misprint for அஞ்செழுத்தும்.

note: Tirumular says the world knows letters on water and no one knows the one letter in the sky, and that even its knowers miss the letter in the flesh; Sivavakkiyar says the flame and the body were born in the one letter and asks that it be known. Both put the one letter in the body.

1180 gives the formula whole: the body does not age if the tongue and nose are folded in, the breath passes along the nada channel and the two are pressed tight, and every direction becomes Brahman. 1387 repeats the second half with a corrupt first line and adds the praise of the two-letter mantra; it reads as a variant of 1180.
audit_text_issue: 1387 line 1 காக்கை மூக்கை ஆமையார் looks like a corruption of 1180's ஆக்கைமூப்பது இல்லையே; line 3 may also be corrupt.

note: Tirumular says that if the two breaths are set in the upper palate Death is gone, the door opens and grey hair turns to childhood; Sivavakkiyar presses the tongue back along the knowledge channel and finds Brahman in every direction, and the sister verse 1180 promises that the body does not age.
audit_text_issue: 1387 line 1 காக்கை மூக்கை ஆமையார் is corrupt; 1180 has ஆக்கைமூப்பது இல்லையே.

note: Kakapusundar warns that those who merely raise the tongue to the palate and stare gain nothing, their eyes burst and the body goes, and that the mind must be set at the palate for the breath to be mastered; Sivavakkiyar's verse gives the tongue practice with the praise of the mantra as its condition. The two agree on the method but Kakapusundar limits it.
audit_text_issue: 1387 line 1 (காக்கை மூக்கை ஆமையார்) is corrupt; 1180 has ஆக்கை மூப்பது இல்லையே.

note: Both mock the worshipped stone: 1458 asks whether the planted stone will speak while the Lord is within, as a burnt pot knows no taste of curry; 1388 lines up the broken stone, the doorstep and the puja stone and asks which one pleases the Lord.

Tirumular says that for one who seeks to be saved pearl, ash, rice, flowers or sand can all be made the linga, the Father's body; Sivavakkiyar asks which of three identical stones the Lord could be pleased with. The conflict holds if 1388 rejects image worship outright; it eases if Tirumular's point, that the material is indifferent, is taken as Sivavakkiyar's too.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1719 கொத்தும்அக்கொம்பு and கோமளம் are obscure, but the list's sense is clear.

note: Tirumular says they wander everywhere in the land seeking Nandi, who is fragrant within the body, and do not know the purpose that stands in the body; Sivavakkiyar asks where they run saying 'he is not in this town' and places the Lord in the six centres within.

Both give the Siddhanta pairing of paths and fruits: Tirumular has salokam and samipam from sariyai and sarupam as the way to the formless Supreme; Sivavakkiyar lays out all four, chariyai to salokam, kiriyai to samipam, yoga to sarupam and jnana to sayujyam.

Agappeychittar tells the inner demon that chariyai will not do and that doing kiriyai gains nothing; Sivavakkiyar grants chariyai salokam and kiriyai samipam. The conflict holds if Agappeychittar denies the lower paths any fruit; it eases if he means they do not reach the final release, which 1400 also reserves for jnana.
audit_text_issue: 1666 is unmarked in the corpus; only its Tamil is available.

note: 1400 states the four paths with their four fruits as a ladder; 1401 says there is no reaching by the rightness of the four steps, and that those who reach Siva's state are those who received grace, then tells them to make the four firm. Grace becomes the cause and the paths its expression.

Tirumular's Siva-siddhas cast off the three graded releases as flawed and stand firm with 'I' and 'mine' changed; Sivavakkiyar denies that the order of the four steps is what reaches Siva's state and credits grace. Both put the attainment above the graded scheme.

Tirumular's bindu, kindled by the fire in the root, is raised above the throat and becomes cool nectar at the moon; Sivavakkiyar raises the root channel, opens the three bolts and has the nectar come down, with the Lord then appearing to his servants.

Tirumular's yogic god is the mouth, body, life and eye and is earth, water, fire, air and sky; Sivavakkiyar's speaker says 'I will become fire, air, water, earth and the long sky', and those bathed in the guru's flood know him by his mark.

Both use the myth of the gods who could not find Siva's limits: Arunagirinathar names Vishnu on the serpent who could not find the feet in the depth of the netherworld, Sivavakkiyar has Mal dig the earth and Ayan fly the sky for the root and the crown and find nothing. Sivavakkiyar adds the lesson, know the middle.

The Kural says cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; Sivavakkiyar asks what can hold on to the one that has no holding, and answers that learning cannot, only asking those who have reached. The paradox is the same; the Kural treats it as method, Sivavakkiyar as a question about who can teach it.

Tirumular says to leave the cleverness of reciting the shastras and turn to look within for a moment; Sivavakkiyar asks whether the Lord's feet can be seen by learning and sends the hearer to those who have gained them. Both set learning aside for a direct seeing.
audit_text_issue: Siddhar 1411 line 3 கற்றிதாலோ is a misprint for கற்றதாலோ.

note: 1357 asks whether temple, tanks and waters are not all one and says those who know this body become the vision; 1407 gives the inner version of the tank: sitting in the primal chakra the Lord bathes in the holy water within, once the breath is set right.

Both make learning worthless without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning has gained if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge, and Sivavakkiyar tells the book-reciting yogis that there is no knowledge other than the Lord who stands as knowledge.

Tirumular says no purification is needed for one who stands free of தொடக்கு, and Sivavakkiyar says those who fall into water over தொடக்கு should instead learn where pollution arose; both move purity from the rite to the inner state, and both use the same word.

The Kural's many who bathe like the distinguished with impurity in their minds are Sivavakkiyar's 'dumb ones' who fall into water over pollution; the Kural's point is hypocrisy, Sivavakkiyar's that bathing cannot reach where impurity began.

The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes from what they do; Sivavakkiyar argues the same from breeding: a Brahmin and an outcaste woman produce a child with no mark of difference, unlike a buffalo and a cow.

The Naladiyar calls 'good caste' and 'bad caste' mere words, made real only by tapas, learning and effort; Sivavakkiyar denies caste a basis in the body itself. The Jain text keeps a replacement standard, the Siddhar offers none.

Tirumular says that for those who have set Nandi in love there is no caste (குலமில்லை); Sivavakkiyar says that whoever looks into the clans finds nothing but semen. One removes caste at the end of the path, the other denies it at the root.
audit_text_issue: 1426 மனு எரிக்க is unclear; 2957 பலமன்னி is obscure.

note: Tirumular lists copper, brick, bilva, gold and the rest and says any one of them, clearly known, can be the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar calls those who see excellence in brick, copper and stone fools. audit_text_issue: Tm 1720 தென்தியங்கு ஒன்றை is obscure, but the list of materials and the predicate சிவலிங்கமே are clear.

note: Tirumular has the devotee seek through lands, towns and temples and then find the Lord taking the joined heart as his temple; Sivavakkiyar says those who run about in service die of it and the Lord was within all along. Tirumular lets the outward road lead inward; Sivavakkiyar denies the road any part.

Tirumular saw the true substance within the body and came to cherish it as the Lord's temple; Sivavakkiyar searched within himself and found nothing other than the Lord and himself. Both locate the finding inside the body.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show; Sivavakkiyar tells those who prepare seats and smear ash to first know where knowledge of the Lord arises and subsides. Both put inner state before outward preparation, though the Kural's is moral and the Siddhar's is gnostic.

The Naladiyar separates those who collect books and fill the house from those who understand them; Sivavakkiyar's book-carriers babble lies and do not know where birth and death occur. Both make possessing books a different thing from knowing.

The Kural asks what an appearance high as the sky can do if the heart sinks into a known fault; Sivavakkiyar asks what reciting transcendent knowledge does while a thieving heart remains. Both make the inner fault cancel the outward height.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart and those who do not bathe there wander over hollow and height; Sivavakkiyar says those who climb seas and mountains to see the Lord act from ego, when his feet can be held within. Both turn the pilgrim's road inward.

Both verses argue from spittle: 1423 that the mantra itself is spittle from the mouth, 1442 that honey, milk and the body are spittle too. Together they make the pollution rule self-defeating from two sides, what the ritualist utters and what he eats.

Tirumular makes the heart the temple and, for those clear through and through, the soul the Sivalinga; Sivavakkiyar tells those who run after holy water, linga and image to see the soul within as the linga. Both use the same identification and the same condition of clarity (தெளிவு).

The Kural says the one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Sivavakkiyar reports the day he stood with 'I' destroyed in the ocean of silence. The Kural's is an ethic of renunciation, the Siddhar's an experience, but the thing removed is the same.

Tirumular says there is no need to cry out once the meaning is grasped and no need of sounded chant once samadhi is in hand; Sivavakkiyar asks what use polishing bells, sitting in a corner and wailing with closed eyes can be. Both dismiss the noise of practice once its point is seen.
audit_text_issue: 1448 line 3 எட்டிரண்டும் பத்தலோ is cipher; the link does not depend on it.

note: Both use the cipher 'eight and two' (எட்டும் இரண்டும்): Tirumular says those who do not know the eight and two miss the step of the Siddhanta path, Sivavakkiyar says the god became the linga when eight and two joined. Neither explains it; the shared figure, read as the letters அ and உ, ties the two texts.

Tirumular says that if one door is closed inside the bag of the body, light shines within and the temple is lit; Sivavakkiyar lists the nine gates and the shut gate and says that going through the gate of knowledge to the boundary gate ends birth. Both make the body's openings the yogic path.

Tirumular says that by one letter he became everything, by two he joined as two and by three letters the light springs up; Sivavakkiyar speaks of the one letter that moves, the three letters from which the light sprouted as three, and the four letters on the tongue. The counting of letters as stages of the light is shared.

Both use the frog that stays slimy in water: the Naladiyar for readers of flawless books who never gain discernment, Sivavakkiyar for bathers who never scrape the dirt from the mind. The image makes the same point in two domains, that immersion does not clean.
Tirumular ranks those who know only bathing lowest and says they cannot join him; Sivavakkiyar's tank-bathers never clean the mind. Both put bathing below inner clarity.

Both use the ladle that cannot taste what it stirs: the Naladiyar for the fool who mocks teaching he cannot savour, Sivavakkiyar for the stone and pot that cannot know the Lord they are made to hold. The same kitchen image serves ethics in one and the critique of idols in the other.

Tirumular lists lamps, flowers, bell and the bathing of the image and calls the work of the temple the servant's path (சரியை); Sivavakkiyar asks what mantra it is that circles a planted stone with four flowers, since the stone will not speak. The conflict holds if Sivavakkiyar denies temple rites any place; it eases if he mocks only those who stop there, since Tirumular too ranks சரியை lowest.

note: Arunagirinathar describes the body as filth wrapped in skin, a hut of nine gates perishing faster than a bubble, and regrets desiring it; Sivavakkiyar says the body rots without its salt and asks his mind how it can desire it. The Naladiyar scorns those who see that life may leave in a blink and still do no good; Sivavakkiyar scorns those who know all that is born dies and still talk of 'our property and yours' as if deathless. Both treat denial of death as the root folly of householders.

Tirumular says that though one recites the Vedas and Agamas, what is ours lies in one letter of the Lord; Sivavakkiyar says the labour of reciting the Vedas is wasted while the Lord is within. Tirumular still keeps a letter to master; Sivavakkiyar keeps only the inward look, though 1485 and 1488 give him the five letters too.

The Kural says that as this world is not for those without wealth, that world is not for those without அருள்; Sivavakkiyar says that where there are hands and wealth and no அருள், there is no Supreme, only a waste hell. Both make compassion, not rite, the condition of the beyond, and both set it against பொருள்.

Arunagirinathar describes lovemaking and asks to see clearly how to leave that embrace for Murugan's feet; Sivavakkiyar says no god has not joined a woman's shoulder and that human life flourishes in that union. The conflict holds on whether union with a woman is an obstacle to the way; Arunagiri's plea assumes it is, Sivavakkiyar's verse denies it.

Tirumular says Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while body and senses remain; Sivavakkiyar says people count the siddhar mad because heaven and earth are one to him. Both describe how the knower looks to those who cannot read him.

The Kural says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next will be a good guest to the gods; Sivavakkiyar says the guest who comes becomes the Lord and grants life. Both make hospitality a path to the divine, the Kural by reward, the Siddhar by identity.
Tirumular asks whether wasting oneself away is tapas; Sivavakkiyar tells the hermits chewing dry leaves that their body wastes and anxiety grows. Both deny that self-starvation is austerity.

note: Arunagirinathar asks not to wander the earth in ochre, enter forests and punish the body, but to be given Murugan's feet; Sivavakkiyar asks whether those who leave their land to clear forests and hills will see the Lord's feet, and answers that none has gained release that way.

Tirumular makes the earth the base, the sky the linga, the sea its bathing hall and the directions its garment; Sivavakkiyar says that after wood, stone, turmeric, cloth and dung there is no god but the open space. Both replace the made image with the cosmos, though Tirumular keeps the linga's form and Sivavakkiyar keeps none.

The Kural says not killing one creature to eat is better than a thousand sacrifices with oblations; Sivavakkiyar says the goat and cock offered at the Pidari shrine do not cure, since the deity is not the cause. The Kural's ground is non-killing, the Siddhar's is futility, but both set aside blood sacrifice.

The Kural's hidden conduct is a hunter in a bush snaring birds under cover of austerity; Sivavakkiyar's pious thieves make puja and vows flourish while seizing others' property. Both describe religion used as a blind for predation.

The Kural's hypocrite is red as the kunri seed outside and black at the tip; Sivavakkiyar's is white with ash outside and a liar within, his ash the dust where a donkey rolled. Both are judgements of the outward sign by the inner fault.

Tirumular says that by chanting the five letters, through grace, copper becomes gold; Sivavakkiyar describes the man who promises to make gold and runs off with the fee. Sivavakkiyar does not deny transmutation, but his verse makes the alchemist's promise the mark of a fraud, which narrows what Tirumular's line can be taken to license.

Tirumular says the eight siddhis come through eightfold yoga by mastering the breath; Sivavakkiyar describes men who learn the eight siddhis as a stage trick, float upward for show, fall to lust and die. The powers are real for both; Sivavakkiyar's verse says they can be counterfeited and that display is the sign of counterfeit.

The Naladiyar's sages who see the body as a bubble in rain and resolve to end their wandering are the model; Sivavakkiyar's drummers who preach that the body is a bubble and then rob their hearers are the parody. The same image is held sincerely in one text and sold in the other.

Tirumular lists earrings, rudraksha, bowl, seat, yoga band and staff as the ten emblems of the yogi; Sivavakkiyar lists ochre, matted hair, pots, seat, rudraksha and staff and calls their bearers oxen who desert their wives to beg. The conflict holds if Sivavakkiyar condemns the garb as such; if his target is only those who use it to abandon a household and beg, it is a qualification, and Tirumular's own chapter on false garb (1655 to 1660) agrees with him.
audit_text_issue: The count of ten in 1664 depends on whether கட்டி is a separate item.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Sivavakkiyar's matted-haired, ochre-robed men have kept the hair and not given up the fault. Both deny the outward mark any weight.
Tirumular says the false garb is worn for the sake of eating; Sivavakkiyar says the swami's garb is put on to fatten the belly daily. The motive assigned to false renunciation is the same in both.

The Kural says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth; Sivavakkiyar asks whether plunging the head in countless rivers makes a pure jnani and answers that devotion does. Both deny water the power to make the inner clean.

Tirumular says that by the five letters the Lord made the five elements and the many wombs of birth and bears the world; Sivavakkiyar says the world was born, the moving and unmoving dwell and lives rise in the five letters. The cosmogony of the five letters is the same in both texts.

Tirumular's chakra chapter gives further orders of the five letters ending in a form beginning வசி; Sivavakkiyar's closing verse chants சிவாயவசி, the five letters reordered to end in வசி. Both texts permute the pancakshara to bring out the வசி/வாசி, read by tradition as the breath, and both attach power to the permuted form.

note: Both ride the breath as a horse with twelve legs: Tirumular says bind it fast and drink and the body lasts a thousand years; the Azhuganni binds its four legs with a rope and asks whether he could then rule the eight-sided land. The Siddhar keeps the claim in a question.

Tirumular's lord of the five, chief of the town, has a horse to ride to salvation that throws the false; the Azhuganni's horse is a burden even when let go and must be caught in the street. The town and the horse are the same body and breath.

The Azhuganni laments losing the practice at the needle-point gate at the crown; Tirumular says talk of the breath and the needle is useless until desire and attachment are cut. Tirumular names the condition the Siddhar's lament lacks.

Moss on a pond stands for the mind's clouding in both: Tirumular's worshippers have minds like a stone dropped in a mossy pond, without love; the Azhuganni's moss is the Mother's own delusion on clear water, which lifts to leave the water as it was.

Both count the ninety-six under the five: Tirumular's five ministers and their ninety-six who mean to rule, the Azhuganni's ninety-six taken as one with kin and parents. Both treat the body's constituents as a company that must be ruled or will leave.

Tirumular's five ministers rule the body with their ninety-six and exact tribute; the Azhuganni follows the five kings to their death and asks how the warrior kings died, which Tirumular's verse does not reach.

Melting wax in both: Tirumular's rising fire works on the body as melting on wax and leads to knowing the mother; the Azhuganni, not knowing the deathless head, melts to wax in a moment before the Mother. The same softening is attainment in one and collapse in the other.

Both pair the five letters with the rising of sun and moon, the two breaths: Tirumular says at that hour none knows the fitting mantra but the five letters can be recited; the Azhuganni makes the five letters the arrow for the hunt in the grove where sun and moon have gone.

The Kural begs all who beg not to beg of those who conceal; the Azhuganni, baring his teeth to the base for goods, asks the Mother for wealth so that he need not go to them. Both find the shame of begging in the giver as much as in the asking.

Tirumular praises the worship that rises above the six-and-six supports as a splendour gained through Nandi's teaching; the Azhuganni's guru burns the six supports and the fifty-one letters as a fort of deceit. On the reading that the adharas are the ladder of yoga, one text climbs it and the other burns it.

note: Tirumular says those who recite, worship and heap flowers without love have minds like a stone in a mossy pond; the Azhuganni, having sung and studied, drops the flowers and the pilgrim's running and loses his form. Both set the outward rite below what happens in the heart.

Both place the practice in the central channel between root and crown: Tirumular's sushumna running under the rising fire with sun and moon on their way, Ramadevar's breath between foot and crown within the six, at the root that bears the maiden.

note: Three letters that bring the light: Tirumular says by three letters the light springs up, Ramadevar that the way appears by uttering the three letters at the root. Which three letters is not fixed in either text.

note: Both set the maiden at the root as the power to be met: Tirumular's transmuting maiden who rouses the form rising from the root region, Ramadevar's first root-gem who is the maiden within the triangle.

note: Both texts turn mantra and drawn figure to a magical end and promise a visible result: Tirumular's palm-leaf figure smeared with wax and warmed for stambhana, Ramadevar's seed set in a figure and recited a lakh of times against enemies. The Tirumanthiram's chakra tantra is the precedent for the Siddhar rite.

The Kural says not killing is the whole of virtue and that killing brings every other evil; Ramadevar's rite is a procedure meant to bring an enemy's death and calls its teaching a secret for being saved. On any reading of 1534 as a killing rite, the two are incompatible.

Both set a practice by the calendar: Tirumular's breath runs left or right by the weekday and the fortnight, Ramadevar's rite is good on Revati, on the eighth day and in the waxing moon. The timing is shared; what is timed, breath against rite, differs.

Both name Manonmani: for Tirumular she is one of the names by which the great goddess stands as many; for Ramadevar she is the Mother who is all the paths of the pure space, the formless fullness the puja addresses.

The Naladiyar sees the body as a bubble in pelting rain that forms and bursts, and praises those who resolve to end their wandering; Kaduveli calls the body a bubble on water and asks the mind for a means to stay unattached. The Naladiyar's bubble argues for ending rebirth, Kaduveli's for a method of non-clinging in this life.

Tirumular's potter shapes pots from the tank's clay and notes that a broken pot's shards are kept while a broken body is not; Kaduveli's mendicant begs a pot of the potter and breaks it dancing. Both make the body a potter's vessel, but Tirumular's point is how the dead are discarded, Kaduveli's that the living break the body by their own revelling.
audit_text_issue: 1544's parable has no key in the text.

note: Pattiragiriyar asks to become the Lord's subject before this salted pot breaks and takes a womb again; Kaduveli tells of the pot begged from the potter and broken in dancing. Both poets make the body a pot that will break; Pattiragiriyar adds the return to the womb that Kaduveli leaves out.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will burn the sastras and make the four Vedas false in order to see the one formula; Kaduveli tells the mind to stand by the rule of the Veda. The conflict holds if Kaduveli's வேத விதி means the Vedic injunctions themselves; it softens if 1564's 'false Veda' shows he means only a true core against false teachers, but even then he keeps what Pattiragiriyar burns.
audit_text_issue: 1548's சாத நிலைமையே is unclear (perhaps சாது).

note: The Kural says to forget anger toward anyone, since evils are born from it; Kaduveli tells the mind to subdue and kill the vile anger. Both make anger the fault to be destroyed outright rather than measured; Kaduveli adds a caste slur to name it, which the Kural does not.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:1548 சாத நிலைமையே சொல்லு is unclear.

note: Pattiragiriyar asks when he will see with resolve the bare void that grew in the open space and become clear; Kaduveli tells the mind to become clear in the pure open space of Vedanta. The same வெட்டவெளி and the same verb of clearing (தேறு, தெளிவு), but Kaduveli names it Vedanta's, which Pattiragiriyar elsewhere leaves behind.

The Naladiyar says nothing goes with a person but the deeds they have done; Kaduveli says nothing comes along at all, and that bearing the body is itself the trouble. The Naladiyar's exception for deeds is what Kaduveli's own pallavi relies on, since Yama comes for sin, so his flat 'nothing' is rhetorical, not a denial of karma.

Pattiragiriyar asks when, burning off the five senses in which the ego hides, he will gain bliss; Kaduveli tells the mind to cut the forest of thieving senses, set fire and burn it to see the house. Both burn the senses; Kaduveli adds the siege of the fourfold inner fort as the step before.

The Kural makes understanding an inner fortress that enemies cannot destroy; Kaduveli has a fourfold fort within that must be captured from the enemy before one can rule the land. The Kural's fort is a possession that protects; Kaduveli's is held by the enemy and must be stormed, so the same image runs in opposite directions.

Pattinathar asks his heart what ash and bathing are worth when it has not learned the way to be born differently, lying in the river without knowing the ford; Kaduveli asks whether Kasi and the Ganga remove karma or the manifold difference of being born. Both tie the futility of bathing to rebirth, not only to sin.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart, and that the deceitful who do not bathe in them wander over hollow and height; Kaduveli asks whether going to Kasi or bathing in the Ganga ends karma. Both deny the outer river's power; Tirumular supplies the inner bathing that Kaduveli only implies.

Tirumular says the eight great siddhis are not hard for him because the Lord gave grace and cut off his birth; Kaduveli says the eight siddhis succeed for anyone by Siva's act through bhakti. Both make the powers a consequence of grace rather than a goal of technique, and both set release or the cutting of birth above them.

Sivavakkiyar says that if one regards within oneself the god who became the linga when eight and two joined, one crosses the sea of birth; Kaduveli says that weighing the eight and the two and discerning the Vedas as one within, one reaches the open space and the flood of bliss. Both place the eight-and-two cipher inside the body and make it the key to the goal.
audit_text_issue: Both flagged uncertain as to the cipher's sense.

note: Tirumular says to know by gathering the eight and the two and set Nandi within knowledge; Kaduveli says to weigh the eight and the two and find the Vedas one within. Both treat the cipher as something gathered inwardly; Tirumular adds the five who danced becoming kin, Kaduveli the open space and the flood of bliss.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will stop drinking ganja, opium and toddy and drink the five-fold nectar instead; Kaduveli tells the mind not to smoke ganja or drink the liquor that stupefies. Both renounce the drugs from within the Siddhar tradition; Pattiragiriyar names the inner nectar as the replacement, Kaduveli leaves it to 1563.

Sivavakkiyar describes frauds who smoke ganja at set hours and eat opium to be esteemed as kaya-kalpa men, roaming like dogs; Kaduveli forbids ganja and liquor outright. Sivavakkiyar's is a portrait of the abusers, Kaduveli's a rule for the hearer; together they show the drugs were a live problem among the Siddhars' own.

Tirumular makes the thirty-six tattvas the rungs of a ladder to release, climbed into the inner light; Kaduveli sets up a ladder called bhakti and stretches it to the place free of the pairs. The same ladder, but the rungs differ: Tirumular's are the constituents of the world known in order, Kaduveli's a single devotion that also drives off the sects.

Tirumular lists the eight limbs, yama, niyama, postures, breath control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samadhi; Kaduveli only tells the mind to discern the incomparable eight-limbed yoga well, and adds that its truth is enjoyment. Kaduveli presupposes Tirumular's list and adds a judgement on its fruit.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will reach the thing that lies beyond eight-limbed yoga and beyond what is beyond it; Kaduveli commends eight-limbed yoga as the thing to discern and know. Not a contradiction, since Kaduveli does not call it final, but Pattiragiriyar's stanza marks the limit of what Kaduveli recommends.

The Kural says birth is alike for all beings and distinction comes only from the difference in what they do; Kaduveli tells the mind to know the many castes said to be unequal as one and declare it as kinship. Both deny difference by birth; the Kural keeps a difference by work, Kaduveli names none.

Tirumular says that for those who set Nandi in love by knowledge there is no impurity, no pride, no caste and no good to seek; Kaduveli asks the hearer to know all castes as one and teach it. Tirumular's casteless state is the knower's condition; Kaduveli's is a truth to be realised and preached.

The Kural says many with impurity in their minds bathe as though distinguished and go about concealed; Kaduveli says not to put on a false guise or wet one's obligations in many Gangas. Both pair ritual bathing with concealment: the bath is the disguise.

1555 asks whether Kasi and the Ganga remove karma; 1573 turns the question into a rule and sets the bathing beside the false guise and plunder. The second stanza treats pilgrimage not as useless but as a kind of fraud.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will see the bare void in the open space and become clear; Kudhambai asks what a title-deed is to those who hold the open space as truth. For both the வெட்டவெளி is the real; Kudhambai draws the consequence for ownership.

Sivavakkiyar describes frauds who smoke and eat drugs so as to be esteemed as kaya-kalpa men; Kudhambai asks what kalpa drugs are to the jnani who has seen the true thing. Sivavakkiyar attacks the pretenders, Kudhambai sets the drugs below knowledge even when genuine; both place the medical craft outside the goal.

note: Pattiragiriyar asks when he will sleep without sleeping and gain bliss; Kudhambai asks what a mudra is to those who have lost sleep and stay in remembrance. The same wakeful state; Kudhambai adds that the seals of yoga are needless once it is reached.

Tirumular says that with the shambhavi and khechari seals joined, the great Siva-state is the gain of the eight siddhis; Kudhambai asks what a mudra is to the sleepless and aware. The conflict holds on the reading that Tirumular's seals are the means to the state and Kudhambai's aware one is in it; it dissolves if Kudhambai only means the seals are spent after use, which is her method throughout.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 642's சங்கட்டம் is obscure (variant சக்கட்டம்).

note: Pattinathar describes the guru's teaching as a chakra not drawn, a mantra not spoken, a lingam not built, a puja within thought that does not fail; Kudhambai asks what a mantra is to those who stand in the place of tantra. Both make the inner station replace the spoken formula.

Kaduveli tells the mind to climb the path of true knowledge and be clear in the open space; Kudhambai asks what jnana itself is to those in bliss and awareness. Not a contradiction if jnana is the path and bliss the arrival, but Kudhambai's stanza marks the point at which Kaduveli's counsel runs out.

The Agasthiyar verse places the fire in the triangle and in the six, two and eight, and makes the jiva the five letters; Kudhambai asks what the hexagon is to the jnani sprouted in the triangle. Both use the triangle as the place of origin in the body; Agasthiyar keeps the six as a further station, Kudhambai dismisses it.

note: Kaduveli tells the mind to discern the incomparable eight-limbed yoga well and know it; Kudhambai asks what the eightfold prostration is to the jnani who knows eight-limbed yoga. audit_text_issue: 1595: முட்டாங்கம் is unexplained.

note: Pattiragiriyar asks when he will reach the thing beyond eight-limbed yoga and beyond what lies beyond it; Kudhambai asks what yoga itself is to the jnani who has restrained the rush. Both place the goal past yoga; Pattiragiriyar as a longing, Kudhambai as an arrival already made.

Tirumular says the Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while body and senses remain, unlike the ritual purifiers and the monkey-glad knowers; Kudhambai asks what hand-cymbals are to the jnani who wanders like the dead. The same figure of the corpse-walker; Kudhambai turns it on the bhajan singers, Tirumular on ritualists and false knowers.

Pattiragiriyar asks when, having seen the Father's dwelling, he will wander daily like a dead corpse; Kudhambai asks what hand-cymbals are to the jnani who wanders like the dead. Both make the corpse-walk the knower's outward form after the inner finding.

Kaduveli promises that daily celebration will come on earth to the one who sets his gaze on the heavenly state; Kudhambai asks what celebration is to those who stay with attention. The two uses of கொண்டாட்டம் differ, inner gladness in Kaduveli and festivity in Kudhambai, so the stanzas rub rather than clash.

Tirumular calls pure Saivas those who go beyond outward garb to Siva's side without show; Kudhambai asks what adornments or guises are to those who have conquered Death. Both make the costume something the realised have left behind, Tirumular naming Siva as the goal, Kudhambai the victory over Death.

Tirumular tells of drinking the nectar that is milk at the upper place, reached by driving bindu and nada; Kudhambai sets mango milk on the mountain against coconut milk. Read in the coded way, the milk on the height is the same yogic nectar; Kudhambai leaves the code unstated.

Tirumular describes the teacher who cut through the heavens as a solitary man in this world with no house of his own; Kudhambai's knower has no property and no house, and so no household shrine. Tirumular makes homelessness the guru's mark, Kudhambai the reason household worship falls away.

Tirumular says that when one knows oneself and becomes one with Siva, malam and the gunas die and birth ends; Kudhambai says that for those who know themselves and join the Lord no desire remains. The sequence, self-knowledge then union, is the same; Tirumular counts the bonds that die, Kudhambai only the desire.

The Kural makes giving up craving the cause of an unshifting nature; Kudhambai makes the end of desire the consequence of knowing oneself and joining the Lord. The Kural asks for the renunciation first, Kudhambai expects it to follow.

Sattaimuni ends by telling the mind to look at the root; Thirumula Nayanar Njanam says how: look at the foot called the root within the subtle, through the adharas, to the place between the eyes and the brow.

Both make the body-siddhi (காயசித்தி) follow initiation: here after the five dikshas and vaasi yoga there is no obstacle to it; the Valluvar text says its first initiation was done and the siddhi burned off karma.
