note: Here the Vedas practised in vain search and stand as mere void; the Valluvar text allows that the Veda's hidden knowledge, if it becomes true perception, leads by grace to the state. The two texts in the same collection disagree on whether the Veda can be a path.
audit_text_issue: 1620 line 2 (பொருளாகுங் காட்டும் போதே) is a fragment.

note: Two Siddhar invocations that place the guru in the body: Romarishi's protection is the guru's foot that is the root circle; here the guru is praised beside the lotus of the sushumna and Guha within the kundalini.

The Kural's invocation names one Primal Lord as the first of the world; the work that borrows Valluvar's name invokes Brahma, Vishnu, the sun-moon light, Agastya, the guru and Guha in the body's channels, which is one reason the attribution is not taken seriously.

Sivavakkiyar asks what a Paraiyar woman is and what a Brahmin woman is, finding no mark on flesh or bone; the Valluvar text answers the slur of low birth from the other side, by knowing the cosmos in the body and so destroying the way they called him low.

The Naladiyar says good and bad caste are only words and that austerity and learning make a lineage; the Siddhar text makes knowledge of the cosmos in the body the thing that destroys the charge of low birth. Both answer caste with attainment, in the ethical and the yogic domains.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which gets ahead of any other plan; the text that borrows Valluvar's name says it burned the fate-deed that was there from the first. On the reading that 1635 claims karma itself destroyed, the two are incompatible; the Kural's own 620 (seeing fate's back by toil) is the nearer relative.
Kural 620 says the untiring will see fate's back; 1635 turns that into the Siddhar claim of burning fate-deed and the triple void outright by unpanicked effort.

Both say the one who does not open the inner door perishes: Tirumular says one becomes weak if the inner door is not opened; this text says Yama is Death for those who do not know the whirl and the root.
audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 593 line 4 (கோய் திறவாவிடில்) is obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: Kaka Pusundar's chapter turns from silence to buying rock salt and opens an alchemical sequence; here rock salt is the thing humans eat and die of and is said to be in the mind. Both use கல்லுப்பு as a cipher whose referent the text never gives.
audit_text_issue: 1637's last line ends abruptly at உன் (presumably உன்னு, 'think').

note: Tirumular's Siva-water drunk for a year makes the body shine and turn gold; here the moon's urine drawn off and heated gives strength. Both are claims about a fluid of the body as the medicine of the body, and tradition reads both as cipher for the yogic nectar.
audit_text_issue: 1638's opening இந்துப்பாகும் is obscure.

note: Both make leaving women the precondition of the bliss of release: Romarishi will speak the path only to one who has left desire for women, and here great bliss comes once their nearness is removed.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:1641 போசைவிதி is obscure, likely corrupt; siddhar:2457 lines 1-2 are obscure.

note: The Tirumanthiram gives earth gold, water white, fire red, air black and the sky smoke-coloured; Agappei's 1652 to 1654 give the same table with air as நீலம் and the sky as மஞ்சு (cloud). The Siddhar takes the Tirumanthiram's meditative table as settled doctrine and then, in 1660, says none of it is the Lord.

Tirumular says that by three letters the light springs up and by the great letter (ம) delusion came; Agappei says ம is maya and impurity while சி is the root. Both read the letters of the mantra as a key to bondage and release, and both assign delusion to ம.

Tirumular counts fifty-one letters, eighty-one words and the rest as the way the adhvas, the paths the soul traverses, came to be; Agappei says the fifty-one letters are falsehood and are not to be believed. The conflict holds if Tirumular's verse treats the letter-path as real; it dissolves if his count is only descriptive of what the knower must pass beyond.
audit_text_issue: 1658: அத்தி வரை obscure.

note: Tirumular says salokam comes with sariyai and sarupam by the further paths; Agappei accepts that sariyai yields salokam and adds that this is nothing gained. He keeps the Siddhanta mapping and strips it of worth.

Sivavakkiyar gives the full ladder, sariyai to salokam, kiriyai to samipam, yoga to sarupam and jnana to sayujyam; Agappei names the first rung and says kiriyai gains nothing, and in 1676 denies yoga too. Where Sivavakkiyar grades the paths, Agappei discards all but knowing oneself.

Tirumular says Saivam is knowing oneself and reaching Siva, and leaving what does not reach him; Agappei says that when you know yourself you join with nothing. Both make self-knowledge the heart of Saivam and detachment its sign; 1696 makes the identification explicit.

Sivavakkiyar says that in clear yoga one reaches sarupam, the Lord's form; Agappei asks what use yoga held for any length of time is and whether it yields release, expecting no. The conflict holds if sarupam counts as release; it eases if Agappei, like Tirumular in 2525, treats sarupam as a graded state short of it.

Tirumular makes the stillness in which there is no moving (அசைவு இல்லாமை) the mark of sanmarga; Agappei's one formula is சும்மா இரு, be still, and the place where one stays still is the thing pointed to. Both end the path in motionlessness, though Tirumular reaches it through removing pasu and pasam and Agappei by stopping.

Tirumular says that when bindu and nada meet the moon, nectar wells up in the inner sky; Agappei states the key, the moon is nectar and white, the sun poison and red. The same cipher of the inner moon as nectar is used, but Agappei only names it and in 1702 denies that working the breath brings the Lord.

Tirumular asks whether wasting oneself away is tapas; Agappei asks what hard tapas in forest and hill achieves and whether it opens release. Both deny that severity of place and body is the way, and both put something inward (the Siva-state, the truth) in its stead.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether those who leave their land to clear forest, hill and hollow will see the Lord's feet and says none of them has gained release; Agappei asks what hard tapas in forest and hill will give and whether release is laid open by it. The two Siddhars make the same case against ascetic wandering.

Tirumular defines Saivam as relation with Siva, knowing oneself and reaching Siva; Agappei asks whose Saivam is and answers that it belongs to those who know themselves. Both take Saivam out of sect and into self-knowledge; Agappei adds the guru's feet as its place.

Agasthiyar's stanza instructs: join the standing breath to the space, join the chief fire, join sun and moon together; Agappei says that even one who has mounted the breath will not have the thing of the sky come to him. The conflict holds if 2387 means that the breath practice itself delivers the goal; it eases if the breath there is only preparation.

Arunagirinathar asks for that which the four Vedas say they cannot reach even at their height; Agappei says the four Vedas do not see the Lord and that their end is the guru's foot. Both place the real past the Vedas' reach, and both give it through a teacher (Murugan as guru to Siva, the sadguru).
audit_text_issue: thiruppugazh:347 வெருபம் may be garbled.

note: Sivavakkiyar names the place where one stands without mind, life, Shakti, Sambhu, caste distinction, release, root and root-mantra; Agappei says there is no root and no three categories, and that release would exist only if a root did. Both reach a state in which even the ground of release is denied.
audit_text_issue: 1009 மூத்தியற்று and விலைந்ததே are misprints for முத்தியற்று and விளைந்ததே.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks what caste is, since all water is one water and all gold ornaments one gold; Agappei says there is no caste distinction for those who stand as themselves. Sivavakkiyar argues from the sameness of matter, Agappei from the state of the knower, and both deny caste.

Tirumular says that for those who by knowledge set Nandi in love there is no impurity, no pride, no caste and no good to seek; Agappei says there is no caste distinction for those who stand as themselves, and that even for the learned there is nothing. Both make casteless-ness a property of the one who has arrived, not a social programme.

Tirumular lists eighty-one words, fifty-one letters and seven crore mantras as the way the adhvas came to be; Agappei calls the eighty-one words and mantra alike Indra's net, conjuror's illusion, and says to shut one's mouth. The conflict depends on Tirumular's verse treating the pada-path as real; as a description of what is to be crossed, the two would agree.

Sivavakkiyar asks the fools crying 'puja, puja' where in the self the puja was received; Agappei says puja is a ghost and knowledge crookedness. Sivavakkiyar's attack is a question about the recipient; Agappei's is flat denial, extended to the Lord as maya.

Sivavakkiyar's place without Shakti, Sambhu, mukti and root keeps the Siva-mantra at its close (சிவாயமே); Agappei goes one step further and denies self, Lord and sadguru in a single stanza, with no mantra left standing. The later Siddhar pushes the elder's negation to its end.

Tirumular says knowing oneself is knowledge and anything known afterwards is a ghoul's knowledge (பேயறிவு); Agappei repeats the line almost word for word, you must know yourself and all else known is பேயறிவு, with the pun that his addressee is the demon. The stanza is a direct borrowing of the Tirumanthiram's half-verse.

The Kural says that even with the fivefold awareness there is no benefit for those who lack true perception; Agappei asks what use study or doing is, since all the told ways are only pointers. Both deny that acquired knowledge avails without the inner seeing, though the Kural keeps learning and Agappei discards it.

The Kural says those called freed are those freed of craving and no others; Agappei says begging does not end birth and the Lord is where desire has ceased. Both put freedom in the ending of desire rather than in the outward act of renunciation, and both deny the title to the one who has only given up possessions.

Tirumular says the Siva-siddhas cast off the three graded releases as flawed, lose pride and change 'mine' and 'I'; Agappei says those who have become pure consciousness want no moksha, no release and no initiation. Tirumular rejects the lesser releases for the sake of union; Agappei's knowers want nothing at all, release included.

Sivavakkiyar says those who can melt sun, moon and stars into the one letter in the incomparable void (ஒப்பிலாத வெளி) and stay there are not born again; Agappei says appearances are void and appear without appearing in the pure space (சுத்த வெளி). Both name an open space beyond the lights of the inner sky as the ground of release.

Tirumular says that though one recites the Vedas and Agamas, what is ours lies in one letter of the Lord, to be mastered; Agappei says not to recite the Veda, not to trust the feet, and in 1707 not to open the mouth for mantra at all. The conflict holds if Tirumular's one letter is a mantra to be practised; it eases if the letter is read as the Lord himself.

Both name the Supreme as a void: Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to know Brahman as சூனியம், and Sivavakkiyar says that for devotees ripe in love the one in the Supreme is பாழ். Both make the void the object of devotion, not its negation.
audit_text_issue: 1374: அர்ந்திருந்தது looks like a misprint for அமர்ந்திருந்தது, and the first line is unclear.

note: Idaikkadar says that without tapas there is no strength to reach God; Tirumular says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva if one has the fellowship of those already in Siva's bliss. The conflict stands on the plain reading of 1644, that company can replace tapas; it softens if 1644's last line, that the mind becoming Siva is the fruit of tapas done, is taken to mean tapas was done earlier.

Both claim escape from death through practice: the Kural says leaping past death is possible for those who have gained the power of tapas; Idaikkadar asks whether Antaka can approach one who holds the ineffable Lord within night and day.

Both place the முப்பாழ், the triple void, beyond speech and the faculties as the thing to dwell in: Tirumular locates the final experience in the three voids where words cease, and Idaikkadar asks the herdsman to keep the triple void beyond the three faculties in thought. An editor's gloss on 1741 takes the term as the three mayas instead.
audit_text_issue: 2483 நாடிஒண் முப்பதும் obscure.

note: The same reversal of attachment: the Kural says cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go, and Idaikkadar says hold (பற்றி) with love the one who stands free of attachment (பற்றற்று) so that agitation flies off.

Tirumular says that when the mind becomes Siva, siddhi and release follow; Idaikkadar warns that the mind merely brought under, like a tamed bull, is not yet release. The warning draws a line between a subdued mind and a mind become Siva.

Both make the death of desire the decisive step: the Kural says giving up craving at once gives a nature that never shifts, and Idaikkadar says that when the cow called desire is slain one sees and knows the whole cosmos, where taming the mind and killing anger (1745, 1746) were not enough.
The body as a vessel of filth: the Naladiyar's pot that seeps from nine openings, which the fool mistakes for a beauty, and Idaikkadar's body-pot whose nature is a jar of excrement.

Idaikkadar, having ordered attachment cut (1751), keeps one small unwavering desire for Brahman; the Kural keeps one clinging, to the one without clinging, as the means of letting the rest go. Both admit a single desire as the lever against desire.

Both set the guru's spoken word above the written or heard scripture: Sivavakkiyar tells the mutes bewildered at the womb-gate to mark the word the guru spoke, and Idaikkadar says the Veda no ear has heard becomes plain when the guru speaks it.

The same inventory of what will not last: Sivavakkiyar's cattle, calves, wealth, wife and children in the mansion when Death's messengers strike, and Idaikkadar's cattle, houses, children, kin, gold and horses that do not stay. Idaikkadar adds the alternative, the way of Siva.

Both deny that wealth lasts; the Naladiyar argues it from the rich man who comes to beg gruel, Idaikkadar from a list of twenty possessions with the single verb 'they do not stand'. The Naladiyar's chapter draws the lesson of giving; Idaikkadar draws that of joining the Siva-way.

Both list what falls away on attainment: Tirumular says recitation, desire, dying and wandering are no longer needed once the Life of life is within, and Idaikkadar says enjoyment, eating, meanness, delusion and thirst all go when one reaches Brahman. Idaikkadar's list is of experiences that end, Tirumular's of practices that become needless.
audit_text_issue: பிரமரத்து in 1756 line 4 is a misprint for பிரமத்து.

note: The same inner campaign: Kaduveli says take the fourfold fort within and cut and burn the forest called the thieving senses to see the house; Idaikkadar cuts the forest of ignorance with the sword of tapas and builds his own fort against death. Kaduveli captures a fort, Idaikkadar builds one.

Both keep the five senses from straying into their field: Tirumular turns back the five so they do not go into the millet field, and Idaikkadar drives the five goats out of the forest of taste, light, touch and sound and pens them in the space of yoga. Both master the senses by turning, not destroying them.
audit_text_issue: 1760 வீறு where smell is expected may be corrupt.

note: The two attachments Idaikkadar cuts are traditionally 'I' and 'mine', which the Kural says must be cut to enter a world above the gods'; Idaikkadar names what follows: the higher pleasure and union with the Supreme.

Both describe the seal at the palate by which the body's nectar is drunk: Tirumular raises the tongue to its shoot so the body's water rises like cane juice, and Idaikkadar closes the palate within and drinks the nectar. Idaikkadar adds that this is still subordinate to true knowledge.

Both climb the six centres to reach what lies above them: Tirumular counts the petals from the root and finds the feet of the Lord who has seen time at the end, and Idaikkadar seeks the gods of the six supports and then the Primal One above them.

Idaikkadar uses the mother twice for the Lord: here he is more loving than a mother and never leaves those who love, and at 1809 he guards every life as a mother does. The second extends the care from devotees to all lives.

Idaikkadar's two cowherds agree on the void: Thandavaraya Konar says Brahman must be known as சூனியம், and Narayana Konar tells the cow to cling to the one that became the void, past pointing. In both the void is the Lord to be held, not an absence.
audit_text_issue: 1777's சூனியமானவத்தை needs to be split as சூனியமான அத்தை.

note: Both call a human being who lacks the essential thing a tree: the Kural those without courtesy, however sharp, and Idaikkadar those who do not reach Siva by their own minds. Idaikkadar's tree also puns on தானு, Sthanu, the fixed one they fail to reach.

Both compare the Lord to the pupil of the eye: for Tirumular he is like the pupil to those who can see, and Idaikkadar praises the great light thought of as the jewel within the eye. In both the image places the Lord at the seeing centre, not among things seen.
audit_text_issue: 2823 flagged uncertain.

note: Oil in sesame as the pervasion of the Supreme: Pattirakiriyar asks when he will know the end of the Veda that is in all things as oil in sesame, and Idaikkadar tells all to praise within the one that fills everything so. Pattirakiriyar longs to know it; Idaikkadar makes the knowing the ground of praise.

Both promise a lasting gain from keeping the senses under: the Kural says that withdrawing the five like a tortoise gives protection through seven births, and Idaikkadar says karma wears away for those who do not let the grazing senses rise above them.
audit_text_issue: 1792 line 1 syntax (பொறிகடமை) is loose.

note: The mind as a monkey seized by a ghost: the Njanak Kummi's mad monkey of a mind gripped by a frenzied spirit, and Idaikkadar's possessed monkey that sets its desire on the world. The kummi prescribes a medicine to tame it; Idaikkadar only asks whether its roaming does any good.

The magnet and the iron, turned two ways: Pattirakiriyar asks the Lord to seize him as a magnet draws iron to its feet, and Idaikkadar makes the mind the magnet drawing in many things that do not last. The same pull is liberation when the Lord exerts it and bondage when the mind does.

Kudhambai asks what need the true jnani has of kalpa preparations; Idaikkadar says it is by the kalpa state that one crosses the ages. The conflict stands if Idaikkadar's கற்பநிலை is the state given by the kalpa medicines, and dissolves if it is a state of mind lasting a kalpa.
audit_text_issue: 1797 flagged uncertain; சொற்பநிலை மற்றநிலை unexplained.

note: On the reading that japa and tapas wear the body away and yoga keeps it, Idaikkadar takes Tirumular's side: Tirumular nurtured the body because true knowledge cannot be won once it perishes. On the other reading of 1798, which doubts yoga alone, the link weakens.

Idaikkadar says true learning is learning to be silent; Tirumular sets a condition on that silence: if only speech is still one is merely mute, and silence is speech and mind both stilled. The learning that ends in silence must quiet the mind, not only the tongue.

Two lamps addressed to the same petty knowledge: at 1805 knowledge is already a lamp for the dark room and must be set in grace, and at 1807 it carries a hand-lamp into the sea while the true lamp is inside. The first asks knowledge to become the lamp; the second rebukes it for looking past the lamp it has.

Tirumular says the Lord is kinder than a mother to those who love well; Idaikkadar says the Primal One guards every life with love as a mother does, and release comes from seeing him. Tirumular restricts the nearness to lovers, Idaikkadar extends the care to every life.

Tirumular counts a hundred sects within six and says the supreme path is no path of theirs; Idaikkadar tells the cuckoo that the many religions are falsehood and that the Noble One is hard to see. Both reject the sects as a whole rather than one in favour of another.

Tirumular says the sages who waited for release by praise alone did not know the fruit that tattva-knowledge gives; Idaikkadar says those who have mastered all the tattvas will burn, and only the root mantras bring greatness. The conflict holds on the reading that தத்துவங்கள் தேர்ந்தவர்கள் are those who know the tattva doctrine, which Tirumular's verse prizes and Idaikkadar's dismisses.
audit_text_issue: Idaikkadar's மாதவங்கள் போலும்பலன் வாயா is obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: 1818 says those who perform the practices (சாதனங்கள்) will die; 1855 tells the herdsman to hold the practices well in hand and keep to them. The conflict holds if the two verses mean the same practices; it dissolves if 1818 means outward rites and 1855 the inner disciplines of the herding songs.
audit_text_issue: 1818 is a hard verse; வேவார் and வாயா are uncertain.

note: The Kural says a household life that keeps to virtue has more endurance than those who do penance; Idaikkadar says household life is affliction and the good dharma is renunciation. The conflict is direct on the ranking of the two dharmas, which the Kural's chapter on household life argues one way and this verse the other.

Pattinathar says that forest, rags and bowl gain nothing without inner love, and that true lovers reach the home of knowledge even staying in the house beside their women; Idaikkadar says household life is sorrow and renunciation is the good dharma. Both make devotion the condition, but they disagree on whether leaving the house is the better dharma, Pattinathar denying that the outward state decides and Idaikkadar ranking it.

Tirumular makes devotion and the knowledge that is dispassion the seed of the supreme siddhi; Idaikkadar says that without devotion there is neither release nor siddhi and that renunciation is the good dharma. The pair of conditions is the same in both.

Both use heated iron. In Tirumular the heat that stays after the fire is withdrawn is the stain of karma that lingers even in turiya, a warning; in Idaikkadar the glow of the heated iron is the soul made to shine by practice, an encouragement. The same image carries opposite lessons.

Tirumular says that for those to whom silence has come, release comes too and the powers stand before them; Idaikkadar says that in the state of silence release comes to be. Both make silence the state in which release is found rather than a vow that precedes it.

The Kural says the domain of the five must be crushed and all that one has wanted let go; Idaikkadar says those who let the senses loose like dogs are demons. Both make the restraint of the five the first condition, the Kural in the chapter on renunciation and the Siddhar in a herdsman's song.

The Kural says that drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is protection for seven; Idaikkadar says untied dogs are never fit for guarding. Both treat restraint of the senses as protection, the Kural from the side of the one restrained, the Siddhar from the side of what the senses are for.

Both use the snake asleep in its box. In the Sivavakkiyam the sleeping snake is the danger lust wakes, with the coiled power as the coded sense; in Idaikkadar the snake is the demon-mind charmed down into the box by the flute. The one verse warns against loosing the snake, the other shows how it is settled.
audit_text_issue: 1464 line 1 (சுட்டெரித்த சாந்து, திட்டநெட்டு) is unclear.

note: The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Idaikkadar blows the flute so that neither 'mine' nor 'I' remains. The pair of words is the same; the Siddhar's means is to play the flute as the Lord's own.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will kindle the root fire in the hall of the moon and bring down the milk and drink it; Idaikkadar milks the milk that is in the head so as not to die. Both use milk for the nectar of the crown, Pattiragiriyar from the side of longing, Idaikkadar as a work-song for the yogi who has it.

Tirumular says that when the tongue-tip is pressed up into the middle, soul and Siva dwell there and the flesh does not die; Idaikkadar milks the milk that comes above the palate and oozes in the great egg so that torment ends. Both place the deathless nectar above the palate, and both claim an undying body from it.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will drive the wind-cow to the place and tie it; Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to pen the one cow that is the mind. The cow to be tied is the breath in the one and the mind in the other, and both poets make the herdsman's rope the figure for yoga.

Tirumular sets out the three classes of souls by their malas, those with two being the Rudras and the sakalas having three; Idaikkadar turns the classes into cattle, the one-mala being to be tied aside and the herdsman's own two malas driven off. The doctrine is Tirumular's and the herding is Idaikkadar's.

Tirumular says that for those who delight in the nada that shines at the crown there is no Yama; Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to see the great light in the brahmarandhra and sit in silent nishta. Both place the goal at the top of the head, Tirumular as sound and Idaikkadar as light.

Tirumular says a magic mirror has risen in the mind, yet people do not see even its reflection and will not polish it; Idaikkadar says that without the eye of knowledge the mirror itself cannot be seen. Both make the inner mirror something present but unseen, and both blame the faculty of the viewer rather than the mirror.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will see and know as light within a mirror instead of measuring distances; Idaikkadar says the mirror can be seen only with the eye of knowledge. Both make the mirror the figure for immediate inner seeing, and Idaikkadar adds the condition Pattiragiriyar leaves implicit.

Tirumular says the Lady of the tattvas makes her way through the flesh and dwells within us, and the body becomes Siva's temple; Idaikkadar says Shakti and the Supreme are blended within oneself and are seen there in nishta. Both locate the divine pair in the body; Tirumular has her come in by grace, Idaikkadar has her already there to be seen.

Both use the owl. In Pattinathar the sun is darkness to the owl's eye, so the owl is the unknowing man blind to a light that is present; in Idaikkadar the herdsman is told to stay like an owl and reach silence, so the owl is the still, night-waking sage. The same bird is the figure for blindness in one and for watchful silence in the other.

Tirumular says silence is when speech and mind are both still, and that silence of the tongue alone is mere muteness; Idaikkadar tells the herdsman to be like an owl, achieve silence, and so cut off birth. The owl's stillness is of the whole creature, which fits Tirumular's demand that mind as well as speech be quiet.

Konganar makes the mute letter the body and Om the life; Sangili Siddhar, in the same kummi diction, makes the Omkara circle the body and the mute letter the life. Read as assignments of the two letters to body and life, the two stanzas contradict each other; read as saying only that both letters make the person, they agree.

Tirumular says that by the five letters the Lord made the five elements, the wombs of birth and the world; Konganar says the five letters created the world and the soul and ended and restarted the age. Both give the mantra the Lord's own acts, Konganar without naming the Lord.

Pattinathar praises the Lord who stands as the five letters, the eight letters and the fifty-one syllables; Konganar's stanza has the same three counts in the same order, as stages of the letters' growth. The shared triad shows a fixed Siddhar formula.
audit_text_issue: 1882 நிலையாமலந்த likely corrupt.

note: Tirumular runs the letters downward: the fifty letters are the Vedas and Agamas and, known, become the five. Konganar runs them upward: five become eight and then fifty-one. The two are the same correspondence read in opposite directions, contraction toward the mantra against expansion from it.

note: Tirumular says the human body is the Sivalinga, Chidambaram, Sadasiva and the dance; Konganar says those who know the Chidambara chakra must know the deity within it. Sangili Siddhar tells the woman that this is a filthy corpse, a salted pot and a leather bellows to be crossed; Konganar tells her not to think it a filthy corpse or a salted pot, since for those who have seen there is no filth in it. note: The Naladiyar calls the body a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, admired only by a fool dazzled by its skin; Konganar says those who have seen find no filth in it and should look within it. Thirumular Njanam names the root adhara as the circle of three lights and the triangle with three channels, and tells the reader to know the letter A there; Konganar puts the three-flamed lamp in the root mandala and says its flame is the Maiden. Tirumular puts fire, water, air, sun, moon, Vishnu, Brahma and Rudra all within the heart; Konganar's stanzas 1895 to 1899 distribute the five gods along the body, Sadasiva at the brow, Maheswara at the throat, Rudra in the heart, Vishnu at the navel and Brahma at the root. note: Tirumular says that when the silent letter meets the spoken letter the five draw in like a tortoise and Om gains an inner light; Konganar says the mute letter is within Om and that knowing it is the task. Both make the unsounded letter the inside of the sounded syllable.

note: Tirumular says those who can tie in its stall the frisking calf that butts at the sack will find how the fruit ripens; Konganar says the untied bull must be tied, desire cut and the breath joined before the body fails. Pattinathar's Puranamalai opens by confessing that he forgot his understanding by not praising the Maiden within the triangular chakra that rose at the root; Konganar says the Maiden sits in that cornered round chakra and is reached by breath in the root mandala. A later stanza of the same song says mother and wife are the same, for both gave, and asks whether raw fruit and ripe are equal; this stanza makes the Maiden mother, wife, sister and in-law in turn. The later stanza draws the moral the list implies: the goddess gives through every woman alike.

note: Tirumular says the three malas cover the soul as bran and husk cover the sprouting grain, and tells the reader to separate the bonds; Konganar, citing Avvai, says that rice without its husk will not sprout. This stanza puts a saying in Avvai's mouth and asks whether it holds; the later stanza of the song says that whoever speaks what is apt and fits what is lacking, as Avvai did, is the guru. The appeal to Avvai is made general: the proverb-poet becomes the model of the teacher.

This stanza says there is no man without woman, as no sky without earth; the later stanza answers those who say a child comes from man and woman joining by saying the two joined became one seed without difference. The dependence of one on the other becomes their identity in the seed.

This stanza says there is no deity above the Maiden; the later stanza of the same song says that though the Maiden is great she is not the master, and Siva is greater. note: Pattinathar says wife, children and wealth reach only as far as one's own mouth and kin as far as the cremation ground, and that a sesame seed of austerity rules the road; Konganar says the wife comes to the common ground and the children to the burning-ground's edge, and the dharma of service joins one in between. Pattinathar asks who would trust this birth while the hoard lies there and the wife is at the door, having seen the death-rattle; Konganar says Death may seize us as we laugh with soft women on the mattress and we are at once a corpse. Both set the deathbed in the midst of enjoyment, not after it.

note: The Naladiyar tells the wealthy to give, since the span cannot be exceeded and tomorrow the funeral drum may sound; Konganar says the one who has must feed the one who has not and must not say 'tomorrow', and gives the four Vedas as authority. note: The Kural says do virtue without saying 'later', for it is the companion that does not perish; Konganar says that if fortune has come, do charity quickly and finish temple work, and 1947 adds that those who finish it do not die. Both make haste the whole of the counsel; the Kural's reward is a companion at death, Konganar's a kind of deathlessness.

Sivavakkiyar asks what is a Paraiyar woman and what a Brahmin woman, whether a number is marked on flesh, skin or bone; Konganar asks whether any body carries a difference marking it as god, and says ghee, curd and buttermilk come from one milk. Both deny caste by appeal to the body's sameness; Sivavakkiyar's test is pleasure, Konganar's the common source.

The Naladiyar says cows differ in colour but their milk does not, so virtue is one though its ways are many; Konganar says the one milk became ghee, curd and buttermilk, so caste differences are products of one substance. The image runs the opposite way: in the Naladiyar many sources give one thing, in Konganar one source gives many.

Pattinathar says that while the Lord of Arur is right here people wander from town to town for festivals, looking for fire while the lamp burns; Konganar says that while the means is inside your own house you run about to the neighbour's. Both make wandering the failure to look where one already is; the kummi keeps the plain sense of house and neighbour alongside the coded one.
audit_text_issue: யூகம் printed for ஊகம்.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks the sastra-reciting Bhattar whether the Veda will help when the sweat and gasping come; Konganar says the world laughs when those who studied all the sastras die like anyone, and that the knower must join the gods even in dying. Both test learning at the moment of death and find it wanting.

Tirumular says those who have looked over mantra, tantra, yoga and jnana yet do not make them clear and go blind for the sake of food are false gurus; Konganar says the one who knows no fullness, lies and recites crores of mantras is only an instrumental guru who grabs goods. Both make the false guru a man of many mantras and a living, and both test him by what he knows, not by what he recites.

Pattinathar says those who call the Lord sky or cosmic egg, speaking knowledge with the mouth alone and saying 'it is I', are idle talkers who do not know themselves; Konganar says those who call themselves all-knowing full gnanis run about to feed their bellies. Both make the claim to knowledge the mark of its absence; Konganar adds the motive.

Pattinathar says the Fullness is spread through everything like sugar in milk; Konganar says Vaalai stands in all she created like oil in sesame. Both images are of a pervasion that is hidden in the substance and needs pressing or tasting to be known; in Konganar the pervader is the goddess, in Pattinathar the impersonal Fullness.

Pattinathar says people wander from town to town for festivals while the Lord of Arur is here, seeking fire while the lamp burns; the kummi says people go in turn to see the lamp of Annamalai while it is inside them. Both use the lamp against pilgrimage, Pattinathar as a figure, the kummi as the actual festival lamp.

Tirumular says the form of the human body is Chidambaram and the holy dance; the kummi says the dance of Chidambaram is inside you, so serve it there. Tirumular's identity becomes the kummi's instruction, and the kummi draws the practical conclusion in 1978 that there is no need to travel.

Pattinathar says that while the little hall and Siva are close at hand we went seeking an empty hall; the kummi says the Lord dances with lifted foot inside you, so why go to Chidambaram. Both make the journey to Tillai a mistake about where the hall is.

Both poets use oil in the sesame seed for an unseen presence that fills the whole: Pattiragiriyar for the end of the Veda embracing all that moves and stands, Pambatti for the Lord filling every life. Pattiragiriyar asks when he will know it; Pambatti tells the snake to think on it until devotion rises.

Tirumular tells the disciple to give the guru the goods he has, his body and his life; Pambatti's guru has already received body, goods and life (உடல் பொருள் ஆவி) as a gift. The formula of surrender is the same, and both make it the mark of the true guru relation.

Both define the false guru: Tirumular as the fool without inner feeling who never sees the Veda-Agama path and reviles others, Pambatti as the preacher of false religions. Tirumular only condemns; Pambatti's true guru talks sense to the false ones and sends them onto the good path, a gentler ending to the same diagnosis.

Tirumular lists the body entering another body among the eight siddhis; Pambatti credits the same power, leaving one cage for another, to the guru and asks who can tell its measure. Both treat it as a siddha's attainment, and Pambatti adds that the same guru shows the way to release.

Tirumular's yogi in the eighth year shows no grey hair or wrinkles; Pambatti's guru has a strong body that no defect can touch, harder than diamond. Both hold that practice perfects the body itself, not only the mind.

The boast of making the eight nagas dance in the hand is carried out in the dialogue of 2014 to 2018, where the eight are named, set in the eight directions of a chakra with letters and mantra, and the Siddhars are told to take the hooded ones in hand so they spit their poison.

Tirumular's eight siddhis begin with being an atom within the atom and greatness; Pambatti's pillar made a straw and straw made a pillar are the same pair of powers as a stage show. Tirumular presents them as attainments of yoga; Pambatti's own verb, make it appear, admits they are appearances.

Tirumular says he has learned the way of sending moon, fire and sun up the path, the inner alchemy of the breath; Pambatti boasts of turning the three worlds to red gold and cooling the sun. Both move the alchemist's vocabulary from metal to cosmos, Tirumular inward and Pambatti outward.

Tirumular says letters, songs and the sixty-four arts do not remove birth; Pambatti, having known the sixty-four, says he knows the one art above them and has a mind without attachment. Both set the whole curriculum below one knowledge, which Tirumular names as the way of the breath and Pambatti leaves unnamed.

Tirumular's chakra is drawn with eight lines across eight, a letter of the Lord set in the middle and the five letters recited quickly; Pambatti's Siddhars score the eight directions as chakras, set letters at the angles and recite the mantra. The procedure is the same in outline; Pambatti's chakra is peopled by the eight nagas instead of the fifty-one letters.

Pattinathar measures how far each possession follows the dead: property to the house, wife to the street, children to the burning ground; Pambatti asks whether country, house and cattle will seek one out when Yama comes, and answers that the cage once gone they are no use. Both end at the Lord's feet.

The Naladiyar's kings who rode elephants under moon-like umbrellas were carried off and spoken of as dead; Pambatti's elephants, armies, chariots and horses are no help when Yama comes. Both take the king's army as the strongest case of a protection that fails.

Pattinathar says the wealth kept hidden will not come when Yama breaks the frame and takes the life; Pambatti asks whether those who keep mountains of gold will sweep it up when Death comes. Pambatti adds the counter-claim that those whose heart rests on the Father do not perish.

Pattinathar: wife, children and wealth reach only one's own mouth, kin only as far as the cremation ground, and nothing is a companion for the road; Pambatti: children, wife, kin and sons-in-law do not die with one. Pattinathar asks what the companion is; Pambatti answers with the Maker who gave the world.

The Naladiyar's kin arrive unasked and leave wordlessly, leaving the body to its own people like a bird leaving its tree; Pambatti's kin simply do not die with the dying. Both state the limit of kinship as a fact of nature, without reproach.

The Naladiyar tells the lover not to desire the woman for her spear-like eyes, since she too will stoop over a staff; Pambatti says her beauty is turmeric fading in sunlight and the lover will flee when the body goes like the parrot from the silk-cotton pod. Both argue from the beauty's end to the desire's emptiness.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one' because its dark skin dazzles him; Pambatti's lovers call a skin that will shrivel a round breast like Meru and fall into the stinking well. Both oppose the flattering name to the anatomy, and both blame the eye that is dazzled.

Pattinathar says karma took the form of a woman, rounded into the breasts men speak of, and pushed him into the pit of filth and blood; Pambatti says the breasts are shrivelling skin called Meru and the womb a stinking well that ruins those who fall in. Pattinathar confesses the fall; Pambatti warns against it.

The Naladiyar refuses the men who call eyes water-lilies, carp or spears, having seen the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit; Pambatti says those without strength of mind call an eye that oozes filth a sword. The same simile (the eye as a blade) is rejected by the same means, a look at the organ.

The Naladiyar's untaught men call smiles jasmine buds and pearls, and the poet answers with the teeth and bones scattered in the burning ground; Pambatti's owl-men call spittle nectar and a mucous nose a bud. Both reduce the praised mouth to its fluids and remains.

note: Tirumular's potter shapes pots from the tank's clay, and when the body breaks no one keeps it even a moment; Pambatti's potter takes clay from the pit of filth and mixes it with blood, and the vessel is not worth a dry stick. Tirumular's image is of the body's end, Pambatti's of its making; the valuation is the same.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will become the Lord's subject before this salted pot breaks and takes a womb again; Pambatti describes how the pot was made, from filth-pit clay and blood by the potter. Both use the pot for the body and both set the Lord against its breaking.

The Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; Pambatti's pot of pus, blood and fat breaks and dog, jackal, ghoul and vulture eat it as their own. The broken vehicle and its scavengers are the same lesson against praising the body.

The Naladiyar's firm-minded see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; Pambatti's body is a bubble rising on water that will surely depart, and the hearer is to hold the Creator. The image is the same; the Naladiyar draws renunciation from it and Pambatti devotion.

Tirumular says those who know only bathing cannot join the Lord, who is within the mind; Pambatti says bathing in many rivers no more removes the body's impurity than washing removes a fish's stench. Both deny that holy water purifies; Tirumular offers the inner holy waters instead, Pambatti the knowledge of the Lord's state.

The Kural says outer purity comes through water and inner purity is seen through truth; Pambatti says the body's impurity does not leave by bathing in rivers. Pambatti goes further than the Kural, denying even the outer cleansing, since the stench is in the fish; but both locate real purity elsewhere than in water.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will throw off this bellows that the wind blows and reach the Lord; Pambatti's body is a torn nine-mouthed bellows in which the great wind produced speech, food for the burning earth for those who do not know the Lord. Both use the smith's bellows for a body animated only by breath.

Tirumular counts eight that go out and eighteen that come in through the nine gates, with the snake and the horses of the breath; Pambatti's bellows has nine mouths and lives by the wind that entered it. Both count the body by its nine openings and its breath, Tirumular as a yogic puzzle and Pambatti as a memento mori.

Pattinathar tells his heart to hold the wretched body as a puppet show and life as water from an overturned pot; Pambatti's body is a clay puppet on the string of the soul, falling the moment the mover behind the screen stops. Pattinathar names the show, Pambatti names the puppeteer.

Tirumular says Hara makes the elements he spread dance like the deed that makes a false puppet dance, and so settles the soul in awareness; Pambatti's hidden mover behind the screen works the string of the soul, and the body falls when he stops. Both put the puppeteer behind life and death; Tirumular calls it grace, Pambatti only says the body falls.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will put kin away like the lotus leaf spreading on the water; Pambatti tells the snake to push away desire for the world as water does not stay on the lotus leaf, and worship the Light's feet. The same leaf, as a question in one poet and an instruction in the other.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will become like the ripe tamarind, firm within its shell yet apart from it, though he lives with troublesome women; Pambatti says to stay among kin like the tamarind fruit in its shell, without ties, and to stand in the stainless Supreme. Both apply the image to living among one's own without attachment.

Tirumular tells people to hold the reins of the running horse firmly and drop the garb; Pambatti bridles the horse called mind with the intellect and rides it to clarity. Both make the mind a horse to be reined, and both put that above outward practice.

Bathiragiriyar longs to let the unbridled horse run into the inner space; Pambatti bridles his horse and rides. The horses differ: Bathiragiriyar's is the breath set free, Pambatti's the mind brought under control, the two senses the Siddhars' horse carries.

Kakapusundar says that drinking the kalpa called the self is a samadhi in which one can watch Death's dance from the crown; Pambatti says the kalpa-sword drove off Death. Both make கற்பம் an inner attainment that defeats Yama rather than a drug.

Tirumular says the true guru is the lord who gives his feet, and by giving them grants self-knowledge and quells the bonds; Pambatti sees Siva's raised foot and the light, and says the foot placed on his head is the true guru's. Both identify the Lord's foot with the guru's act of initiation.

Both verses name Kasi as the far end of a futile walk: Bathiragiriyar confesses he went as far as Kasi and wore his legs out instead of watching the breath, and Pambatti asks what fruit comes of running till the legs ache and sets the ghat of Vedanta in its place.

Tirumular says there are many holy waters within the heart and that those who do not bathe there wander over hollow and height; Pambatti lists forests, mountains and rivers run to in vain and names a different ghat. Both move the bathing-place inward.

Tirumular says love itself is Siva and only the ignorant make them two; Pambatti says no one with less than a sesame seed of love gains release. Both make love the condition rather than one practice among others.

Sivavakkiyar says release and siddhi are a pair and tells the reader to recite and realise the Lord with love every day, with the five senses mentioned in between; Pambatti puts love first and the cutting of the senses' bonds second as the way to release. The same two elements in the same order.

note: Both use the magnet drawing iron, but in opposite directions: Bathiragiriyar asks the Lord to seize and draw him to his feet as a magnet draws iron, and Pambatti tells the practitioner to join his own mind to the Thing as iron to a magnet. Grace pulls in one, effort joins in the other.

Bathiragiriyar asks when the chiselled stone, the red paste and the tamarind-scoured copper will ever become the Real; Pambatti uses the same chiselled stone and tamarind-scoured copper as comparisons for the fool who has no feeling and whose fault will not come off. Tirumular asks what it is to build a thousand temple towers when nothing equals a meal given to a jnani; Pambatti says those who build a temple in every country and worship daily never see the Lord's feet. Both rank temple-building below what reaches the Lord.

Bathiragiriyar calls those who speak knowledge with the mouth and say 'it is I' idle talkers who do not know themselves; Pambatti says those who do not know themselves are the ones who display themselves, while the knowers hide. Both make self-display the mark of not knowing oneself.

Bathiragiriyar asks when he will stand unobstructed in the sushumna between ida and pingala; Pambatti tells the snake to stand at the whirl-point in the breath and see the all-pervading light. The same standing-place, longed for in one and commanded in the other.

note: Tirumular says there is no dharma that leaves out the Veda and that the wise recited it and gained release; Pambatti lists the Vedas, shastras, tantras, puranas and Agamas and calls them all vain books. On the plain reading of both, one makes scripture the way to release and the other denies it any worth.

Agasthiyar says the four Vedas contradict one another and are a path made in vain for their reciters' livelihood; Pambatti calls the Vedas, shastras, Agamas and all other books vain. Agasthiyar gives a reason (contradiction, self-interest) where Pambatti gives only the verdict.

note: Tirumular says kin is one and God is one; Pambatti says the differences of religion and caste belong to worldlings and not to true sadhus, and tells the snake to learn the Siddhas' Siddhanta. Both dissolve sect and caste into a single truth, Tirumular's stated flatly and Pambatti's restricted to the realised.

Bathiragiriyar asks when he will go about without any division of caste, as Kapila's agama says; Pambatti says caste differences do not touch true sadhus whose minds have reached the summit. Both make casteless living the mark of the realised, and both ground it in a teaching (an agama, the Siddhas' Siddhanta) rather than in protest alone.

Sivavakkiyar tells those who prepare seats, smear ash and do penances to know where the Lord's knowledge rises and subsides and then do puja, keeping puja on a condition; Pambatti asks whether puja brings pure awareness at all and answers with the end of desire. Sivavakkiyar reforms the rite, Pambatti sets it aside.

Tirumular calls the teaching beyond the tattvas one that cannot be told, and adds that if it is told it is Siva the Supreme; Pambatti says flatly that those who tell have not seen. Both hold the truth to be untellable, but Tirumular leaves room for a telling that is itself the Lord.

Valluvar asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Pambatti asks what all merits achieve if the heart does not think of the One's feet. The same 'what use' question, with merit and penance in place of learning.

Sangili Siddhar and Pambatti both set மணக்கோலம் against பிணக்கோலம், the wedding array against the corpse's array, in a household of wife and children. Sangili mocks the one who does not know it will come; Pambatti blames the one who has seen it and still does not renounce.

The Naladiyar's wedding drums become funeral drums for the bridegroom on the same day; Pambatti's wedding finery becomes the corpse's finery. Both use the one body dressed for marriage and for burning, and both draw renunciation from it.

Both name a great medicine (மாமருந்து, பெருமருந்து) that is no drug: for Tirumular it is the Lord's pair of feet, for Pambatti the knowing of how the mind's lock opens. One finds the medicine in grace received, the other in an act of knowing.

Tirumular calls false gurus those who have looked over mantra and tantra but do not reflect on them; Pambatti says those who speak the single mantra do not know its meaning and that mantra-chanters circle the wall without finding the gate. Both separate handling the mantra from knowing it.

Within Pambatti's own song: the wooden ship of ten nadis, ten airs and seven dhatus lurches and falls, and the reader is told to sail the fitting ship on the one flood; here the clay ship steered by knowledge crosses the sea of Vedanta to the feet. The body is the ship both times, first doomed and then rightly sailed.

Bathiragiriyar longs to launch the ship of love on the sea of knowledge; Pambatti's ship has knowledge for its sail and crosses the sea of Vedanta. The ship and sea are shared, but the cargo differs: love in one, knowledge in the other.

Tirumular gazes steadily at the space between the brows and finds there the Supreme's seat; Pambatti stands looking above the nose between the eyes and seeks the supreme light. The same gaze practice, with the same thing found at its end.

note: Pattinathar confesses that not keeping his eyes open on the tip of the nose spoiled his body and understanding; Pambatti tells the practitioner to stand looking above the nose. The same fixed gaze, regretted as neglected in one and prescribed in the other.

In 2063 the golden pillar in the middle street is garlanded with no key given; here the pillar is named the pillar of Om and the practitioner stands on its summit. The later stanza supplies the cipher the earlier one left open.

Both make the mind a horse: in 2057 it is bridled with the intellect and ridden to clarity, here it gallops in the street of the five senses and is made one-pointed. The same image from control to concentration.

Valluvar tells the reader to cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging; Pambatti ends his stanza with பற்றானைப் பற்றி, holding to the one who holds nothing. The same paradox, compressed into two words.

Agappei says to stay still, that the formula has been told and the place of stillness is what was pointed to; Pambatti, after the forge and the gold-making, says that by not babbling and staying still he joined Parapara. Both put சும்மா இரு, simply being still, at the end of the method.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:2101 line 4 (கருதி யருகல்வி ஒப்பஞ் செய்வோம்) is obscure, possibly corrupt.

note: In 2078 caste differences belong to worldlings and not to true sadhus; here the poet will set fire to caste divisions and go into the houses he should not. The earlier stanza says the realised are untouched by caste; this one acts against it.

Bathiragiriyar asks when the letters va and ma will become the sword and he will stand contained in the letter a with si; Pambatti shuts the snake in the pot of ma, pushes away the pots of va and becomes the form of si. Both make the syllables of the five-letter mantra places one passes through.

The golden pillar in the middle street of 2063 returns as the ruby pillar on which the snake is set dancing, now with a fort of fire below and a ladder up. The same central pillar, given its place in the ascent.

Both place seed syllables in the body: Agasthiyar sets ஆம், ஓம், வாம், பாம் at the suzhumunai, the moon, the brow and the bow, and Sangili makes Om the body, its mute letter the life, and ரீம், ஸ்ரீம் the way. In both the body is made of mantra, and both leave the key to tradition.

Tirumular counts letters, one, two, three and the great letter, to say how the world, the pair, the light and delusion arise; Sangili makes the letters of Om into body and life. Both verses give only the counts or the letters and leave the decoding to tradition.

Both ride the vaasi: Pattiragiriyar would ride it instead of wearing out his feet on the earth, Sangili's mind mounts the horse called தேசி once the breath is known. In both the horse is the breath and the ride replaces another kind of travel.
audit_text_issue: 2115's 'மனது கந்து' looks like a misprint, probably மனது உகந்து.

note: Both place the breath's work at the navel: Tirumular raises the prana that stands with the navel whorl to the summit and becomes Siva; Sangili sets the Brahmin's seat in the navel lotus and makes the breath-quest something the knowers never give up.

Both deny that performing worship reaches the Lord by itself: Tirumular's reciters and flower-gatherers have minds like a stone in a moss pond; Sangili says whatever puja one does, the stilling of thought comes by Sadasiva's feet. Tirumular names love as the missing thing, Sangili the stilled mind.

Both turn the great saying into the first person: Tirumular's 'you are that' ripens into 'I have become that' by Nandi's grace; Sangili knows the Siva-Supreme that fills all as 'I myself am I'. Sangili's 2118 has just made the feet the means, so in both the identity is granted, not asserted.

Pattiragiriyar knows all he sees as 'I am he' and still asks when he will take refuge; Sangili knows the Supreme as 'I myself am I' and calls that the supreme quest. Both hold the identity and the search together.

Both run the four paths as a ladder that ends in jnana: Tirumular's devotee goes from kiriyai and chariyai through yoga to the jnana by which the mind becomes Siva; Sangili says that past chariyai, kiriyai and achieved yoga, nothing is of use without jnana. Tirumular credits each rung to grace; Sangili grants grace to the yogi and still says it is not enough.
audit_text_issue: ஞானவி சர்க்கம் is obscure and may be a copyist's slip (விசாரம்?).

note: Sivavakkiyar gives the four paths their four fruits and makes jnana, in all four, reach union; Sangili says the three lower paths and even grace yield nothing without jnana. Both put jnana above the others; Sivavakkiyar grants the others their fruits, Sangili grants them none.
audit_text_issue: 2121: ஞான விசர்க்கம் is obscure, possibly a slip for விசாரம்.

note: Both count the nine gates and look past them: Sivavakkiyar's nine gates of trouble are left for the good gate and the gate of knowledge, through which one is not born again; Sangili's nine-gated one takes on beauty and shows eight places to those who walk by it. In both the ordinary body's openings are the starting point of a cipher of inner gates.
audit_text_issue: siddhar:1074 அருத்தடைந்த வாசல் and சொம்மிவிம்மி are unclear.

note: The Naladiyar's body is a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, and the fool who praises it is deceived by its skin; Sangili's nine-gated one 'takes on beauty' for those who know it. The same nine openings, loathed in the one text, are in the other the thing to be known; Sangili's 2125 then uses the Naladiyar's disgust too.

Both call the body a salted pot (உப்பிட்ட பாண்டம்): Pattiragiriyar asks to become the Lord's subject before it breaks and takes a womb again; Sangili lists it among the things to see beyond. The pot is cured yet brittle in both.
audit_text_issue: The marked reading of 2125 takes இதுதாண்டி as தாண்டி (beyond); it is இதுதான் + டி.

note: Pattinathar's catalogue, the filthy body, the torn bellows stuffed with flesh and the pot filled with wind, is the source of Sangili's three names; Pattinathar confesses to having loved and carried it, Sangili tells the listener to see past it.
The Kural asks whether the life lodging in the body has no home of its own; Sangili looks for a body that is his own and finds none. Both make the body a place one stays in without owning.

The Naladiyar's wedding drums sound the same day as funeral drums for the bridegroom; Sangili's wedding show (மணக்கோலம்) becomes the corpse show (பிணக்கோலம்). Both rest on a single word changing while the scene stays.

Tirumular's unfired vessel returns to clay when the rain falls, as people die past counting; Sangili sees that all things have their origin in earth and (2132) that what is born of earth perishes. Both argue impermanence from clay.

Tirumular says a broken pot's shards are kept but the broken body is not kept a moment; Sangili says the entombed body's earth is dug up, fired into a pot and serves the world. Sangili does not contradict the abandonment of the corpse, but gives the body's earth a use that Tirumular's verse denies it.

Both use oil in sesame for pervasion: Pattiragiriyar for the end of the Veda that embraces all that moves and stands, Sangili for the Lord clinging in every thing that is earth. In both the pervading thing is present everywhere and visible nowhere.

Tirumular's Lord stands mingled everywhere like jaggery in sugarcane, ghee in milk and scent in the flower; Sangili's Lord clings in all things like oil in sesame. Sangili adds the step that all things are first reduced to earth, so the pervasion holds even of dust.

The Kural calls the lowest understanding the one that takes the impermanent for permanent; Sangili lists what perishes, what is born, what is kept, what is seen, and tells the listener to know it. The Kural judges the error, Sangili supplies the inventory.

Both ask whether parents, body, kin, wife and the rest are சதம், lasting: Pattinathar denies it seven times and affirms it only of the Lord's feet; Sangili asks it five times and answers in 2134 that no one is. Sangili's list is Pattinathar's shortened.

The Kural's life leaves the body as a bird leaves its குடம்பை; Sangili's soul leaves the கூடு, the cage or nest, and goes. The same image of the body as a bird's left dwelling, used by the Kural for the thinness of the body-life bond and by Sangili for the unreality of all who remain.

Pattiragiriyar asks when he will stand unobstructed in the sushumna that moves between ida and pingala; Sangili says those who know the suzhumunai have found the way of ease while crores wander. The same channel is the way in both, as a longing in the one and as a finding in the other.
audit_text_issue: 96's சலித்தருப்பது is doubtful.

note: Agasthiyar's guard verse subsides in the unceasing suzhumunai and goes by the vaasi to the summit; Sangili makes knowing the suzhumunai the one way against the world's wandering. Both make the central channel the method itself and not an aid to it.
audit_text_issue: The source divides 2485's lines unevenly (மகத்தான runs over).

note: The Kural says the domain of the five must be crushed and all one wanted let go at once; Sangili says to burn off desire and attachment and then do yoga and live in this world. The letting-go agrees; Sangili's yogi stays in the world where the Kural's chapter is on renunciation.
audit_text_issue: வீண் ஆண்மையைத் தான்சுட் டறுத்து த்தள்ளி has a doubled consonant (த்தள்ளி) and is uncertain in sense.

note: Tirumular's long-haired lady dances where there is neither night nor day, and one who sleeps there becomes a child age does not touch; Sangili turns night into day and sees the single expanse. In both, night and day are read by tradition as the moon and sun breaths, and their ending is the yogi's state.
audit_text_issue: 2138 flagged uncertain.

note: Pattinathar says the Lord showed him the place where night and day are no more; Sangili tells the listener to make night day and see the one expanse. The same place, given by grace in the one and reached by method in the other.
audit_text_issue: 2138 flagged uncertain.

note: Pattinathar asks 'what if there is a town, good people, the mother who bore one, the wife, glory', and Sangili asks 'what if the parents live, what if wife and children are there'; both use இருந்தென்ன and both answer that none of it avails. Sangili names what does avail, tapas, and what otherwise owns us, Yama.

Tirumular ranks temple, bathing and breath below clear knowledge, in whose mind the Lord dwells; Sangili grants the holy bath, the temple rounds and the darshan and asks whether the fourth, silence, has come. Both leave the acts standing and set the test elsewhere.

Pattinathar went as far as Kasi and wore out his legs because he did not watch the breath; Sangili asks whether bathing, temple rounds and darshan have produced silence. In both the pilgrimage is not false but beside the point.
audit_text_issue: 2140 flagged uncertain.

note: Kakapusundar says forest or town, what matter, once silence is seen, and a lamp carried outside is wasted; Sangili says forests and hills and ritual observance gain nothing for one whose mind still runs. Both make the place of practice indifferent and the stilled mind the whole matter.

The Kural says a spotless mind is the whole of virtue and all else noisy show; Sangili says forest wandering and ritual acts yield no supreme arising to one whose mind runs. Both locate the test in the mind and treat the visible acts as secondary.

Kanjamalai Siddhar warns that desire for women will not do, that its delusion does not go easily, and that one burns in the fire of desire-bonds; Sangili says those who have not burnt away the world's maya and the infatuation for women never reach release. The same two delusions, and fire on both sides, to be burnt in or to burn away.

Sangili says only those who know the higher silence reach undying release; the Puranamalai lists 'those who say the release called silence' among the people who do not know the Lord's name. On the reading that 751 rejects silence taken as release, the two make opposite claims about mounam; on the reading that it rejects only the saying of it, Sangili's knowers of silence are exempt.

Tirumular's silent ones (மோனர்) whose mind has become full of Siva are the Siva-freed, beyond the powers just listed; Sangili's knowers of the higher silence reach undying release where knowers of the arts and of jnana's ways do not. Both place silence above knowledge and attainment.

Both make the identification flatly: Tirumular says Nandi declared the guru is Siva and people do not grasp it; Thirikonar opens by naming Siva himself as the supreme guru and preceptor, and ends the chapter with Siva taking a guru's form.

note: Tirumular's six sects are roads to one city, and those who call one good and another bad bark like a dog at a hill; Thirikonar's Lord is the great faith that sees no difference among the sects that need disputing scriptures.

note: Pattinathar addresses the Lord as the one who stood as ida, pingala and the sushumna themselves; Thirikonar says the Lord walks at the root beyond the reach of ida, pingala and the whirl-point. note: Both set the Lord at the root: Tirumular has the yogi take up ida and pingala and twist at the root in the triangle to see his feet; Thirikonar's Lord walks at the root's end, where the channels cannot reach him.

Both refuse every predicate of size and colour: Sivavakkiyar's cause is not great, not small, beyond black, red and white; Thirikonar's yogi cannot be called small or great, red or black, short or tall.

note: Sivavakkiyar asks what caste is when all water is water and all ornaments one gold; Thirikonar's guru tramples and grinds the whole order of caste underfoot. One argues, the other describes the act, but both deny caste any standing.

Tirumular says that for those who set Nandi firmly in love there is no impurity, no pride and no caste; Thirikonar has the guru wipe out sect-hatred and caste order in the disciple together with egoism in 2182.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'; Thirikonar's guru cuts egoism (ஆணவம்) out by the root. The Siddhar makes the guru the cutter where the Kural leaves it to the renouncer.

audit_text_issue: 2193 is a broken fragment of a kalivenba (உட்கோட்டை யும்கூத்து / வாடியிடும்) whose sense the marker flags as uncertain; 96's சலித்தருப்பது is also doubtful.

note: Sivavakkiyar says the shastras recited and the books tied in bundles ended as nothing once he knew the Lord; Thirikonar's old woman tells the awakened girl to refuse the book-ghosts. Both set realised knowledge against text, though Thirikonar's girl has first mastered the southern and northern books (2215).

The conflict holds if 2223 to 2224 reject the paths themselves and not only their proud practitioners; on the narrower reading, both could stand.
